en: Preface to the *Jingtu ganzhu* (The Azure Pearl of the Pure Land).

I have heard that among the myriad phenomena of the world, none exist outside the realm of form and number. Thus, in ancient times, the sage-kings beheld the markings on the back of a dragon horse and drew the Eight Trigrams (*bagua*);
they obtained the auspicious tortoise shell and set forth the Nine Categories (*jiuchou*). These truly constitute the governing principles of all existence and the fundamental laws of all phenomena.
It is the pivotal axis [of all teachings]. As for the single gateway of the Pure Land, it is a supramundane dharma that is simple, easy, direct, and straightforward;
it does not even fall into the ranks of gradual stages. Why, then, employ such numerical designations as one, two, three, four, a hundred, a thousand, ten million, or a hundred billion?
It is simply because the capacities and roots of those in this defiled world who practice the Pure Land method vary; therefore, the lands where they realize the fruit differ accordingly.
The four lands and nine grades manifest spontaneously; how could they ever exist outside of these numerical categories?

The Elder Xuzhou of Fanchang Mountain realized the essence of the School of Mind early on and extensively propagated the profound wind of the Dharma. He was truly a leader of the monastic community and a bridge for the age of the Final Dharma.
Now, I have compiled into a single volume those phrases and passages concerning the Pure Land found within the sutras and treatises that pertain to these numbers.
It is titled *Jingtu Gan zhu* (The Azure Pearl of the Pure Land). This title is derived from the meaning of Zhang Yan-gong’s record of "never forgetting what one has learned.
In the past, masters such as Tiantai Zhizhe, Tianru Weize, and Hanshan Deqing were all great artisans of the Chan school, whose pedagogical approaches were lofty and rigorous.
Yet, when it comes to instructing others, he again takes up this gate and exhorts them tirelessly;
is this not because his compassionate heart is so urgent and his desire to deliver others is so pressing, pointing out the swift shortcut to the essential?
Those who read this compilation in the future must also recognize the master’s profound and earnest concern. Written by Lulian Jushi in the late summer of the Ji-mao year.
Autobiographical Account, Autumn of the Year Jīmōu (1679). While I was staying at Fǎchāng, the mountain moon cast its white light in the night and the incense smoke curled in azure spirals.
Seated in meditation upon my single mat, all sounds were hushed. A guest knocked at the door; entering with a graceful air, he bowed and said, "My Master..."

He inherited the lineage of Linji and bore the great Dharma upon his shoulders. Seated upon the lion throne and wielding the fly-whisk, he employed the universal radiance of wisdom through horizontal and vertical staffs and shouts for over forty years;
yet among the eminent disciples at his Dharma assemblies, not a single person was heard to have attained the status of a true master.

Is it that the tradition of this school is so lofty and steep that there are no steps by which to ascend? Is it that the faculties of those in these degenerate times lack the strength to take up the burden?
Is the handle [of the teaching] exhausted here? Or is it that the conditions for the Dharma have not yet ripened? An ancient worthy said:

"If one were to exclusively exalt the teachings and the sect, the grass before the Dharma Hall would grow a fathom deep. Why not lower your cloud-head and, through simple and expedient means, receive and guide beings according to their capacities?"
[The Master] said, "Continue. I replied, "I wish to hear your explanation. The guest said, "The Tathāgatas of the ten directions cherish and pity sentient beings as a mother remembers her child.

If the child has fled far away, what can the mother’s remembrance accomplish? But if the child remembers the mother as the mother remembers him, then throughout successive lives, mother and child will never be separated or distant from one another.
If the minds of sentient beings remember the Buddha and recite the Buddha's name, then in the present and in the future, they will certainly [attain liberation]."

To behold the Buddha and, not far from him, to attain the opening of the mind spontaneously without relying on expedient means—this is the beginning of the Great Perfect Penetration (Mahāpariśuddha-samādhi) that dates back to kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

What is the Samādhi of Recollecting the Buddha? It is defined as the concentration of thought and the stillness of contemplation. When thought is concentrated, the will becomes single-minded and undisturbed;
when contemplation is still, the vital energy (*prāṇa*) becomes empty and the spirit becomes luminous. When the vital energy is empty, wisdom shines with tranquil clarity; the spirit...

When it is bright, there is no hidden corner it does not penetrate; these two are the profound symbols of nature itself. They converge in oneness to bring forth utility, and by relying on cultivation, one concentrates the spirit;
through the accumulation of practice, one transforms one's nature. This was the beginning of the assembly of the Lotus Society in China.

Subsequently, hundreds and thousands of masters of successive generations have proclaimed and expounded [these teachings], and those who have been reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss are beyond counting.

Ten thousand times ten thousand. If a person’s faith is pure and ultimate, their fundamental cause is solemn and resolute; they deeply contemplate birth and death and earnestly reflect upon the cycle of transmigration.

When delusive conditions disperse like clouds and distracted thoughts melt away like ice, they raise a single invocation of the Buddha’s name, and directly beneath it, there is no longer any other view.
This is precisely the Buddha’s mindfulness. Like the blade of the Great A-sword, it is held level across the threshold of the hall.
This mindfulness of the Buddha is like a great wheel of fire; stars fly upward as its flames blaze fiercely. Should any thing encounter it, it is consumed; should anything touch it, it is wounded.

When this mindfulness is cultivated for a long time, there is no Buddha apart from mindfulness, and no mindfulness apart from the Buddha. Body and mind become one, and both subject and object are forgotten. This may be called "shattering" [the barriers].
It is the thunderclap that awakens those hibernating in the cave of birth and death; it is the sun and moon that illuminate the dark alleys of delusion.
If one can proceed directly in this manner, Chan and Pure Land are never two; their cultivation and realization ultimately converge into one.

Why does my teacher not employ this Dharma-gate of Pure Land to gather and transform those with whom he has a karmic affinity? Pray, consider this and strive to lead them all forward together. I remained silent for a long while.

After a long time, he presented this "Azure Jewel" (*gāñjú*). Having perused it, the guest said: "From this day forward, I recognize the compassionate toil with which you, Master, have bestowed this upon me.
As a student of shallow and inferior learning, I had dared to speak with unrestrained arrogance. He bowed in thanks and withdrew.
I have therefore compiled the guest’s questions to serve as a preface, and appended them with a verse: [Verse follows]
In the past, one has already endured inexhaustible suffering; In the present, one now endures endless suffering;
In the future, one shall endure limitless suffering. Even across hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, these are difficult to calculate.
There is but a single gateway for transcendence: Recite the Buddha’s name to be reborn in the Land of Peace and Bliss.
Having personally beheld the Tathāgata Amitāyus and heard the subtle, wondrous, and true Dharma,
they suddenly awaken to unsurpassed Buddha-bodhi; endowed with all-encompassing wisdom and supernormal powers,
they travel and sport throughout the worlds of the ten directions, making offerings to the Buddhas and receiving their predictions of enlightenment.

Returning to enter the Sahā world to deliver the multitudes, thereby repaying even a ten-thousandth part of the Buddha’s grace—this is what is called a "good son" (satpuruṣa); this may also be called "great liberation";
one may be called a "great man" (mahāpuruṣa), and only then is one truly named a "Great Bodhisattva."

Preface: Among the works recording numerical categories within the Buddhist scriptures, there is the *Three Pitakas’ Dharma Numerals*, which compiles a rather extensive range of material.
This compilation, however, selects only those phrases and terms related to the Pure Land dharma-gate that pertain to numerical categories, and has been compiled accordingly.
Regarding the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land: since its great exposition by Master Huikang, successive generations of superior practitioners have followed in his footsteps to proclaim and expound it.

There are treatises and literary works, as well as biographies, records, commentaries, and sub-commentaries; there are also poems, songs, gāthās, and hymns of praise, each providing its own elucidation.
This work, however, is the first to categorize these materials numerically; though its volume is small, it encompasses the entirety of the six perfections and myriad practices.
This is sufficient.
From one to ten, although the details vary between extensive and concise, they can all be enumerated;
as for numbers beyond ten, they shall be recorded as they appear, ceasing at forty-eight. Anything remaining is not pertinent to the three gates of faith, practice, and aspiration.
Such matters are generally set aside and not recorded.
That Chan and Pure Land practitioners establish separate banners and harbor mutual animosity and fault-finding is because they do not recognize that the return to the source is non-dual.
Furthermore, when one practices the methods of śamatha and vipaśyanā, cultivating both samādhi and prajñā together, how could Chan and Pure Land ever be different?

This compilation provides particularly detailed explanations regarding the two gates of Contemplation and Visualization, with the sole aim that practitioners may aspire toward both "Pure Land" and "Chan," realizing the same realm of tranquil light (jiguang).
Zhang Yan Gong of the Tang dynasty said: "In my youth, I studied extensively across many fields, yet I suffered from a poor memory. A guest once presented me with a deep blue bead;
whenever I held it in my palm, everything I had read became clearly visible. Therefore, it was called the 'Bead for Retaining Affairs.
Now, taking the meaning of 'not forgetting,' I have named this [work] accordingly."

Reflecting upon myself, I am both shallow and ignorant; moreover, my preservation of materials lacks corroboration, and my collection has not been extensive, such that I cannot avoid the reproach of omitting ten thousand things for every one retained.
As for completing this work as a perfect vessel, I leave it to future scholars of broad learning and refined erudition.

Commentary by Xuzhou Dezhen. Compiled:

*The Mind of Single-mindedness* (The Amitābha Sūtra). If there are good sons or good daughters who, upon hearing the teaching of Amitābha Buddha, hold fast to His name with single-mindedness and without distraction, then at the time of their death, Amitābha Buddha, together with [His holy assembly]...

The assembly of noble ones will stand before them at the time of their death; their minds will not be inverted, and they will immediately attain rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Amitābha Buddha.
*Ichinen* (The Master Jishō’s Teaching): The ancients taught that one should draw near to a true teacher and seek out a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).

Yet, such a spiritual friend possesses no secret dharma-gate to be transmitted orally or bestowed from mind to mind; they merely untie the person’s adhesions and remove their fetters—this itself is the secret.
Now, simply uphold the Name with single-mindedness and without distraction. These eight characters are themselves [the secret].
This secret dharma gate for untying adhesions and removing fetters is the grand, majestic highway out of birth and death.
Whether recollecting in the morning or evening, while walking or sitting—let every thought follow the next in continuous succession, and you will spontaneously attain samādhi.

Regarding the One Vehicle (as explained by Master Lianchi): A person who practices the recitation of the Buddha’s name seeks only the fruit of Buddhahood of the One Vehicle as their goal, harboring no vain expectations for other vehicles.
To give rise to such a mind and thereby cultivate the Pure Land is what constitutes the correct cause.
If it were otherwise, then even if one were diligent in reciting the Buddha’s name, the causal ground would not be true, and the resulting fruit would be circuitous.
The Patriarch Cizhao said: "This Way is most profound and most subtle; it is also most simple and most easy. Because it is so simple and easy, those of lofty intelligence overlook it.
Indeed, birth and death do not depart from a single thought-moment, and even the myriad dharmas of the mundane and supramundane worlds do not depart from a single thought-moment.
To now take this very thought-moment to recite the Buddha's name—how intimate and close is this!"
This is essential. If you can see through the place where this thought arises, it is the Amitābha of one's own nature; it is the very intent of the Patriarch’s coming from the West.

Even if you do not attain awakening, by virtue of the power of this mindfulness, you will be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, thereby cutting across birth and death and no longer undergoing saṃsāra;
ultimately, you shall surely attain great enlightenment.

Regarding the "Single Thought" (from the *Lianzong baojian*): In a quiet chamber, sit upright with the body straightened. Clear away distracting conditions and sever the dust of emotional attachments. Open your eyes wide;
do not be attached to external objects, nor dwell in internal meditative absorption. Turn the light back upon yourself and take one glance;
when both interior and exterior are utterly still, then silently and continuously bring forth the thought: "Namo Amitābha Buddha," three or five times. Then turn the light back.
Looking at the clouds himself, he said: "To see one's nature is to become a Buddha. Ultimately, which of these is my original nature, Amitābha? He then examined it again:
"From where does this single thought that is currently being raised arise? Having seen through this single thought, he saw through it once more:
"Who is it that is looking? [He] investigated. After a long while, he again brought up the thought: "Nan."
"There is no Amitābha Buddha. Furthermore, observe thus, investigate thus, and apply yourself with urgency to the practice without interruption.

Remain alert and unclouded, like a hen brooding over her eggs. Whether engaged in any of the four postures—walking, standing, sitting, or lying down—raise this thought, look thus, and investigate thus.
Suddenly, while walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, or when hearing sounds or seeing forms, [the truth will manifest].
Suddenly, there was a clear awakening; he personally beheld the Original Nature Amitābha. Body and mind, internal and external, were simultaneously liberated.

Throughout the entire universe and the great earth, all the myriad phenomena were the Western Pure Land; everything without exception was one's own self. In stillness, there was no lack of illumination;
in movement, there was no departure from quiescence.
The Great Matter (spoken by Master Cizhao): All those who practice the Pure Land path must resolutely confront birth and death;
it is not a matter of merely speaking of it and then leaving it at that. One should reflect that impermanence is swift and that time does not wait for anyone;

only by treating this as a "Great Matter" can one succeed. If one advances only half-heartedly and retreats half-heartedly, or is caught between belief and doubt, how could such a person ever achieve liberation?
Regarding such a matter, how can one escape saṃsāra? If you can truly believe this, then from this very day forward, arouse great courage and great diligence;
do not concern yourself with whether you understand or not, nor with whether you have seen your nature or not.
Simply maintain the single-minded recitation of "Namo Amitābha Buddha. It will be like leaning against Mount Sumeru;
it will be as immovable as if one were shaking it. Concentrate the mind and unify the intent.

Whether through investigative mindfulness, contemplative mindfulness, recollective mindfulness, ten-fold mindfulness, silent mindfulness, focused mindfulness, or mindful prostration—let the thought remain fixed upon this very object. Constantly remember and constantly recite, morning and night.
Be mindful while standing; do not fail to be mindful. Be mindful while walking; be mindful while sitting. Let mindfulness never pass in vain.
Hold the Buddha without letting Him leave your mind. Day after day, at every moment, do not let go. This is precisely what is meant by "pure mindfulness succeeding one another.

When you further add the illumination of wisdom, you will know that the Pure Land is none other than your own mind. If you can grasp this firmly in this way, you will become the master and find your reliance.
Steadfast. Even when encountering circumstances of suffering or joy, adversity or favor, simply recite the name of Amitābha Buddha.
Do not have a single thought of wavering, do not have a single thought of indolence, and do not have a single thought of distraction.
Continue until the end of this life, never harboring another thought, with the firm resolve to be born in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss. If one can truly act in this way...

By applying oneself to this practice, the karmic obstacles of birth and death and the ignorance accumulated over kalpas will naturally dissolve; the habitual taints of worldly toil will naturally be purified until nothing remains.
One will personally behold Amitābha without departing from one's original mindfulness, and when merit is perfected and conduct fulfilled, [one will attain rebirth].
Supported by the power of vows, at the time of death, one will certainly be reborn in the highest grade.

Regarding the *ekākāra-samādhi* (from the *Mañjuśrī-prajñā-sūtra*): in Sanskrit it is *samādhi*, which in Chinese means "concentration of straightening and rectifying," or alternatively, "right concentration.
As for the *ekākāra-samādhi*, it refers exclusively to focusing on a single practice to cultivate right concentration; that is to say, the cultivation of the practitioner—
A person should dwell in a secluded place, abandon all distracted thoughts, and fix the mind upon the true principle.
Contemplating a single Buddha, they should single-mindedly recite His name. Facing the direction where that Buddha resides, they should sit upright and turn toward Him.

If they can maintain this continuous flow of mindfulness toward a single Buddha without indolence, then within a single thought-moment, they will be able to see all Buddhas of the ten directions and attain great eloquence.
Furthermore, regarding the practice of the Samādhi of One Aspect (*ekalakṣaṇa-samādhi*) according to the *Ratnarāja-śāstra*:

one should maintain mindfulness without forgetting while walking, standing, sitting, or lying down. Even when falling into deep sleep, one should continue to maintain mindfulness while sleeping; upon awakening, one should immediately resume it.
One does not allow other karmic activities to intervene, nor does one allow greed, anger, and so forth to create a gap.

One repents immediately upon committing an offense, without a lapse of mindfulness, without a shift in mindfulness, without a lapse of a day, and without a lapse of time. Moment by moment, one is never separated from the Buddha;
moment by moment, one is pure and perfectly luminous. This is precisely the attainment of the Samādhi of the Single Characteristic.
Regarding the practice of the "Contemplation of the Sun" (*rìguān*) for practitioners according to the *Lianzong baojian*:
One must stay in a quiet place, sever all external conditions, sit upright with the mind collected, and clearly contemplate the solar disc as if it were present before one's eyes.

Focus the mind on this single object until it becomes still and tranquil, like beholding one’s own reflection in a bright mirror. If the mind wanders, restrain it and bring it back; once the mind has ceased its agitation, let it abide.
Concentration: One immediately attains samādhi.
(As the Patriarch Cizhao said: Deluded thoughts are the illness; mindfulness of the Buddha is the medicine.

A chronic illness cannot be cured by a single dose, and accumulated delusions cannot be eliminated by a momentary thought. The principle is one and the same: do not concern yourself with those deluded thoughts.
They fly about in confusion. It is simply a matter of reciting the Buddha’s name with precision and intensity. Each character must be distinct; each phrase must follow the next without interruption.

Only by holding fast with all one's might does one have a portion of the path before them. As it is said, through "true accumulation and long-term effort," there comes a sudden, expansive realization.
This is certainly not a falsehood, as illustrated by the analogies of grinding a pestle into a needle or forging iron into steel. There are many gateways for entering the Way, but...
This single method is the most direct shortcut; it must not be neglected, it must not be neglected.
To concentrate the mind and recite the Buddha’s name, desiring to swiftly achieve samādhi, the method for counteracting dullness and distraction is that counting the breath is most essential.
Whenever one wishes to sit in meditation, first visualize one's own body within a circle of light, and observe silently.
Focus on the tip of the nose and contemplate the inhalation and exhalation. With each breath, silently recite "Namo Amitābha Buddha" once.
Skillfully regulate the breath, neither too slow nor too fast, so that the mind and the breath are mutually dependent, following its movement in and out.
This may be practiced while walking, standing, sitting, or lying down; do not allow it to be interrupted. Constantly maintain this practice in a subtle and continuous manner until you enter deeply.
In meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), both breath and thought are forgotten; this very body and mind become equal to empty space.
After long practice until it is fully matured, the eye of the mind opens and penetrates, and samādhi suddenly manifests before one. This is precisely the Pure Land of Mind-Only.

A Single Phrase (as spoken by Master Hanshan): Whenever reciting the Buddha’s name, first set aside all the various discursive thoughts within your chest at once, until there is nothing further to set aside.

Then, single-mindedly hold up the single phrase "Namo Amitābha Buddha," making it vivid and distinct, uninterrupted in the mind like beads strung on a thread, or like the nocks of arrows joined together.
Without even a hair’s breadth of gap in between, exert yourself in this way and remain steadfastly fixed.

At all times and in every situation, do not allow yourself to be led astray or distracted by external conditions. Whether in daily activities of motion or stillness, let there be no confusion or disorder; let it be as it is even in dreams.
When you reach the moment of death, if your mind is single-minded and undisturbed, that is precisely the time of transcending birth into the Pure Land.
(As Master Hanshan said: Apart from two periods of formal practice each day, simply take the single phrase "Amituofo" and place it across your chest;
do not forget it from moment to moment, and let every thought remain clear and unclouded. As for all worldly affairs...
Do not entertain any thoughts at all. Take this single sound of "Buddha" as your very life-root; clench your teeth with determination and never let it go.
Whether eating, drinking, rising, resting, walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, let this single sound of "Buddha" be ever-present before you.
Should you encounter circumstances that are adverse or favorable, joyful or angry, or when the mind becomes unsettled due to afflictions, take hold of this very [sound].
At the single sound of "Buddha," one lifts up and applies pressure; immediately, afflictions are seen to be extinguished on the spot.

Since every thought-moment of affliction is the root of the suffering of birth and death, now, by using the recitation of the Buddha's name to extinguish these afflictions, this is precisely where the Buddha delivers one from the suffering of birth and death.
If one can extinguish afflictions through the recitation of the Buddha's name, one can then resolve the matter of birth and death; there is nothing else.
The Dharma.

(As spoken by the Repentance Master Ciyun): For laypeople who are preoccupied with the bustle of worldly affairs, every morning after dressing, they should face west with palms joined and recite "Namo Amitābha Buddha. Let one full breath constitute one recitation.
These ten recitations are performed simply by following the length of the breath, with the breath reaching its limit as the measure.

The sound of the recitation of the Buddha’s name should be neither too loud nor too low, but adjusted to be perfectly balanced. These ten recitations are to be continuous and uninterrupted, with the intention of preventing the mind from scattering;
this is the merit of single-minded devotion. This clearly demonstrates that one relies on the breath to bind the mind.

A Single Thought (by Master Hanshan): If you are truly urgent regarding birth and death, and every thought is like saving a house from fire, yet you fear that once this human body is lost, it will be difficult to regain it for a hundred kalpas—then you must bite down firmly on this single invocation of the Buddha's name.
You must resolutely overcome forgetfulness and delusion so that, in all places, the mindfulness remains present at every moment, unobstructed by discursive thoughts. Acting in this way...

Through arduous and earnest effort, after a long time, one becomes thoroughly proficient; then, it naturally accords with reality. Without seeking to form a continuous state of mind, it spontaneously becomes a single, unified whole.
(Master Ouyi said: Throughout one’s life, the presently manifest mind that is capable of mindfulness is fundamentally free from fault and transcends all negation; there is no need to eliminate it.

Cultivate a state of mental attention that is detached and free from conceptualization. The Buddha who is presently being brought to mind is, by nature, beyond the reach of the emotions and transcends all calculation;
why then labor over discoursing on the sublime or discussing the profound? It is simply a matter of being able to believe with certainty and maintaining a steady composure.

Proceed directly with recitation—whether ten thousand, five thousand, or three thousand times a day and night—taking it as your standard that the practice be resolute and without deficiency. Vow to maintain this until the end of this life.
There is no change or alteration. If one were not to attain rebirth [in the Pure Land], the Buddhas of the three periods of time would be guilty of speaking falsehoods.
This single point of true nature (the very core of the Chan school) consists simply in reciting the Buddha’s name with a single mind, without being distracted by any worldly affairs.
When the mind is undisturbed, the breath naturally becomes still; when the breath is still, the spirit naturally becomes clear; when the spirit is clear, the ears are free from false listening.
Let your gaze be free from deviance; let your mind and mouth be as one. Then hand, mouth, mind, and body will merge into a unity.
After the attainment of Great Samādhi, my spirit shall be your spirit, and my breath shall be your breath.
Forgetting the self to become you, and forgetting you to become the self—these two are one, and this one is two. It is neither this appearance nor that appearance; it cannot be defined.
It is perceived through form and sound, yet cannot be sought within the physical body. Thus, in a state of profound, undifferentiated wholeness, one naturally attains union with the essence;
movement follows the mind, and the spiritual mechanism remains unimpeded.
One must necessarily rest in stillness and contemplate one’s own original single point of true nature, ensuring that one recognizes how the great white ox plows the field. Every evening, as before...

When traveling on this journey, it is as if one were sitting in a great forest hermitage for seven days; within no more than a period of seven days, the nature of the mind will naturally attain realization.
Thus, even without looking at the scriptures, there is not a single moment when one does not recite them, nor does one fail to recite the Buddha’s name with the mouth.
Yet there is not a single moment when the mind is not Buddha. If you practice this evening, you will benefit this evening; if you practice tomorrow morning, you will benefit tomorrow morning.
(A saying of Chan Master Dadian): "If you wish to know where the Buddha goes, it is right here in these very words. This is for those who have not yet attained realization.
Listen to these words: who is it that is speaking right now? The Sūtra says: "There is a world named Sukhāvatī;
in that land there is a Buddha, titled Amitābha, who currently dwells and expounds the Dharma. Contemplate this truthfully:
every sound flows from within your own breast, uninterrupted from moment to moment. Throughout the twelve periods of the day, constantly recite this sūtra and call upon the Buddha’s name.
One sound responds to one sound; the original face is too clearly manifest. If one can be thus, it is called returning to the root and restoring the source.
What is the source? "The flow of water originally lies in the sea; the setting moon does not leave the sky."

As stated in the *Ekottarika Āgama*: "If a person were to offer the four most excellent things as an offering to Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas filling a great trichiliocosm, the merit obtained would not equal that of a person who joins their palms and utters the name of the Buddha once.
It would not reach even a hundred-thousand-millionth part; it cannot be matched by calculation or analogy. To utter the name of the Buddha once—
If the merit of merely naming [the Buddha] is already thus, how much more so the merit of recollecting the Buddha for ten moments, one day, one month, one year, or even one lifetime?
In this present life, one will dwell in peace and security, be protected by the multitude of sages, and be freed from all calamities; such merit is immeasurable.
A former master once said: "The Buddha-dharma is not a dead fish; one need not fear it rotting away.
It is like peeling a plantain tree: peel one layer, then another; peel one layer, then another, until you reach the point where there is nowhere left to apply the knife.
Only then do you achieve a single seamless whole. After that, you can don your robes, eat your meals, and answer the call of nature."
Whether urinating, moving or still, speaking or silent—there is not a single moment that is not this very Amitābha Buddha.
From this point on, the flower of the mind blossoms brilliantly, illuminating the ten directions like the bright sun adorning the sky or a clear mirror set upon its stand.

Without transcending a single thought-moment, one suddenly attains perfect enlightenment. Not only does one clarify this great matter, but there is nothing—whether the Buddha-dharma or worldly dharmas—that remains obscure.

Yet, even so, one must not dwell in attachment; one must seek realization and awakening. When a master meets the student with the appropriate trigger and grants certification, neither sage nor ordinary person is established, and both grasping and rejecting are forgotten. Throughout the entire Dharma-realm, there is only this very self, Amitābha.
The entirety of empty space is this Pure Land of Mind-Only.

Regarding the two minds (as taught by Chan Master Yongming) and the nine grades of the sutra text: while there are natural variations in their elevation or decline, these encompassed levels—from high to low—do not transcend these two minds.

First is the concentrated mind (*ekāgratā-citta*); as when one cultivates meditative visualization (*samādhi-vipaśyanā*) for rebirth in the superior grades. Second is the single-minded devotion (*ekānta-citta*); it consists simply in mindfulness [of the Buddha].
Regarding the Name: it is perfumed by a multitude of virtues. Through dedication and the making of vows, one attains the final stage.

Nevertheless, one must take refuge for the duration of one's life and practice with diligent cultivation until the end of one's term. Whether sitting or reclining, one should always face west. When reciting the Buddha’s name and making vows:
With earnest and sincere devotion, free from all other thoughts: whether imprisoned in a cage, pursued by enemies, or beset by water or fire,
one should single-mindedly seek deliverance, vowing to escape the wheel of suffering, swiftly realize non-arising, extensively save all sentient beings,
perpetuate and honor the Triple Gem, and vow to repay the four debts of gratitude.

Regarding the two types of single-mindedness (as explained by Chan Master Zhenxie): the method of reciting the Buddha’s name is a direct path of practice that accommodates those of the highest faculties while also drawing in those of middling and lower capacities.
Therefore, the teaching of "single-mindedness without distraction" encompasses two meanings: principle single-mindedness (*li yixin*) and practice single-mindedness (*shi yixin*).
If it is practice single-mindedness, everyone is capable of performing it; it requires nothing more than a single moment of mindfulness, like a dragon [arising from the water].

Obtaining water is like a tiger relying on a mountain; this refers to the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*: "By recollecting the Buddha and mindfulness of the Buddha, one will certainly see the Buddha in the present and in the future.
Without relying on expedient means, one spontaneously attains the opening of the mind. If one maintains single-mindedness in principle, it is likewise not some other method.

Take simply these four characters, "A-mi-t'o-fo," as your *huatou*. Throughout the two-and-six periods of the day, from the moment of the ten recitations at dawn, maintain this directly and continuously.
Do not contemplate with a mind of existence; do not contemplate with a mind of non-existence;
do not contemplate with a mind that is both existent and non-existent; do not contemplate with a mind that is neither existent nor non-existent. Thus, sever the continuity of the past and future.
When not a single thought arises, one does not traverse the stages of cultivation but directly transcends to the Buddha-ground. Is this not the seeing of the Buddha in the Pure Land?

Is it not more simple and direct than the Gate of the Patriarchs (Zongmen)? One can truly know that whether in the Teachings (Jiao) or in Chan, both the Buddhas and the Patriarchs all cultivate pure karma and return together to a single vow.
Once one enters this gate, one is able to enter all the infinite Dharma-gates.

Regarding the second practice (as taught by Master Shandao): Sentient beings have heavy afflictions; their objects of perception are subtle while their minds are coarse. Their consciousness drifts and their spirits fly away, making it difficult to achieve meditative visualization.
Therefore, out of great compassion, the Great Sage exhorted them to cultivate the exclusive recitation of the Name. This is precisely because reciting the Name is easy.
If one continues this practice in succession, such that it flows from moment to moment until the end of life, ten will be reborn for every ten, and a hundred for every hundred.
Why is this? Because they are free from external distracting conditions and attain right mindfulness; because they correspond with the fundamental vows of the Buddha;
because they do not contradict the teachings; and because they accord with the Buddha’s words. Those who cultivate mixed practices may rarely succeed even once in a hundred attempts.
Out of one or two thousand, only three or four may be found. Why is this? It is because they lose right mindfulness due to the agitation of various distracting conditions;

because they do not accord with the original vows of the Buddha; because they contradict the teachings; because they do not follow the words of the Buddha; and because their focused mindfulness lacks continuity.
Even though they perform wholesome deeds, their minds lack continuity as they fail to maintain mindfulness of repaying the Buddha’s kindness. Although they practice virtue...

[This is] practice. Because it is constantly associated with fame and profit, one delights in frequenting distracting conditions, thereby obstructing oneself and obstructing others from giving rise to correct practice.
Second, regarding "holding" (as explained by Master Ouyi): there are two types of holding. First, "holding by means of the thing" (shih-ch'i) refers to believing in the existence of the West...

While one has not yet reached the state where "this mind makes the Buddha" and "this mind is the Buddha," because one resolutely vows to seek birth [in the Pure Land], constantly remembering it without a moment's forgetfulness—just as a child remembers its mother—this is called "factual retention" (*shih-ch'i*). Second, regarding "principle retention" (*li-ch'i*):
one believes that the Amitābha Buddha of the Western Quarter is fully possessed within one's own mind and is created by one's own mind.
One should take the sublime name, which one possesses and has cultivated within one's own mind, as the object for binding the mind, ensuring it is not forgotten for even a moment;
this is called "retaining through principle" (*li-chi*).

Second, [Master] Xi Ming (the layman Jushi) said: "In practicing mindfulness of the Buddha (*nianfo*), one should seek rebirth in the Pure Land. As the saying goes: 'Plant melons and you shall reap melons; plant beans and you shall reap beans.'"
Beans. One naturally attains Buddhahood through the practice of nianfo (reciting the Buddha’s name), yet worldly people do not know that the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss is accessible to everyone.
Their minds are first filled with doubt and confusion; instead, they contemplate the karmic rewards of future lives. Consequently, their lifelong practice of nianfo comes to nothing.
This is not because the Buddha speaks deceptive words, but because one is unwilling to accept the responsibility for one's own liberation and thus strays onto a mistaken path. [End of] Preface.

I exhort those who practice *nienfo*: if they reach the full ten degrees of faith, the full ten degrees of aspiration, and the full ten degrees of practice, they will certainly attain a place within the lotus womb of the nine grades.
One should widely perform various good deeds while practicing *nienfo*. This Sahā world is like a sea of suffering; *nienfo* is like boarding a boat;
being born in the Pure Land is like reaching the other shore; and accumulating goodness is like the sails, oars, and travel provisions. (From the *Sūtra*)
Although it is stated therein that ten recitations at the moment of death can lead to rebirth while still carrying one's karma, this results from cultivation in previous lives;
a single thought turning back toward the light allows for an instantaneous transcendence of the triple world, and is not something attainable by mere luck.

If one clearly knows that evil must not be committed yet still acts recklessly and arbitrarily, then even if one were to achieve ten recitations in the brief moments of death, [the heavens, earth, and ghosts...]
How could the gods permit such cleverness? Often, when the realm of karma manifests before one, one cannot even utter a single word of "Buddha," let alone perform the ten recitations.
I urge those who practice nianfo to take the eight characters "Commit no evil;
practice all good" as their lifelong guide and to embody them throughout their entire lives.
Second, the two types of goodness (as explained by Dharma Master Yanlun). All Mahāyāna sūtras that encourage rebirth in the Pure Land encompass two kinds of goodness:

first, concentration (*samādhi*); second, distraction (*vikṣepa*). "Concentration" refers to contemplating the Buddha with the mind alone. One visualizes the environment and inhabitants, the principal and the retinue of the Western Paradise as being inherently complete within the mind.
At that very locus, all is empty; the whole is provisionally existent; neither of the two extremes can be found, and even the Middle Way does not exist. Third...
The truths are perfectly interfused; thus, the one mind is fully endowed with all. Therefore, the Samādhi of Mind-Only is the essence of the perfect and eternal contemplation.
One thoroughly understands that the pure land—both its environment and its inhabitants, as well as their form and mind—is entirely the inherent merit of my own mind-nature.

Taking the objective realm itself as the contemplation, there is no Buddha outside the mind and no land outside the nature. By contemplating this incessantly, one realizes the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). "Scattered" refers to the purity of application.

The mind believes that the Western Land exists. With single-mindedness and without distraction, one binds the mindfulness upon Amitābha. For one day or seven days, the voice does not cease and the thought-moments are uninterrupted.
At the time of the end of life, the Buddha and the assembly of sages appear before one. This practice consists solely of visualizing that land;

however, because it lacks the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*), it is termed "scattered goodness" (*vikṣiptakuśala*). Whether in a state of meditative concentration or distraction, and whether one possesses sharp or dull faculties, [the result remains the same].
All are causes for the Pure Land; all shall proceed toward non-arising and never again regress.
Second, regarding the two types of transcendence (as discussed by Master Tongjiang): there are the vertical and the horizontal.

As for the vertical transcendence, it refers to practitioners of the Three Vehicles who, relying upon the Four Truths, the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, and the myriad practices of the Six Perfections, traverse the various stages and positions, much like one seeking academic degrees, which necessarily requires...

Regarding talent and learning: just as when one is promoted through successive appointments in office, it must be based on actual merit and achievement; whereas "transcendent emergence" refers to the practice of reciting the Buddha’s name to seek rebirth in the Pure Land.
This is like receiving a hereditary appointment based on the service of one's ancestors, where the merit derives from the forebears regardless of whether one possesses learning.
It is also like a general amnesty that results in universal promotion, where the merit derives from the sovereign and is not contingent upon the depth or duration of one's prior service.
Regarding the two practices (from the *Ten Doubts Treatise*): if one wishes to be born in the Pure Land, one must seek the two practices of revulsion (*nirveda*) and aspiration (*abhinanda*).
The first is the practice of revulsion: constantly contemplate this body as pus, blood, excrement, urine, and foul secretions—stinking, filthy, and impure.

First, observe that worldly beings are born from emotional desire and craving; this is impurity of the seed. Second, observe the union of the father’s semen and the mother’s blood; this is [impurity of the womb].
1. Impurity of conception; 2. dwelling within the mother’s womb, which is impurity of the dwelling place; 3.

while in the mother’s womb, consuming only the mother’s blood, which is impurity of food and drink; 4. after ten months have elapsed, emerging from the birth canal, which is impurity of initial birth;
5. the pus and blood within the internal body, which is impurity of the entire physical form; 6. [and so forth]. Seven.
After death, the body swells and decays; this is its ultimate impurity. Just as one contemplates the body in this way, so too should one contemplate persons.
Next, one should contemplate the defiled realm of Sahā, where all manner of sufferings converge, and cultivate weary detachment toward it. As soon as weary detachment arises,
The Pure Land will certainly be attained. Second is the practice of joyful aspiration: seeking rebirth in the Pure Land for the sake of rescuing and delivering all sentient beings from suffering.

Therefore, one should cultivate a yearning mind and give rise to mental images, joyfully taking as an object of focus the Western Pure Land, adorned with a hundred jewels, with golden ground and jade-like forests, radiant flower ponds, and sovereign spiritual powers, traveling freely to other regions and forever severing [the bonds of saṃsāra].
Regarding birth and death: there are no further afflictions, and one experiences all manner of bliss; therefore, one must rejoice.
Second, regarding non-birth (*A-sambhava*) [in the Pure Land] (Pure Land Dharma Words): If you seek what constitutes my sincere instruction, nothing is more essential than the words of Yang Cigong:
"If love is not deep, one will not be born in Saṃsāra; if mindfulness is not single-minded, one will not be born in Sukhāvatī. Now, as for this mindfulness...
The Buddha unifies the mind through earnest recitation of the name, with single-minded focus and no distraction; this is that upon which I must exert my utmost effort.
Yet, there may be times when one forgets and cannot bring it to mind, or when one brings it to mind but cannot maintain single-mindedness.

This is due to nothing other than being dragged away by the attachments of worldly emotion. One must therefore diminish such attachment to block its delusions, sever the root of emotion, and liberate oneself from craving.
This is what I must devote my whole heart to. Yet, there are times when I think of it but cannot forget it, or when I try to forget it but cannot let go.
This is due to nothing other than the inability of the thinking mind to achieve single-mindedness.

Therefore, for those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha seeking rebirth in the Pure Land, if they habitually harbor even a slight attachment to this Sahā world, then at the moment of death, because of this—
If one cannot be reborn when led astray by a single instance of attachment, how much less so when there is much attachment?
Likewise, if one cannot be reborn when turned away at the moment of death by a single inconsistent thought, how much less so when there are many such thoughts?
Now, as for that which constitutes love, there are degrees of lightness and heaviness, thickness and thinness, primary retribution and secondary conditions.

To enumerate its categories: parents, wife and children, brothers and friends, fame and achievement, wealth and honor, literary works and verse, arts and crafts, clothing and food, houses and dwellings, fields and gardens, forests...
There are spring flowers and plants, rare jewels, and playthings—various exquisite things beyond counting. Some are as massive and heavy as Mount Tai;
others are as minute and light as a goose’s down. Yet there is not a single object that one does not cherish with love, nor a single thought that one does not harbor with affection.
If there is even one object of love remaining in the breast, the mind will not be unified; if there is even one such thought...
If these two do not return to a single unity, then birth [in the Pure Land] cannot be attained.
Regarding the two types of mindfulness (as taught by Master Liangche): first is mindfulness of the Buddha’s mind-nature; second is mindfulness of the Buddha’s physical form and name.
Mindfulness of the mind-nature is to behold the True Buddha; it does not preclude visiting the Buddha of radiant marks and signs.

Regarding the Western direction, those who contemplate the name of the body perceive the response-body Buddha (nirmāṇakāya). They are also able to behold the Buddha of self-nature and original truth beyond the phenomenal realm.
Thus, both the fundamental and the manifest are presented together, and principle and phenomena share a common source.

Second, the Exhortation (from *The Morning Bell of the Pure Land*): To resolve that it is thus and must be practiced is called faith; to resolve that it is thus and to act accordingly is called cultivation.
If one knows what can be practiced yet fails to do so, and if one’s cultivation lacks vigor, then even if there is faith, no realization will manifest.

Therefore, I urge you with urgency. This exhortation has two meanings: first, the exhortation for self-benefit; second, the exhortation for the benefit of others. [In] the vast and boundless sea of birth and death...
Within this, there is only one’s own self prior to the kalpa of emptiness; this is my original nature.

If I do not contemplate and recognize it early on to seek the gate of liberation, I will willingly sink into ruin. Who shall bear the blame? Furthermore, if I do not cultivate it myself, how can I exhort others to cultivate it?
Indeed, the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land benefits both oneself and others; thus, one should cultivate it for the benefit of both oneself and others. Oneself and others...
Because one practices both [self-benefit and benefiting others], one must exhort both oneself and others.
Second, regarding admonition (*cetanā*): the Buddha said, "Human life is impermanent, briefer than a breath; youth is likewise. (From the *Yunqi Fahui*)
How much more so for old age! I have now come with earnest sincerity to admonish you: you should contemplate this body—its eyes grow dim and its ears deaf; its hair turns white and its face wrinkles;
its back bows and its waist curves; its bones ache and its tendons contract; its gait becomes unsteady and its spirit grows clouded and obstructed.
It is like the setting sun shining in the west, its light lasting but a moment; like withered grass welcoming autumn, falling away in an instant.

Carved. This body will not last long; the path ahead is vast and boundless, and we do not know where it leads. It would truly be as if one had already accomplished what was to be done, which is beyond the measure of a fool like me.
If this were not so, why not vigorously reflect upon impermanence, tremble with awe and exert oneself, contemplate the Pure Land with clarity, and resolve to be reborn there?
Cast aside all worldly attachments and single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name. (From the *Lao Tang Jingce*) The Buddha said:
Human life is impermanent; it is as brief as a single breath. This is true even for those who are healthy, let alone for the sick.
I have now come to you with earnest exhortation: you must contemplate this body. The four elements are no longer in harmony, and the hundred joints of the frame are about to fall apart.
Food and drink gradually diminish, while medicine loses its efficacy. You are confined to a bed by the need for toileting, groaning upon your pillow and mat—like a fish swimming in a cauldron.

Internally, in an instant, one is bound like a plantain tree; like a lamp before the wind, it is extinguished in a moment. This body will not last long, and the path ahead is vast and obscure, its destination unknown.
If this were truly as you say—that all matters are already settled—then it would not be within the measure of a fool like me.

If, however, this is not so, why do you not vigorously contemplate impermanence, remain trembling with awe and diligent resolve, and reflect deeply upon the Pure Land, vowing with determination to be reborn there?
Set aside all worldly concerns and single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name (*Bingtang Jingce*).
Second, regarding the two powers for rebirth in the Pure Land (*Jingtu Shiyi Lun*): one must rely on two kinds of power. The first is self-power; the second is other-power.
As for self-power, although one may cultivate the path in this world, one has truly not yet attained birth in the Pure Land. Therefore—

The *Ratnavyūha Sūtra* states: From the very beginning, an ordinary person bound by all fetters—who has not yet recognized the Triple Gem and does not understand the causes and effects of good and evil—first gives rise to the bodhicitta.
Taking faith as the foundation, they dwell in the family of the Buddha; taking the precepts as the foundation, they receive the Bodhisattva precepts.
As their bodies succeed one after another through successive lifetimes, their practice of the precepts remains without deficiency for the duration of one, two, or three kalpas.

From the very beginning of the stage of Initial Resolve, one practices immeasurable vows and deeds, such as the ten faiths and the ten pāramitās, in continuous succession for ten thousand kalpas; only then does one finally reach the sixth stage, the Stage of the Right Mind.
If one further advances to the seventh stage, the Stage of Non-retrogression (*avaivartika-bhūmi*), this refers to the stage of spiritual lineage (*gotra-bhūmi*).
According to the perspective of self-power (*sva-bala*), one has not yet attained birth in the Pure Land. Regarding other-power (*para-bala*:

if one believes that Amitābha Buddha, through the power of his great compassionate vow, embraces those sentient beings who practice mindfulness of the Buddha, one is then able to give rise to the bodhicitta and practice the samādhi of mindfulness of the Buddha, becoming weary of and detaching from the three realms...)

Regarding the categories of realms: one initiates the practice of giving, precepts, and the cultivation of merit. Within each individual practice, one dedicates the merit with the vow to be reborn in that Pure Land of Amitābha.
By riding upon the power of the Buddha’s vows, when the capacity of the practitioner and the resonance of the response coincide, one immediately attains rebirth there.
Regarding the two paths (*Dvividha-mārga*) [from the *Ten Doubts about the Pure Land*], the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"In this world, there are two kinds of paths for practicing the Way: first, the path of difficulty; second, the path of ease.

As for the path of difficulty, in this world of the five turbidities, it is extremely difficult to attain the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*) even over the course of immeasurable Buddhas; its difficulties are incalculable."
They are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and cannot be fully described; briefly stated, there are five: first, those who outwardly appear virtuous but who disrupt the Dharma of Bodhisattvas;
second, unprincipled evildoers who destroy the superior virtues of others; third, those whose perverted "good" fruits can ruin pure conduct (*brahmacarya*);
fourth, Śrāvakas who seek their own self-interest and thus obstruct great compassion; and fifth, those who rely solely on their own power and lack...

The Support of Other-Power (*parāśraya*). For example, it is like a lame person walking on foot; in a single day they travel no more than several *li*, undergoing extreme hardship—this is called the power of self-effort (*svabala*).
The "Easy Path" (*sukhāpratipad*) refers to those who, trusting the Buddha’s words, are taught the *nien-fo* samādhi and aspire to be born in the Pure Land.
Being sustained by the power of Amitābha Buddha’s vows, they will certainly attain rebirth without doubt. It is like a person...
By way of water travel, because one relies on the power of the boat, one reaches a thousand *li* in an instant;
this is called "other-power. (The Patriarch Chunyang said: These two types of illness—this is the most perfectly interfused and most direct gateway to the Dharma.
One must first still the breath until not a single thread remains clinging to one, and then practice with real vigor; good results will naturally follow. However, there are two great illnesses.

Interruptions are not counted among these [successful recitations]. First, regarding my own practice of mindfulness of the Buddha: I detest the excessive talk of others and the excessive distractions of affairs;
before I have even reached one or two strings of recitations, my anger is greatly stirred up. Regardless of how much I recite, it is ineffective.
Even if one performs beneficial deeds, they will merely become an official in the underworld rather than ascending to the Pure Land. Why is this? It is because of the cause of anger (*dveṣa*).
This is the greatest taboo and the most easily committed transgression. As the sutras state: "A single thought of anger can burn away the seven treasures.
How harmful this is! One does not know how many people have been led astray by this single character "anger," and how many have been added to the ranks of the damned.

There are many illnesses. When the liver energy (liver qi) becomes excessively fierce and the fire of phenomenal consciousness (xiāng huǒ) surges forth, at its mildest it gives rise to symptoms of madness, delusion, and confusion;
at its worst, it causes one to lose their original nature, like paper cast into a red furnace, reduced to ashes in an instant.

How could such a person enter the Buddha-land, the cool realm of the Dharma? Second, there is the practice of reciting the Buddha's name with a seeking mind; though one seeks, [it is not yet sufficient].
It is so. Or, as it is said in a later passage: "Though the Buddha does not reproach one, the retribution for one's offenses is difficult to evade.

When an ordinary person practices mindfulness of the Buddha for fifty days, the Three Corpses (trīṇi śavāni) become enraged and jealous, and demonic obstacles will surely arise. This continues until the sixth month, after which the Three Corpses submit and benevolent deities arrive.
They protect you for upholding the Buddha, yet they are angry at you for slandering the Buddha; how much more so since the original purpose of mindfulness of the Buddha lies in the Great [Vehicle]."

This is merely applying effort toward specific goals. If you seek wealth and obtain wealth, or seek children and obtain children, then even if it were efficacious, it would not go beyond obtaining wealth and children;

it would have no connection whatsoever with the Pure Land. You do not realize that if you practice with single-minded devotion for a long time, you will naturally obtain results—wealth will come and children will be obtained of their own accord, without your having to seek them. This is destiny.

That which exists within one's destiny may not be present even if one practices mindfulness of the Buddha; thus, those raised in luxury and fine silks have no intention to practice cultivation because it is not destined for them, yet mindfulness of the Buddha is naturally theirs.
This is why aged masters and renowned monks often spent half their lives in wealth and honor.

Exert yourself! (As taught by the Venerable Shandao): With body, pay homage to that Buddha; with mouth, recite the name of that Buddha; with mind, contemplate that Buddha. When these three karmas are authentic, it is called the "mind of utmost sincerity.
It means to believe and know that one’s own self is fully possessed of afflictions and wanders through the three realms. To believe...
To know that Amitābha’s original vow grants birth even to those with as few as ten recitations, and to possess not a single thought of doubt, is called the "deep mind.
To dedicate all roots of goodness performed in every action toward rebirth in the Pure Land is called the "mind of dedication and aspiration.
Possessing these three minds, one will certainly attain rebirth.

The three minds (from *Direct Pointing to Mindfulness of the Buddha*) are fully present in the single practice of upholding the Buddha’s name: first, the direct mind, because one correctly contemplates the dharma of true suchness;
second, the profound mind, because one delights in cultivating all virtuous practices; and third, the mind of great compassion.
In order to rescue and deliver all sentient beings from suffering.
Third, regarding the three blessings (*Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*): those who wish to be born in that land should cultivate the three blessings.

First, filially supporting one's parents, serving teachers and elders, maintaining a compassionate heart and refraining from killing, and practicing the ten wholesome actions. Second, receiving and upholding the Three Refuges.

First, they are fully endowed with all precepts and do not violate the rules of dignified conduct. Second, they have resolved their minds on Bodhicitta, deeply believe in cause and effect, recite and study the Mahāyāna, and encourage other practitioners to do the same. Third, [they...
