The Three Powers (*Banzhou sanmei jing*): There are three kinds of power for rebirth through mindfulness of the Buddha. First is the power of the inherently existing Buddha-nature;
this refers to the Tathāgatagarbha within the mind of afflictions. Second is the power of compassionate light’s grasping;
this refers to Amitābha’s immeasurable radiance which, through mindfulness of the Buddha, grasps sentient beings and does not abandon them. Third is the power of mindfulness of the Buddha...
The power of samādhi means that by recollecting the Buddha and being mindful of the Buddha, one will certainly see the Buddha in the present and in the future.

Regarding the three grades (*wǔliàngshòujīng*): among the devas and humans of the worlds in the ten directions, those who with a sincere heart vow to be born in that land are divided into three grades.
As for the superior grade: they abandon their homes and renounce desire to become śramaṇas, and resolve upon bodhicitta.
With a mind that is single-mindedly focused on Amitāyus Buddha, they cultivate various merits and vow to be born in that land.
When these sentient beings approach the end of their lives, Amitāyus Buddha, together with a great assembly, will appear before them.
They shall then follow that Buddha and be reborn in his land, where they will spontaneously manifest by transformation within lotuses made of the seven treasures, dwelling therein.
They shall retreat from [lower realms] and possess courageous wisdom and sovereign supernormal powers. As for those of middling capacity:

among the devas and humans of the worlds of the ten directions, should there be those who with a sincere heart vow to be born in that land, even if they cannot become śramaṇas or extensively cultivate meritorious deeds, they should instead give rise to the unsurpassed mind of bodhi and single-mindedly and exclusively recollect Amitāyus Buddha. Much...

If one has cultivated a small amount of goodness— observing the precepts and fasts, erecting stupas and images, providing food for śramaṇas, hanging silk banners and lighting lamps, scattering flowers and burning incense—
and dedicates these merits with the vow to be reborn in that land, then at the time of death, Amitāyus Buddha will manifest a transformed body,
possessing radiance and the marks of excellence exactly like those of a true Buddha, appearing before that person together with a great assembly.
Those of the former [grade] will immediately follow the transformation Buddha to be reborn in that land and dwell in the stage of non-retrogression. As for those of the lower grade:

among the devas and humans of the worlds of the ten directions, if there are those who possess a sincere heart and desire to be reborn in that land, even if they are unable to perform various meritorious deeds, they should resolve their minds upon unsurpassed bodhicitta and focus their intent single-mindedly, even for as few as ten recitations. They should recite:
Regarding Amitāyus Buddha: if one wishes to be born in his land, and upon hearing the profound Dharma, feels joy, faith, and delight,
giving rise to no doubt or hesitation, even for a single thought-moment, and with a sincere heart recollects that Buddha and vows to be born in that land— such a person, at the time of death,
will see that Buddha in a dream and shall likewise attain rebirth there.
The Three Expedient Means (as explained by Master Kumārajīva): One who possesses these three expedient means will be born in the Pure Land.
First, being skilled in one's own practice while not grasping at signs; second, not grasping at realization; third, being skilled in transforming sentient beings.
The Three Doubts (as taught by the Patriarch Cizhao): A practitioner of nianfo who harbors three doubts at the time of death will not be reborn in the Pure Land.
First, they doubt that because their accumulated karma from past lives is extremely heavy and their practice has been shallow for so few days, they may not attain rebirth.
Second, they doubt that they owe debts to others, or have unfulfilled aspirations, or that their greed, anger, and ignorance have not yet ceased, and thus they may not be reborn.
One can attain birth [in the Pure Land]. Third, there is doubt, thinking: "Although I am mindful of Amitābha, I fear that at the time of death the Buddha will not come to welcome me.

These are the three types of lack of faith (as explained by Yang Cigong). There are virtuous persons in the world who give rise to these three kinds of lack of faith and do not seek birth [in the Pure Land].
Regarding the Pure Land, it is all the more lamentable that there are three [erroneous views]: first, "I shall transcend Buddhas and patriarchs;
the Pure Land is not a place where I ought to be born"; second, "Everywhere is the Pure Land; there is no necessity to be born in the West";
and third, "The sacred realm of Ultimate Bliss is a place where we commoners cannot be born."
For three reasons (as taught by Master Liánchí), those among the world who recite the Buddha’s name are many, yet those who are reborn in the Western Land and attain Buddhahood are few.
There are three such reasons. First, although they recite the Buddha’s name with their mouths, their minds are not virtuous; for this reason, they do not attain rebirth there.
I exhort all people of the world: since you practice the recitation of the Buddha’s name, you must act in accordance with what the Buddha has taught.
You must accumulate virtue and cultivate merit; you must be filial toward your parents; you must serve your sovereign with loyalty; you must love one another as brothers;

you must respect one another as husband and wife; you must be sincere, honest, and truthful; you must be gentle, flexible, and patient; you must be impartial and upright; and you must perform deeds of hidden merit.
Regarding skillful means: one must have compassion for all beings; not kill living creatures; not insult those of low station;
and not oppress the common people. Whenever an unwholesome thought arises, one must immediately apply focused mindfulness to resolve it.
Only by doing so is one a person who truly recites the Buddha’s name and will certainly attain Buddhahood. Second, even if one recites the Buddha’s name with the mouth...
With such random thoughts swirling in the mind, one will fail to attain rebirth in the Pure Land. I exhort all people of the world:

when reciting the Buddha’s name, you must restrain the restless monkey of the mind and the unruly horse of the thoughts. Make every syllable distinct and maintain constant mindfulness at every moment.

Act as if your parents were already in the Western Land, facing Amitābha directly, never daring to let your mind wander. Only in this way are you a true practitioner of nianfo; only then can you achieve concentration.
To attain Buddhahood. Third, though you may recite the Buddha’s name with your mouth, in your heart you only wish to seek wealth and status;
or you say, "We are ordinary beings; it is unlikely that we can achieve this. My lot is merely to ensure that in future lives I do not lose my human form.
This does not accord with the Buddha's mind or intent in leading you to be born in the Western Land. You yourself do not even wish to be born there. For this reason...
One will not attain rebirth there. I exhort all people in the world: those who recite the Buddha’s name must resolve to seek birth [in the Pure Land] and must not harbor doubts.
For instance, even when the wealth, honor, and blessings in the celestial palaces are exhausted, one must still fall; how much more so for the wealth and honor of the human realm?
How much time do you have? If you say that as an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) you have no share in the Western Land, then it follows that all sages and worthies were once ordinary persons.

How can you know for certain that you will not be born in the West? You should immediately give rise to a vast and great mind, establish a firm resolve, and vow to be reborn there to see the Buddha, hear the Dharma, attain the unsurpassed fruit, and extensively deliver all sentient beings. As it is said:
These alone are those who practice *nien-fo* (Buddha-recitation). They will certainly attain Buddhahood.
Regarding the "Threefold Specialization" (as taught by Master Shandao): the body must be specialized—worship only Amitābha Buddha and do not intermingle other forms of prostration;
the mouth must be specialized—recite only the name of Amitābha Buddha and do not recite other names; the mind must be specialized—contemplate only Amitābha Buddha and do not... [contemplate others].
If one practices other forms of contemplation, yet practices them with single-minded devotion, then ten [recitations] result in ten births, and a hundred result in a hundred births.
(According to Master Daxing): If the mind thinks only of the Buddha, the Buddha knows it, because of his power of knowing others' minds (*paracittajñāna*).

If the mouth recites only the name of the Buddha, the Buddha hears it, because of his divine ear (*divyaśrotra*). If the body bows only to the Buddha, the Buddha sees it, because of his divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).
Because of the penetration of the eye:
(according to Master Ouyi), hearing the teaching of Amitābha Buddha is the wisdom of hearing; upholding his name is the wisdom of reflection;
and single-mindedness without distraction is the wisdom of cultivation.
Third, the Comparison (from the *Ten Doubts Treatise*): Although beginningless evil karma may be heavy, ten recitations at the moment of death can counteract it.
Now, we shall compare this by means of three aspects. First, regarding the mind: when one commits evil, it arises from false and inverted views;
whereas the practitioner of Buddha-remembrance arises [in mind] through hearing the true merits and name of the Buddha from a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*). One is false and the other is real.

How could they possibly be compared? It is like a dark room that has been shut for ten thousand years: when the sunlight briefly reaches it, how could the darkness accumulated over such a long time fail to be dispelled?
Second, regarding conditions: at the time one commits a transgression, it arises from a mind of deluded darkness, conditioned by illusory objects.
The mind of mindfulness of the Buddha arises from hearing the names and merits of the Buddha, conditioned by unsurpassed bodhi.
The arising of the mind is of two kinds: one is true and one is false; how could they possibly be compared?

It is like a person struck by a poisoned arrow, the shaft deep and the venom cruel, wounding the flesh and breaking the bone; yet upon hearing the drum of the medicine that eliminates it, the arrow immediately comes out and the poison is removed.

How could it be that one does not emerge simply because the arrow is deep and the poison is cruel? Third, it concerns decisiveness: at the time of committing a sin, there is an interval and a subsequent mind;
however, at the time of recollecting the Buddha, there is no interval and no subsequent mind, as one passes away immediately.
Because the wholesome mind is so fierce and sharp, one is reborn [in the Pure Land] right then and there. It is like a great rope ten spans in circumference, which a thousand men cannot restrain.
When a youth brandishes a sword, it is divided in two in an instant. It is also like a thousand-year-old pile of firewood that is completely consumed in a short time by a single grain of fire.
(Said by Master Ximing): One must not associate with heterodox teachings when practicing *nianfo*; *nianfo* is the sublime, orthodox Dharma.
Although this gate appears simple and easy, it in fact encompasses the Perfect and Sudden teachings.
I fear that foolish men and women may grow weary and indolent midway, being enticed by others into the non-active (wuwei) teachings of the Heavenly Lord and other such doctrines;

they would thus regard the single gate of Pure Land as erroneous, incurring grave offenses in life and falling into hell after death—how pitiable and lamentable! I earnestly exhort those who practice the Buddha-remembrance to be sincere and steadfast.
Maintain mindfulness until the thought of mindfulness reaches its fulfillment; with single-mindedness and without distraction, the lotus will naturally bloom and you shall behold the Buddha.

Do not by any means indulge in strange superstitions or seek out spirits, nor give rise to other deluded thoughts; such actions are not only useless but will further harm you. One must not treat the recitation of the Buddha’s name as mere currency.
There is no Great Dharma for transcending the world that compares to the recitation of the Buddha’s name. I often see that the roots of faith of worldly people are not upright, and they all say:
The Buddha whom one has kept in mind can be used as currency after death. Because of this, at the time of death, one becomes deluded;

knowing only that the underworld uses money, one fails to know how to dedicate merit toward the Pure Land. Is this not a great error? I earnestly exhort those who practice *nien-fo* (Buddha-recitation):
you must take refuge in Amitābha Buddha, as well as the Great Bodhisattvas Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta. Ten thousand...
One must not use this Great Dharma that transcends the world merely for the sake of worldly social obligations or the expenses of impermanence.
In the practice of *nianfo*, one must not kill living beings recklessly. *Nianfo* takes compassion as its foundation; if one does not refrain from killing, the efficacy of the practice will diminish.
All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature; throughout kalpas of time, they have all been our own kin. To kill them...
To nourish me—how can my heart bear this? I exhort those who practice *nianfo* (Buddha-recitation): whenever you take up your chopsticks to eat, always maintain this reflection;
then you will naturally abstain from meat and quickly perfect the pure karma. Even if you cannot maintain a perpetual fast, you should at least observe the six days of fasting.
One may still attain rebirth there; however, if one commits the act of killing, it is absolutely forbidden.
Regarding the "Three Strategies" (from *Jingtu huiwen*): the ancients established three urgent measures for self-exhortation: first, repaying kindness; second, resolving the will;
and third, seeking verification. First, regarding repaying kindness: having cultivated the Pure Land, one must contemplate the repayment of kindness toward the Buddha.
The kindness of the state is certainly not something we have leisure to discuss; yet, how can the kindness of one’s parents in raising and nurturing us not be considered a profound kindness?
How can the virtue of one’s teachers in molding and perfecting us not be considered a profound virtue? When you first left the household life, you said you would repay this profound kindness;
later, when you went on pilgrimage, you said you would repay this profound virtue. Having left your hometown and parted from your well, for twenty or thirty years...
Throughout your years, you paid no heed at all to the hardships and sufferings of your parents and teachers. When your parents grew old and sick, you did not care for them;

when you heard of their deaths, you did not return. Now they may be in the three miserable realms, undergoing punishment and suffering, looking to you for rescue and looking to you for deliverance, yet you instead allow your mindfulness to be interrupted moment by moment, so that Pure Land is not achieved.
If the Pure Land is not established, you will be unable to save yourself. If you cannot save yourself, how can you save others?
Since you are unable to help one another, you are ungrateful and disloyal, a person of great filial impiety.
As the Sūtra says, "The sin of unfiliality shall cause one to fall into hell. Thus, even a single thought of interruption is itself the karma of hell. Furthermore, moreover—
They wear clothing produced by silkworms and eat food grown without plowing. Their monastic quarters and bedding are provided for their use as a matter of course.
You should diligently cultivate pure karma to repay the kindness of those who offer their faith and alms. As the Patriarch said: "This is the domain of the donor and his wife."
If you diminish and neglect your practice in the future, your Dharma-eye will remain unclarified. Even a drop of water or a thread of silk must be used to pull the plow and hold the handle;
only then can you repay your debts. If you, however, allow your mindfulness to be interrupted moment by moment, the Pure Land will not be realized.
If the Pure Land is not realized, there will be no way to fulfill your obligations. Thus, a single thought of interruption is itself the karma of an animal. Second Decision.
As for "resolve": if you study with single-minded dedication, your resolve must be decisive. You have spent your entire life practicing Chan;
yet, having failed to awaken through Chan, you turn to the teachings, only to find them likewise obscure. Having reached this point, your deluded thoughts remain undispelled.
Now you wish to utter a few words of Chan, utter a few words of the teachings, write a few characters, and compose a few [verses].
The opening verse: Sentiment hangs between two ends; thoughts branch into four paths. The Patriarch said:
"A thought tied by a hair’s breadth is the karmic cause for the three miserable realms; in a mere flicker of emotion, one is shackled for ten thousand kalpas.

Yet you remain indecisive in your resolve, with many-faceted sentiments and thoughts that interrupt right mindfulness. Thus, a single moment of interrupted mind is itself the shackle of the three miserable realms.
This is karma. Furthermore, while guarding the roots of the precepts, if one’s resolve is not firm, or if one pursues desires through body and speech from moment to moment, the scriptures teach:
it would be better to pour molten copper into one’s mouth than to accept food or drink with a mouth that has broken the precepts;
it would be better to wrap one’s body in hot iron than to accept clothing with a body that has broken the precepts.
How much more so when, due to a lack of strictness in the various precepts, the deviant mind moves recklessly; because of this reckless movement, one interrupts dedicated cultivation.
Thus, a single thought of interruption is itself the karma of molten copper and glowing iron.

Furthermore, regarding the severing of hatred and attachment, if one's resolve is not determined, one will fail to break through self-delusion whenever confronted with empty fame and floating profit; such fame and profit belong to—
I, however, immediately gave rise to craving and attachment. When I perceived that fame and profit belonged to another, I immediately gave rise to resentment and jealousy.

The person on the right said: "To crave fame and profit is to follow the same path as the class of ghosts; to pursue love and pursue hatred is to enter the same fiery pit together. You, moreover, because of this love and hatred—
This interrupts the Pure Land practice. Thus, a single thought of interruption is itself the karma of the hungry ghosts' fiery pit.
Third, regarding seeking verification: once you have studied the practice of exclusive cultivation (*senju*), you should seek spiritual efficacy.

For instance, now that your hair has turned white, your face is wrinkled, and the signs of death are manifest before you, knowing that your end is near and there are but a few days remaining, you must [seek this] in the present.
If you wish to see the Buddha: consider Master Huiyuan of Mount Lu, who throughout his life was thrice graced by the Buddha’s hand upon his head;
or Master Huigan, who upon reciting the Buddha’s name, immediately beheld the Buddha;
or Master Shaokang, who when chanting the Buddha’s name once, the assembly saw a Buddha fly forth from his mouth, and when he chanted it ten times, [the same occurred]. Thus...
Ten Buddhas emerged from his mouth, appearing like pearls strung together. Such miraculous responses are countless—ten thousand, ten million, a hundred thousand.

If your mind remains uninterrupted, it will not be difficult to see the Buddha; if an interrupted thought arises, you will certainly not see the Buddha, for you will lack the karmic affinity with him.
Lacking this affinity with the Buddha, it is difficult to be born in the Pure Land. If one is not born in the Pure Land, one will inevitably fall into the evil realms.
Thus, even a single moment of interrupted thought constitutes the karma for the three miserable realms and evil paths. Be cautious! Be cautious!

Regarding the three strategies mentioned above, you must personally lash yourself with remorse so that your mindfulness does not depart from the Buddha, and the Buddha does not depart from your mindfulness.
Through the mutual resonance of the Way, one manifests the presence of the Buddha. Having seen the Buddha of the Land of Bliss, one sees all Buddhas of the ten directions;
having seen all Buddhas of the ten directions, one sees the Buddha of one's own original nature.

Regarding the "Exclusive Recommendation" (from *The Questions on the Pure Land*): While the Tathāgatas of the ten directions are all accessible for veneration, there are three reasons why Amitābha alone is exclusively recommended here.
First, his vows are profound and weighty; second, he has a karmic affinity with those in this Sahā world; and third, his path of transformation is particularly relevant to us.
Regarding the "Vow of Weightiness," the Sūtra states: In the past, during his causal stage, Amitābha once made various kinds of vast and great vows.

A summary of them says: "If, since my attainment of Buddhahood, there should be sentient beings who wish to be born in my land, or who hear my name, cultivate the roots of goodness, and recite my name—even for as few as ten recitations—and yet are not born [there], I vow..."

"I shall not attain perfect enlightenment. Once those who have been born in my land should experience regression and fail to achieve certainty in their attainment of Buddhahood, I vow not to attain perfect enlightenment.
Therefore, the *Huayan chao* states: "The vows of Amitābha are profound; he specifically receives and delivers the sentient beings of this Sahā world."

Regarding those with the karmic affinity: during the time when our Buddha Śākyamuni was present in the world, there were already many sentient beings who, upon hearing the Buddha’s teachings, turned toward Amitābha.

As for sentient beings in the degenerate age after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa—whether monastic or lay, male or female, noble or humble, rich or poor—among those who have heard even a little of the Buddha’s teaching, there are none who do not believe and turn toward him; as for those who have not yet heard the Buddha’s teaching...
They shall likewise be called by name. Even those who are stubborn, foolish, violent, evil, and devoid of faith—
whether they encounter calamities and perils, or involuntarily utter sounds of praise or lamentation,
or even when children and women, in the midst of play, gather sand, knead clay, or draw upon walls— [shall all be saved].
On the wall, he then fashioned an image of Amitābha Buddha. Even those whose practice was not yet stable and whose speech was not yet formed were naturally able to chant "Amitābha Buddha.
All of this arose without being exhorted and occurred without being taught; how could it be anything other than the presence of a karmic affinity?
The *Sūtra of Immeasurable Life* states: "After this sūtra has ceased to exist, the Buddha-dharma will be entirely gone, leaving behind only..."
The four-character name of Amitābha Buddha saves sentient beings. Those who do not believe and instead slander it shall fall into hell and undergo all manner of suffering.
Therefore, Tiantai said: "One should know that this Buddha has a particular affinity for this degenerate age.
Regarding those who are connected [to him], the former sages stated that the holy ones of the two lands manifest their residence in the Pure Land.
Regarding filth: through the two gates of subduing (*nigraha*) and gathering (*saṃgraha*), one tames sentient beings.
Here, one subdues them by means of filth, suffering, brevity, and manifold demonic afflictions, so that they may come to know what to loathe.

There, one gathers them by means of purity, bliss, longevity, and non-retrogression, so that they may know what to rejoice in. Once there is both loathing and rejoicing, the path of transformation proceeds. Furthermore, I...
Śākyamuni, beyond bestowing the Way upon those of the Three Vehicles, leaves those whose liberation remains incomplete to be saved by Amitābha;
therefore, in various Mahāyāna sūtras, he repeatedly and earnestly extols and exhorts them to go [to that land].
This is because their paths of transformation are interconnected. For these three reasons, he alone is uniquely recommended.
The Three Paths (Pure Land Dharma Words): If one's mindfulness is not single-minded, one will not be born in Sukhāvatī.
There are three paths for this single thought-moment: namely, faith, practice, and aspiration. First, regarding faith: to have no doubt is called faith.
If there is any doubt, the mind cannot attain its unity. Therefore, those who seek rebirth in Sukhāvatī must take the cultivation of profound faith as their foundation.
At the outset, one must read the Mahayana scriptures thoroughly and study the teachings of the patriarchs extensively.
One must investigate and seek out every single work that elucidates the Pure Land, realizing that the Land of Ultimate Bliss is originally the pure land of one’s own mind and not some other land;
and that Amitābha is originally one’s own original nature and not some other Buddha. Once this is realized—

The wondrous existence is all-pervasive and complete, serving as the foundation for delighting in purity. A single realization of true emptiness brings about perfect detachment and liberation, serving as the source for abandoning defilement.
As for the second practitioner: the former stage of deepening faith is like seeing with one's eyes;
the present stage of cultivation is like walking with one's feet. To have faith without practice is like having eyes but no feet; to practice without faith is like...
One may possess feet but lack eyes; therefore, once faith and understanding are complete, one ought to practice the mindfulness of the Buddha.
Only when both eyes and feet are fully provided can one reach the cool pond. Thus, after faith, practice is explained. As for the third vow:
the vessel of the Prajñā of the Pure Land must take faith as its nodding head for testing the waters and practice as its oar.

With oars, sails, and wind, one wishes for the rudder to steer it straight; without dipping the head to probe the water, one will not know whether the passage is open or blocked, or how deep or shallow it is.
Without oars, sails, and wind, one cannot reach the destination; without a rudder to steer it straight, [the boat will not reach its goal].
Thus, there are no restrictive constraints or regulations; therefore, the next practice clarifies the vow.
These three dharmas may be called the grand framework for birth in the Pure Land and the precious raft for beholding Amitābha. All dharma-gates of the Pure Land do not fall outside of these.
Regarding the three modes of recitation (as taught by Master Lianchi): there is silent recitation, there is loud recitation, and there is vajra-recitation (*vajra-japa*).

Loud recitation is perceived as being too strenuous, while silent recitation easily leads to dullness and sleepiness. Instead, one should maintain a continuous and dense flow where the sound remains between the lips and teeth;
this is called vajra-recitation. Furthermore, one must not be dogmatic about it; if one feels it is too strenuous, one should not persist.

It is permissible to recite silently; however, if one perceives a state of mental dullness (*styāna*), it is better not to recite in silence. One must ensure that every phrase leaves the mouth and enters the ear, and that every sound awakens the mind within.
It is like when one person is in a deep sleep and another calls out, "So-and-so! and that person immediately wakes up.
For this reason, the recitation of the Buddha’s name (*buddhānusmṛti*) is most effective for gathering the mind.

Three Exhortations (Spoken by Master Lianchi): 1. Exhorting those with extreme leisure to recite the Buddha’s name: Having completed all matters of marriage and family, and with sons and grandsons capable of managing the household, you enjoy peace and have no affairs to attend to;
this is precisely the time to devote your heart and exert your strength in reciting the Buddha’s name. Recite several thousand times every day.
Even for those with tens of thousands of affairs, I urge even half of those who are neither busy nor idle to practice mindfulness of the Buddha.

Whether they are busy or idle—and though not entirely free from busyness—they may attend to their duties during busy times and practice mindfulness of the Buddha during idle times, reciting the name several hundred times daily, up to several thousand.
Furthermore, I urge even those who are extremely busy to practice mindfulness of the Buddha; though they labor diligently in royal service and run about in haste...

Regarding one's household affairs, although there is no moment of leisure, one must still steal moments from amidst busyness to recite the Buddha’s name. Every morning at dawn, one should perform ten recitations;
furthermore, during the day, one may recite several hundred times.

The Three Barriers (from the *Lianzong baojian*): Chan Master Doushuai Yue presented the assembly with three barriers. First: "To pull back the weeds and investigate the profound is merely to seek the realization of one's nature.
Where, right now, does this person’s nature reside? Second: "Having recognized one's original nature, one seeks to escape birth and death.

When birth and death actually arrive, how will you escape them? Third: "Having escaped birth and death, one seeks to know the place of departure. Fourth: [The fourth barrier is omitted in the source text.]
When the great separation occurs, where will one go? If you penetrate this barrier, you will not be constrained by birth and death, nor hindered in coming and going.
Now, those who practice the Buddha-remembrance should, throughout the twelve periods of the day, hold the single phrase "Namu Amida Butsu," with focused thought and tranquil visualization.
Furthermore, they should turn the light inward and examine for themselves: what is my original nature when the four elements separate and where does it go? When the four elements separate... where?
While dwelling [in this state], one constantly harbors such doubts; yet, upon suddenly recognizing them, one immediately knows their point of resolution.
This is precisely the direct path of cultivation.

(From the *Lianzong baojian*, "The Three Contemplations") Now, ignorance clouds the Dharma-nature, and the sands of affliction obstruct transformative guidance. [This concerns] the views and thoughts...
Obstructed by emptiness and stillness, one accordingly establishes the three contemplations, destroys the three delusions, realizes the three wisdoms, and accomplishes the three virtues.
The contemplation of emptiness destroys the delusions of views and thoughts, realizes all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñā*), and accomplishes the virtue of prajñā.

The contemplation of the provisional destroys the delusions as numerous as motes of dust, realizes the wisdom of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), and accomplishes the virtue of liberation. The contemplation of the middle destroys the delusion of ignorance and realizes the [wisdom of] the...

The knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) accomplishes the virtues of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). When a practitioner recollects the Buddha, the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) serves as the cause and the white tuft of hair and circular halo serve as the conditions;
the mindfulness thus aroused is the dharma that arises. When one contemplates with discernment and the mind of recollection arises, this is a provisional designation (*prajñapti*);
its essence is empty. To penetrate and see this mind clearly is the Tathāgatagarbha; it is the manifestation of that which is free from extremes.
Within this, both the faculties and the objects are the Dharma-realm. All Buddhas and sentient beings universally respond in a single thought-moment;
this is "the middle within the extremes. Where there is no Buddha and no thought, this is the perfect cultivation of the Mahayana—the third contemplation of the Buddha.
Therefore it is said: "Neither form nor emptiness, nor non-emptiness—this is the Tathāgata’s true mark."

Third, [as stated in the *Lianzong baojian*]: Amitābha Buddha possesses vast and great power of vows (*praṇidhāna-bala*) that gathers the sentient beings of this Sahā world and causes them to return to the Pure Land;
this is to cause them to turn back from delusion and realize the Truth. As for the essence of the Way of the Pure Land:
Taking Amitābha as one’s own original nature is its fundamental principle (*tong*); taking the Pure Land as nothing but one’s own mind is its function (*yong*);
and taking benevolence and forbearance as the means to extinguish evil and give rise to good—these three aspects reveal the retribution of cause and effect across the three periods of time.

Regulate its practice so that the mind becomes empty and still; exhaust its principle so that those who have attained the principle may turn back from their delusions, and those who believe in its practice may be transformed toward goodness.

If a single person can practice this Way to instruct their family, the family to guide the village, the village to reach the state, and so on until it is infinite, then the people of the world will be imbued with it.

He swam in the Way and his virtue was harmonious; his spirit truly merged with the ultimate reality (*dharmatā*). He strode loftily through the realm of non-being and reached the pinnacle of the Buddha’s境界 (*buddha-viṣaya*).

How could he be considered merely a "good man" or a "gentleman"? If this is so, then why worry that he failed to cultivate loyalty and filial piety, or that his propriety and yielding were not manifest?

Regarding the "Three Prisoners" (from *The Morning Bell of the Pure Land*), Qian Xiaozhi said: "From time immemorial, the cycle of birth and death within the three realms has been compared to a prison.
Thus, as long as one has not yet escaped birth and death, all are prisoners within the jail of the three realms. There are three kinds of such prisoners."
The first thinks to himself that there is no possibility of survival, so he merely seeks a precarious sense of ease within this state;

yet one day, when the executioner arrives, he quivers in terror as he is led to his death. The second prides himself on being the son of a man worth a thousand pieces of gold and does not spare his wealth.

He manages his livelihood, yet his mind is not fixed; on one hand, he indulges for the time being in the pleasure of stealing from the cauldron, while on the other, he thinks that if the path to rebirth is cut off, he will simply endure it with a willing heart. There is another man of a rebellious and stubborn nature who cannot bear restraint;
watching for a moment when the guards are few, he breaks free from his shackles and chains, charging forward without looking back. Such is his determination.
How could he possibly be willing, before his death, to stealily enjoy the remainder of his life? Whether he emerges or does not emerge, his state of mind hangs between two possibilities.
Alas! This too is a prime example from within the prison of birth and death for those of our kind. This is the first type of person.
Everywhere one looks, there are those who speak only of fame, achievement, wealth, and honor.

Having acquired these through bitter toil, they indulge themselves in the pleasures of palaces, consorts, and attendants. When spoken to about birth and death, they remain indifferent and unconcerned;
when told that there is another path apart from birth and death, they merely respond with a silent laugh. This is because they entirely lack the faculty of faith.
The second type of person is one who, from birth, possesses innate roots of virtue; they pay homage to the Buddha, practice meditation, and protect the teachings of the Dharma.

They build temples and provide for the Sangha, being unstinting with their wealth. Yet, having stepped into the net of worldly affairs, they are bound by the tether of fame and the shackles of profit, like entering a thicket of thorns where they are entangled and cannot attain freedom. Now, the one great matter in a human life is to transcend the world.

Regarding causes and conditions, if one does not apply oneself with single-minded devotion but wishes to reach the goal through mere incidental effort, how could there be such a thing as a "crane of Yangzhou" in this world?
Though they may have performed meritorious deeds throughout their lives, they cannot escape the threshold of birth and death within the realms of humans and devas;
they simply fail to transcend them. This is because, despite their fear of birth and death, their resolve has never been truly sincere. This is like the third type of person.
Do not seek birth into wealth or nobility; simply apply yourself with diligent effort. Only then can one truly seek to transcend birth and death.
Seeing those now bound in fetters calling out to heaven for their lives, who would not pity their folly and regret that they did not seek birth earlier?
I say that while a condemned prisoner seeking life is far too late, compared to us, we are still early.
This is a calculation. A death prisoner is sentenced for execution in the autumn; in a year, there is no more than one day [of execution].

Before or after that single day, everything may be relaxed and at ease. Yet, consider us: within the prisons of the three realms, we may die every year, we may die every month, and we may die every day and every moment.
The lowly die and the noble die; the old die and the young die; the wicked die and the good die.
One will likewise die. There shall be no ranking by noble title, no ranking by virtue, and no ranking by seniority. With a single breath not returning, one is immediately divided from the living;

if you do not prepare yourself early, you must wait for that moment—yet at this very instant, the execution warrant may arrive, and the executioner will stand before you in a state of frantic confusion.
How can you resist it? Nevertheless, once a criminal has entered prison, they seek every moment [to escape].
They emerge because they know that beyond the thorny walls there exist further realms of great peace and bliss.
Currently, sentient beings take afflictions as their home and birth-and-death as their garden;
they do not realize that the Great Iron Ring Mountains are their thorny walls, and that beyond the field of phenomena of the triple world, each has their own native land and place of joy. All...
The Buddha, pitying them, distinguished between the pure and the defiled and pointed out the path for their liberation and return.
Yet, as the journey was long, those who had cast off their karma found no place of refuge. Therefore, the Buddhas further constructed great dwellings to settle them:
one to serve as a road for traveling to and from the gates of hell, and the other to wait eternally outside the prison to maintain and adorn the guest-houses. Thus it is.

What body could possibly repay this kindness? Since the Buddhas do not begrudge lowering their hands to guide and receive sentient beings, why do you, on the contrary, cling to this mere hair-tip of a matter and fail to awaken even at the point of death? Why is this so?
Third, regarding "Waiting" (as taught by Master Jikishitsu): When worldly people wish to cultivate pure karma, they say, "I am too busy now;
let me wait until I have leisure. Or, "I am too poor now; let me wait until I am wealthy. Or, "I am still young and strong now; let me wait until I am old."
If one’s allotted portion is fixed for constant busyness, fixed for poverty, or fixed for an early death, there will be no opportunity to cultivate pure karma.
Should one suddenly perish, what can be done though one regrets it? I exhort all people: while the body is still healthy, strive with diligence to practice.
The Four Kinds of Buddha-Recollection (*Buxian xingyuan ji*): First, *nienfo by reciting the name*.
This refers to reciting the name of Amitābha Buddha with single-minded concentration throughout the day and night, whether ten thousand times or even up to one hundred thousand times.
In this way, as the months and years pass, one’s mindfulness will become uninterrupted, pure and unadulterated.
At the time of death, one will certainly see that Buddha manifest his body to welcome them, and they will definitely be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Second is the practice of *nianfo* by contemplating the image: this means contemplating the physical marks and signs of Amitābha Buddha while vocally reciting the Buddha’s name; thus, the mind—
Without distraction. When the mind is not distracted, the Buddha of one’s original nature will manifest.

Thus, with every thought-moment uninterrupted and purely singular without admixture, at the time of death, one will certainly see that Buddha appear in person to welcome one, and will definitely be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Third is the visualization of mindfulness of the Buddha: this means sitting upright with right mindfulness, facing [the Buddha].

Face the western direction and perform sublime contemplation with the mind. Visualize either the light of the white tuft of hair between Amitābha Buddha’s eyebrows, or even the thousand-spoked wheel mark on the soles of his feet.
In this manner, contemplate from top to bottom and from bottom to top, turning your gaze back and forth.
When your visualization becomes pure and mature, samādhi will manifest before you. At the time of death, you will certainly attain rebirth there.
This is the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Fourth is the mindfulness of the Buddha through the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
This means that by recollecting the Dharma-nature body of Amitābha Buddha, one immediately attains the principle of the true mark. It is formless and signless, like empty space;
the mind and all sentient beings are fundamentally equal. Such mindfulness is true mindfulness. When this mindfulness continues in an uninterrupted succession, samādhi manifests.
It is certain that one will be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Regarding the four lands (*Lotus School Treasure Mirror*): first, the Land of Common Dwelling of Ordinary Beings and Sages.

In this land, those who merely possess faith and aspiration, practice the recitation of the Buddha’s name, do not sever their afflictions, do not abandon their worldly attachments, and do not cultivate meditative concentration, will be welcomed and guided by Amitābha at the time of death.
All shall attain rebirth there, immediately obtain supernatural powers (*abhijñā*), and reach the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*) until they finally attain Bodhi.

Second, O Householder, those of superior skillful means in this land are all of fixed nature (*niyata-gotra*) and possess the faculties of the Small Vehicle (*hīnayāna*). They dread the three realms as they would tigers, ghosts, dragons, or snakes;

they destroy the delusions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *saṃyojana-kleśa*), kill greed, anger, and ignorance, and sever the seeds of the Tathāgata. They are biasedly attached to narrow views.
Sinking into emptiness and lingering in quiescence, one is born into the Tathāgata’s land of pure Mahāyāna subduing, the land of the threefold true recompense and adornment.

In this land, all are Mahāyāna practitioners who have perfected the cultivation of the three contemplations; they are Bodhisattvas of the Dharma-body at the stages of the ten abodes, ten practices, ten transferences, ten grounds, and equal enlightenment, as numerous as dust motes or grains of sand. Each has individually shattered their ignorance and manifested ten bodies.
This is the square realm where Bodhisattvas dwell to deliver sentient beings: the Land of the Fourfold Constant Quiescent Light. This land is the sphere of the Supreme Vehicle.
When delusions are exhausted and emotions forgotten, all phenomena do not arise; even Prajñā does not arise—this is called Great Nirvāṇa.
Dwelling serenely in this land is called the Pure Dharmakāya, called reaching the other shore, and also called one's own true self prior to the kalpa of emptiness.
Regarding the fourfold analysis (as taught by Master Yongming): "If one has Chan but no Pure Land, nine out of ten go astray. If the realm of the shadows...
Present before you, yet in an instant it slips away. With Chan but no Pure Land, ten thousand may practice, yet only a few go.
But if one can see Amitābha, why worry about not attaining enlightenment? With both Chan and the Pure Land, one is like a tiger with horns;
in this life one becomes a teacher of men, and in the future one becomes a Buddha or Patriarch. Without Chan and without the Pure Land, there is only the iron bed and the copper pillar.
Through ten thousand kalpas and a thousand lifetimes, there is no one to rely upon.
(Master Lianchi’s Explanation of the Four Categories of Discernment): To cultivate merit but not recite the Buddha’s name—when merit is exhausted, one sinks back into the cycle of suffering.

To recite the Buddha’s name but not cultivate merit—the path to enlightenment will be fraught with bitter hardship. To have neither merit nor recite the Buddha’s name—one belongs to the throngs of hell-dwellers, ghosts, and animals. [Therefore,] recite the Buddha’s name.
While simultaneously cultivating merit, one shall later realize the state of the Honored One Among Two-Legged Beings.

Regarding the four intentions (as explained by National Teacher Qingliang): Question: Why is it that one does not seek birth in the Flower Treasury World (*Sukhāvatī*), but rather seeks birth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*)?
Answer: There are four reasons. First, because there are specific conditions; Amitābha’s vows are profound, and he specifically receives those from the Sahā world. Second...

First, it causes sentient beings to take refuge with a single-minded devotion. Second, if they were told that all ten directions are wondrous, beginners would be bewildered and have no place to rely upon;
therefore, it uses skillful means to guide them. Third, it does not depart from the Flower Treasury World (*Huazang*).

Although the Land of Ultimate Bliss is ten thousand *koṭis* of lands away from here, the Buddha-lands of the Flower Treasury are as numerous as motes of dust; thus, it does not depart from it. Fourth...
This is because he is the Original Teacher himself. The Sūtra says: "Some see the Buddha Amitāyus surrounded by Avalokiteśvara and others.
The Commentary states: "This praises the virtues of the Honored One Vairocana; the Flower Treasury Sea of Lands is entirely the realm of Vairocana."
If ten trillion lands have not yet emerged from the ocean of world-systems (*kṣetra-vyuha*), is this not the Master [Śākyamuni] manifesting diverse transformations according to names?
(Regarding the "Four Obstacles," as taught by the Patriarch Cizhao: A person who recites the Buddha’s name encounters these four obstacles and fails to be born in the Pure Land.
Yet those of no wisdom say, "I am now reciting the Buddha’s name, yet I still suffer from illness. They thus slander Amitābha. Because of this one...
If one harbors evil thoughts, one will go directly to hell; this is the first barrier.

Although one may observe the precepts and recite the Buddha’s name, if the conditions are such that the mouth speaks of the Pure Land while the mind dwells upon the Sahā world, failing to seek roots of goodness for transcendence and allowing attachment to family ties to flourish, then at the time of death one will encounter illness, fear death and crave life, and come to believe the words of children, calling out to spirits and deities.
As for ghosts: they burn paper money to transform it into horses and slaughter sentient beings.
Because their minds are thus perverted and they lack the protection of the Buddhas, they consequently wander and fall into the three miserable realms; this is the second barrier.
Or, due to taking medicine that requires wine or meat, or being pressured and urged by relatives, such a person lacks resolute faith and loses their roots of goodness. At the time of death...
They are summoned before the King; let the King judge them. This is the third barrier.

At the moment of death, if one dwells upon worldly occupations, clings to wealth and possessions, or harbors attachment to kin and family such that the mind cannot let go, one loses right mindfulness.
Consequently, within the household, one falls into the realm of hungry ghosts. Having become a malevolent spirit, one may become a stingy dog or take the form of a snake to guard [the dwelling].
To protect one’s family as if they were under the sun—this is the fourth gate.
(As explained by the Venerable Master Ciyun, the Patriarch of Repentance: This is the swift path for cultivating the pure karma of the Pure Land, easy to practice.

All Mahāyāna sūtras reveal this essential point, and there are none among the Buddhas of the ten directions who do not praise it. Whether they be bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās, or virtuous sons and daughters of faith...

If you wish to swiftly shatter ignorance and eternally extinguish the grave offenses of the five heinous crimes and the ten evil deeds, as well as other minor transgressions, you should practice this Dharma.
If you wish to attain purity and fulfill all the gates of the *pāramitās* through the major and minor precepts, you should study this Dharma.
If you wish that at the time of death you may be free from all fears and experience peace and joy in body and mind, [you should practice this Dharma].

Joyful as if returning home, the light illuminates one’s dwelling. Exquisite fragrances and music arise as Amitābha Buddha, together with his assembly of holy ones, sends forth a purple-golden platform and extends his hand to welcome [the practitioner].
Crossing the five paths of rebirth and traversing the nine grades, one casts off the torments of heat and finds rest in cool serenity.
Having first escaped the toil of worldly defilement, one immediately ascends to the stage of non-retrogression; without passing through long kalpas, one realizes [enlightenment].

Those who seek non-arising should study this Dharma. Desiring to cultivate even a small portion of the Dharma yet receiving wondrous retribution, they are simultaneously praised by the Buddhas of the ten directions, who bestow predictions of enlightenment before them. In a single thought-moment, they make offerings to countless Buddhas;
returning to their own lands, they sit and eat with Amitābha, discourse with Avalokiteśvara, and walk alongside Mahāsthāmaprāpta. Their bodies possess clear vision and penetrating hearing.
Their measure is boundless; they move freely through the air and possess clear knowledge of their past lives.
They observe the five realms of existence as if seeing reflections in a mirror, entering the inexhaustible samādhi in every thought-moment. You should practice this supreme dharma.

The Four Kinds of Non-Retrogression (as explained by Master Ouyi): Rebirth in the Pure Land ensures that one never regresses. There are four meanings to this: First, non-retrogression of thought (*citta*).

By destroying ignorance and manifesting the Buddha-nature, one is born directly into the land of true retribution and partially realizes the land of quiescent light (*nirabhāsa-prabhāsvara*). Second, non-retrogression of practice (*caryā*).

Once the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāva-kleśa*) have fallen away and the afflictions of the "dust-sand" (*rajas-aṇu*) are likewise destroyed, one is born into the land of skillful means (*upāya-bhūmi*) and advances toward the ultimate fruit.

Third, those who do not regress: they are born with their karmic burdens remaining in the Land of Common Residence (*sahā-loka-dhātu*), where they take form within a lotus flower and are forever separated from conditions for regression.

Fourth, those who ultimately do not regress: regardless of whether one’s mind is focused or distracted, conscious or unconscious, or whether one understands or does not understand—provided that the name of Amitābha or the names of the Buddhas of the six directions pass but once through the faculty of hearing.
If the name of the *Amitābha Sūtra* passes through one's ears even once, then even after ten million kalpas, one will ultimately attain liberation by means of it.
It is like hearing the sound of a drum smeared with poison: those far and near alike perish. Or it is like eating a small piece of diamond:
it is certain that it will not be digested.
Regarding the four-colored lotus flowers (*Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*): In the Land of Ultimate Bliss, there are ponds made of the seven treasures filled with water of eight meritorious qualities.
The bottom of these ponds is entirely covered with ground of golden sand. The steps and walkways on all four sides are composed of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal.
The lotus flowers within the ponds are as large as chariot wheels; those that are blue emit a blue light, and those that are yellow emit a yellow light.
Light: red flowers have red light; white flowers have white light. They are subtle, wondrous, fragrant, and pure. Blue flowers are named *utpala*;
yellow flowers are named *kumuda*; red flowers are named *padma*; white flowers are named *puṇḍarīka*.
These colors are necessarily accompanied by light, as they are produced through the influence of pure karma. This differs from the flowers of this world, which possess color but lack light.

Furthermore, regarding the four types of prayer beads (*akṣamālā*; *Vajraśekhara-yoga-akṣamālā-sūtra*): as for "prayer beads," the Buddha taught that sentient beings who wish to extinguish their afflictions (*kleśa*) should hold a counting rosary and constantly keep it with their person, focusing their minds single-pointedly on the names of the Buddhas; therefore, they are called "counting beads."
Regarding the degree of merit and the relative superiority or inferiority of these [rosaries], there are four distinct types.
One consisting of one thousand and eighty beads is the superior grade. This bead is considered superior because its number is great; if one holds this rosary...
Reciting the name of the Buddha brings supreme and superior merit and benefit. A rosary of one hundred and eight beads is the most excellent;

it is the most excellent because its number follows that of the superior grade. If one recites the name of the Buddha while holding this [rosary], the merit and benefit will be the most excellent. A rosary of fifty-four beads is of the middle grade. This rosary is...
The middle grade is so called because its number follows the preceding one; if one holds it while reciting the Buddha’s name, its merit and benefit constitute the middle grade.
Twenty-seven beads constitute the lower grade. This bead is considered the lower grade because its number follows the preceding one;
if one holds it while reciting the Buddha’s name, its merit and benefit [constitute the lower grade].
The lower grade. However, these are all distinguished into four grades based on the number of beads;
if one can maintain the recitation with single-minded devotion, then the merit will be equal and without distinction.
Fourth, one must not fail to prepare for the great matter. What is most urgent lies in that single stroke at the final moment.
That which was negligent in the past cannot be procrastinated now; that which was deluded in the past cannot be left in confusion now;
that which was superficial and ostentatious in the past cannot be feigned now; and that which has been a forked path in the past cannot be hesitated upon now.

Within this mere square inch, the luminous spirit presides. When awake, the lotus throne appears instantly; when deluded, there is the division between the six realms and the three miserable paths, with their respective purity and defilement.
In a single moment, one may take divergent paths—how perilous, how perilous! Ultimately, the essential secret for grasping this lies in nothing other than the right mindfulness of the one mind.
The Four Gates (as expounded by the Repentance Master Ciyun): First, the Gate of Prostration and Repentance:
To prostrate before the Buddhas and repent, thereby purifying karmic obstacles so that body and mind become as bright and pure as a fertile field. Second, the Gate of Mindfulness:

To uphold the sacred name, stabilize the mind to form practice, establish vows and set timeframes, and plant the primary cause for rebirth, like sowing seeds in the earth. Third, the Gate of Focusing on the Object...
These are the gates. They protect and nurture, causing the sprouts and stems to flourish as if by the pouring down of a drenching rain.
The fourth is the gate of manifold merit, which assists in bringing about luxuriant growth so that flowers and fruit may quickly be produced, as if by the irrigation with rich, fatty soil.
Although it is thus through these mutual conditions, if one has even a little leisure, practicing any single gate will suffice for rebirth.
The Four Teachings on the Severance of Thought (*Jingtu zhigui ji*): Now, the mind does not arise in isolation; it must necessarily depend upon conditions to arise.

When a practitioner recollects the Buddha, the faculty of mind serves as the cause, and the *ūrṇā-kośa* (the tuft of white hair between the eyebrows) of the Tathāgata serves as the condition. The thought thus produced is the dharma that arises.

To contemplate these three characteristics as shifting and moving, such that every moment of thought fails to abide and, when analyzed, is found to be empty—this is the *Zangjiao* (Tripitaka Teaching).

This is the mindfulness of the Buddha according to the Hīnayāna. That is to say, when the mind arises through the practice of contemplating the Buddha, both the subject that gives rise [to the thought] and the object that is given rise to are entirely empty.
To falsely claim that the mind arises, yet to realize its essence as empty—that is it. The marks of the Buddha being contemplated are like images in a mirror; there is neither Buddha nor mindfulness.

This is the mindfulness of the Buddha according to the Mahāyāna of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao). That is to say, the very arising of the mind in the contemplation of the Buddha is itself a provisional name (*prajñapti*).
The mind of provisional names clearly mirrors immeasurable names and characteristics; it realizes that this mind possesses the *tathāgatagarbha*.

Through kalpas of severing delusions and realizing truth, one departs from extremes to manifest the Middle Way, where there is neither Buddha nor thought—this is the *nien-fo* (Buddha-recollection) of the Distinct Teaching of the Mahayana.

Immediately upon contemplating the Buddha, the mind arises as the Immediate Emptiness, Immediate Provisionality, and Immediate Middle. Whether it be the sense faculties or their objects, all are the dust-motes and lands of the Dharma-realm.
In a single thought-moment, the Buddhas illuminate the sentient beings of the six realms, responding universally to the initial aspiration in an instant.

This is precisely the present initial awakening (ādikṣānti). It is like a person of great merit who holds a stone that becomes a jewel; there is no longer any thought of relinquishing it or seeking elsewhere for a state free from thought.

Being the center within the periphery, there is neither Buddha nor thought. This is the mindfulness of the Buddha (buddhānusmṛti) of the Perfect Teaching Mahāyāna, as clarified in the *Śrīgarbha-vyūha-sūtra* (Yíngluò jīng), which explains the sudden realization of the Tathāgata; this is that very dharma.
IV. Encouragement (From the *Longshu Jingtu Wen*): If people come to know this Dharma-gate of the Pure Land, it is as if they have known it themselves;
how joyful would that not be! If people do not know it, it is as if they themselves do not know it; how painful would that not be! Therefore, one can encourage others to cultivate the Pure Land.
By means of these wholesome conditions, one can eliminate and dissolve transgressions, increase merit and longevity, and bring about adornment.

It is suitable for the merit of rebirth in the Pure Land; it is also suitable for the posthumous dedication for the deceased. Provided one offers sincere prayers and vows, there are none who do not obtain their karmic fruits.
Regarding the Four Vows (as spoken by the Patriarch Cizhao): "If there is practice without vows, that practice will surely be solitary. If there are vows without practice..."

If vows are necessarily empty, there is neither practice nor vow; one dwells in emptiness within Jambudvīpa. If there is practice and there are vows, one enters directly into the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
This is the very foundation upon which Buddhas and patriarchs cultivate pure karma.
The Four-Character Instruction (Spoken by Great Master Da Xing): There is a four-character instruction for rebirth in the Pure Land:
namely, that the two characters "faith" (xìn) and "mindfulness" (yì) must not depart from the mind, and the two characters "recitation" (chēng) and "reverence" (jìng) must not depart from the mouth.

In general, one must possess faith; if one has faith in ten thousand [times], one will be born in ten thousand [lives]; if one has faith in a thousand, one will be born in a thousand [lives]. One must believe in the Buddha’s name and keep it inseparable from both mind and mouth.

The Buddhas will immediately rescue you; the Buddhas will immediately protect you. Constantly recollect the Buddha with the mind, constantly invoke the Buddha with the mouth, and constantly revere the Buddha with the body—this is what is called deep faith.
Whether at any time or at dawn, you shall ultimately never again dwell in the realm of Jambudvīpa.

The Four Methods of Cultivation (from Vasubandhu’s Commentary): These four methods of cultivation employ the practices of the three types of mental application and the five recollections to swiftly attain rebirth [in the Pure Land].
First is the Cultivation of Reverence. This consists of reverently prostrating before that Buddha and all the assembly of sages;
hence it is called the Cultivation of Reverence. Taking one's life as the limit, one vows not to cease [the practice]; this is the Cultivation of Constant Time. Second is the... [text fragment ends]

"Exclusive cultivation" refers to exclusively reciting the name of that Buddha, exclusively contemplating him, and exclusively prostrating to him, as well as praising that Buddha and all the assembly of sages, without intermingling other activities;
therefore, it is called exclusive cultivation. Taking the end of one's life as the limit and vowing not to cease is what constitutes "constant-time cultivation.
Third is "uninterrupted cultivation," which means continuously and reverently performing prostrations.
To recite the name, offer praise, maintain mindfulness and contemplation, and dedicate the merit while making vows— continuing this from heart to heart without interposing other activities—
is called "uninterrupted cultivation" (*nirantara-bhāvanā*). Furthermore, not allowing afflictions such as greed or anger to intervene,
but confessing immediately upon committing an offense so that no thought-moment, period of time, or day is left unbridged, ensuring constant purity, is also called "uninterrupted cultivation."
To complete one's life as the appointed term and vow never to desist constitutes "cultivation at all times. Fourth is "cultivation of dedication" (*pariṇāmanā-bhāvanā*):
this means that once a bodhisattva has escaped birth and death, they dedicate all the wholesome dharmas they have performed toward the fruit of Buddhahood; this is self-benefit.
To teach and transform sentient beings until the end of the future is benefit for others. However, the sentient beings of the present age are entirely afflicted by defilements.
Bound by fetters, one has not yet escaped the sufferings of the evil realms, birth and death, and so forth.

Following conditions to give rise to karmic activity, you should quickly turn all roots of goodness toward the vow to be reborn in the Land of Amitābha Buddha. Once you have reached that land, there will be no further fear.
Through these four practices mentioned above, self-benefit and benefit for others will naturally and effortlessly be fully perfected.
The four modes of birth (*catur-yoni*)—as described in the *Lianzong baojian*—are fully present within the single mind of the nine classes of sentient beings.

They are manifested according to one's actions as they arise: being shrouded by the darkness of ignorance constitutes egg-birth; being enveloped by afflictions (*kleśa*) constitutes womb-birth; being moistened by the waters of craving constitutes moisture-birth;
and the sudden arising of deluded thoughts constitutes transformation-birth. To awaken is to become a Buddha; to be deluded is to be called a sentient being. At the moment of death, one should...

When evil arises and the objects of the evil realms appear before you, and though you recite the Buddha's name, the Buddha-realm does not manifest of itself—if at such a time you cannot maintain self-mastery and are constantly driven by deluded thoughts and inverted views, then at the moment the wind and fire of dissolution scatter and destroy you, you will be like a crab falling into boiling water;
how then could you possibly exercise mastery? At that time, you should reflect to yourself: "I am now practicing..."
To practice pure karma is fundamentally for the sake of transcending birth and death. How could the teachings bequeathed by the Buddhas and Patriarchs deceive us?
One should rely upon the True Dharma and maintain a sincere mind, single-mindedly reciting the name of Amitābha and abandoning all that is false and delusive.

Contemplating this morning and evening, with every thought aspiring to be born in the Western Land—doing so, the karmic consciousness of worldly toil will instantly disintegrate and vanish like ice melting away. Upon reflecting inwardly upon oneself...
Since one's own birth and death cannot even be apprehended, what then can be called a "sentient being"? Therefore, the *Sānchan* (Repentance) text says:

"Within a single thought-moment, one attains the Buddha-remembrance Samādhi (*buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*), universally delivering all sentient beings of the six realms throughout the ten directions, so that each may emerge from the wheel of suffering and be born together in the Pure Land. This is precisely what that means.
Fourth, [as stated in the *Pure Land Morning Bell*]: sentient beings are ignorant and deluded.
They believe that formal acts are of great power, yet they do not believe that the power of formless intention is even greater. Why is this? The power of intention is the root of all action;
no undertaking is accomplished without it. Therefore, what one intends is of the utmost urgency, just as water must flow toward the sea, or as fire...
It must blaze upward; it is like a sharp blade that must wound, or like a poisonous drug that must kill—there is no passing by in vain.
The mindfulness of the Buddha is likewise so. How could one practice the mindfulness of the Buddha and yet the Buddha not appear?
One should know that the power of mindfulness is the king among all dharmas.
The Four Kinds of Filial Piety (*Jingtu chenzhong*). There are three kinds of worldly filial piety and one kind of world-transcending filial piety.
As for the first type of worldly filial piety: it is to nourish one’s parents with delicious food and drink. The second is to bring honor to one’s parents through rank and emolument.

The third is to cultivate virtue and exert oneself in conduct, attaining the state of a sage or worthy to bring glory to one’s parents. These are what the world calls filial piety. World-transcending...

Regarding worldly filial piety: one should exhort one’s parents to observe the fasts and precepts, to uphold the Way, and with single-minded devotion to recite the Buddha’s name, seeking rebirth in the Pure Land and to behold Amitābha in person so as to attain the stage of non-retrogression.
For a child to repay their parents, there is nothing greater than this. While the parents are still living in the hall, one should encourage them early on to recite the Buddha’s name;
when the parents pass away, one should maintain the practice for three years. For those who are unable to do so, they may do so for one year.
At one year of age, or even at forty-nine days, it is all acceptable.

(From *The Direct Pointing to Mindfulness of the Buddha*, Section on Precepts, Understanding, Practice, and Direction) Now, precepts, understanding, practice, and direction must necessarily arise from the vow; only then will one be born in the Pure Land.

What is meant by a person who practices the precepts? Once one has cultivated samādhi, if one does not maintain the precepts, then even though one possesses faith, for that reason... [one is still subject to] the world.

In the interim, one is defiled by adverse conditions; they encroach upon and plunder one another. Worldly afflictions are difficult to dispel, destroying the Dharma-body and causing those who understand to fall into error, thereby preventing them from attaining rebirth there.
As the Sūtra says: "If for even a single day and night one upholds the śrāmaṇera precepts or the full set of precepts, one shall immediately attain rebirth.
Therefore, one must certainly uphold the precepts. What is meant by a "practitioner of liberation"? One who cultivates this...

Samādhi. If one seeks birth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, yet does not employ this profound wisdom and subtle understanding to know that the two lands—the pure and the defiled—stand as adversaries facing east and west, truly and without error;

and furthermore, if one does not know that these very two lands, pure and defiled, are entirely contained within my own mind and do not depart from the present moment—by what dharma can one practice so as to attain birth there? As the sutra says: "Recite and chant the Mahāyāna."
One attains rebirth only by understanding the ultimate truth; therefore, one must certainly achieve correct understanding. What is meant by "practice"?

When a practitioner seeks rebirth in the Pure Land, once their wisdom and understanding are correct, they must establish practice based upon that understanding, performing the path during the six periods of the day.
With the three karmas free from deficiency, one should advance directly without retreating, firmly vowing to be born there. As the Sutra says:
"By practicing the six mindfulnesses, dedicating merit, and making vows for one day up to seven days, one shall immediately attain rebirth. Therefore, one must certainly establish these practices.
What is meant by "dedication" (*pariṇāmanā*)? It refers to the practitioner’s desire for certain rebirth.

One dedicates all merits arising from such precepts, understanding, and practice—both those of the present moment and those from beginningless time, including all roots of goodness, whether great or small—to the Pure Land.
Thus, at the time of death, one attains certain rebirth there. As the Sūtra says: "Dedicate [merit] with the aspiration to be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss."
For example, it is like performing tasks for a household; one must return home to make use of them. Therefore, one must certainly cultivate dedication (*pariṇāmanā*).
The meaning of these four great dharma-gates in a single phrase is able to encompass all wholesome dharmas.

For example, just as the grains and fruits that ripen during the four seasons each depend on their essential requirements, and if even one is missing, they will not form, so too it is with these four dharma-gates. If...
If one of these is lost, samādhi will not be accomplished.
Regarding the five ways of reverently practicing the Dharma (*Gānlù shū*): first, reverence for the Buddha with whom one has a karmic connection;

whether walking, standing, sitting, lying down, or attending to the necessities of nature, one always faces the west. Second, reverence for the image-teachings with which one has a karmic connection; one should set up an image of Amitābha.
And to uphold their teachings; third, to respectfully honor teachers and friends with whom one has a karmic connection, because of the need for respectful intimacy;

fourth, to respectfully honor fellow practitioners—that is, those who cultivate pure karma together—because they mutually encourage and benefit one another; and fifth, to always respectfully honor the Triple Gem, as it is the supreme condition for one’s rebirth.
By practicing such reverence, one will certainly attain rebirth there.
Five Kinds of Non-retrogression (*Wubutui*, *Jingtu Shiyi Lun*): First, non-retrogression through being sustained by Great Compassion.
This means that sentient beings who attain birth in the Pure Land are sustained and not abandoned by the power of Amitābha Buddha’s great compassionate vows; therefore, they attain non-retrogression.
Second, non-retrogression through being illuminated by the Buddha’s light. This means that sentient beings who attain birth in the Pure Land are constantly... [text continues]
The Buddha’s light shines and illuminates them; thus, their bodhicitta increases day by day, and they do not regress.

Third, they never cease hearing the sound of the Dharma: those sentient beings born in the Pure Land hear the sounds of the various water birds, trees, forests, winds, and musical instruments all preaching the Dharma of suffering, emptiness, and non-self. Therefore, they constantly give rise to mindfulness of the Buddha.
The mind that recollects the Dharma and the Sangha does not regress. Fourth, one dwells with virtuous friends without regressing;
this means that sentient beings who attain birth in the Pure Land do so because that land consists entirely of bodhisattvas, who serve as their supreme friends.
Internally, there is no burden of afflictions, delusions, or karma; externally, there is no realm of demonic interference or adverse conditions.
Therefore, after one birth, one immediately attains non-retrogression. Fifth is the non-retrogression of immeasurable lifespan:
it means that all sentient beings who attain birth in the Pure Land immediately obtain an immeasurable lifespan, equal and non-dual with that of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. Thus.
After one lifetime, one will immediately attain non-retrogression.

Regarding the Five Gates of Mindfulness (from Vasubandhu’s Treatise): for those who aspire to be born in that land, they are exhorted to practice the Five Gates of Mindfulness; if these are fully possessed, one will certainly attain birth there.
The first is the Gate of Bodily Worship: this means to single-mindedly and exclusively focus one's intent, reverently joining [the palms].
With palms joined, offer incense and flowers in worship, and pay homage to that Amitābha Buddha.

"Homage" here refers specifically to paying homage solely to that Buddha, vowing to do so until the end of one's life without intermingling it with other forms of prostration. Second is the gate of verbal praise:
this consists of single-mindedly recollecting and praising the physical marks and radiance of that Buddha’s body, the physical marks and radiance of all the holy assemblies, and that land.
Second, because of the equal radiance of all jewel adornments. Third, the gate of mental action consisting of recollection and observation:

that is, to focus the mind single-mindedly on the physical marks and radiance of that Buddha and the entire assembly of sages, as well as the adornments of the land, as described in the *Contemplation Sūtra*.
Except for the time of sleep, one should constantly recollect, constantly remember, constantly contemplate, and constantly observe.
Because these matters are equal. Fourth is the gate of making vows (*praṇidhāna*).

This means that with a focused mind, whether by day or by night, at all times and in all places, regarding the merits performed through the three karmas and four modes of conduct, one must—at the beginning, middle, or end—sincerely make a vow from within the heart to be born in that land. Fifth is the gate of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*). This means that with a focused...

With my own mind, I generate roots of goodness; and regarding all roots of goodness performed by those of the three vehicles and five paths—each and every ordinary person and sage—I give rise to deep sympathetic joy (*anumodana*). Just as the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas give rise to sympathetic joy, so too do I.
By means of these roots of goodness from sympathetic joy, together with the roots of goodness I have myself performed, I offer them all to the assembly.
One shares this with all beings. Because one dedicates [the merit] toward that land, upon arriving there, one attains the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*).

Returning to the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), one teaches and transforms sentient beings until the very end of time, never feeling weary or satisfied, even until the attainment of Buddhahood.
This is called the gate of dedication (*pariṇāmanā-mukha*).

Regarding the five delusions (as explained by Chan Master Changlu Ze): "Whether the conditions for practice are present or not—if those of shallow faith in the Western [Pure Land] school give rise to groundless doubts and slanders, I shall venture to discuss this:
among the people of this land, there are none who do not loathe the clamor and vexation of the secular home and yearn for the tranquility of an araṇya.
Therefore, when someone abandons their home to leave the household life, they praise it with earnest devotion; yet, in the Sahā world..."
Amidst manifold sufferings, how could there be more than the clamor and vexation of a lay home? In the leisurely ease of Ultimate Bliss, how could it be merely the tranquility of an araṇya?
To recognize the excellence of leaving the household life yet not wish to be reborn there—this is the first delusion. To toil with hardship across ten thousand li...
They travel far to seek out a spiritual mentor (*kalyāṇamitra*) to clarify the Great Matter and resolve the questions of life and death;

yet, while the World-Honored Amitābha possesses supreme physical and mental karma and a vast, profound power of vows—such that a single utterance of his perfect voice leaves nothing unilluminated or unharmonized—they instead wish to attend upon a mentor and do not desire to see the Buddha.
This is their second delusion. Furthermore, while the great assemblies in the monasteries all delight in finding rest there, those with few followers [seek] the Way...
