To wish not to rely upon [the Sangha], yet to desire that those in the Land of Ultimate Bliss who are in their final birth before Buddhahood (*ekajātipratibaddha*)—who are exceedingly numerous—and all the superior virtuous ones (*sādhu-puruṣa*) should gather together in one place;
to wish to be in close proximity to the forest [of the Sangha], yet not to admire the pure assembly of the ocean-like multitude—this is the third delusion.
The people of this land do not exceed a hundred years in maximum lifespan, yet they are [afflicted] by childhood ignorance and old age.

In old age and amidst successive illnesses, one dwells in a state of stupor and sleep for more than half the time. Even Bodhisattvas remain obscured by the "shading of the womb," and Śrāvakas still lack clarity upon emerging from it.
Thus, of every inch of jade and every moment of time, nine-tenths are lost before one attains the stage of non-retrogression—this is truly cause for heart-rending anxiety.
As for the people of the Western Land, their lifespan is immeasurable; once they take refuge within the lotus calyx, there is no further [rebirth].

The suffering of death continues without interruption until one reaches Bodhi; this may be called attaining *avaivartika* (non-retrogression), for the stage of Buddhahood can then be expected with certainty.
Yet, while the fleeting moments of the Sahā world pass away, one remains lost in the Pure Land for a long time. This is the fourth delusion.

As for those whose rank is non-retrogressive and who have realized the fruit of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), they are free from desire even amidst desire and dwell within the dust of the world.

Only when one is free from defilement can one give rise to objectless compassion (*anālambana-maitrī*) and exercise coessential pity (*sahaja-karuṇā*), returning to enter the realm of worldly toil (*saṃsāra*) and harmonize with the light amidst the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*).
Yet, those who have heard only superficially or possess but single-minded wisdom, or who associate with minor virtues, may claim to have forever emerged from the four currents (*catasra oghāḥ*).
They claim to have transcended the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) and revile the Pure Lands, while remaining attached to this Sahā world;

thus they close their eyes and return in vain, wandering aimlessly as if side-by-side with oxen and horses, following in the footsteps of hell-beings. Unaware that this is their own condition, they compare themselves to Bodhisattvas of Great Power (*mahopāya-kauśalya*). This is their fifth delusion.
The Five Inconceivables (Expounded by Master Ouyi): By means of faith, aspiration, and the holding of the Name, one directly ascends to the stage of non-retrogression.
There are five points of inconceivability: first, transcending the three realms horizontally, as there is no need to wait for the severance of afflictions;

second, the four lands are horizontally present within the Western Pure Land itself, rather than being realized through gradual stages; third, merely holding the Name, without relying on meditative contemplation.
Because of these various skillful means, the period required is four, one, or seven [lifetimes]; it does not depend upon many kalpas, many births, or many years and months.
Fifth, by upholding the name of a single Buddha, one is immediately protected and remembered by all Buddhas; this is no different from upholding the names of all Buddhas.

(From *The Morning Bell of the Pure Land*): Now that we have fortunately attained this favorable time, we are unwilling to practice; yet when we encounter unfavorable circumstances, we cannot help but practice.
When in a state of prosperity, we are unwilling to practice; yet when we encounter adversity, we cannot help but practice.
When free from illness and pain, we are unwilling to practice; yet when our illness becomes grave and we are on the verge of death, we cannot help but practice. While we are in the prime of youth...
One is unwilling to recite [the name] now; yet when one reaches old age and decline, it cannot be dispensed with. Even as the eyes grow dim and one is about to die, one is unwilling to recite;
yet when turning over to enter the coffin, at the time of burial and the funeral rites, it cannot be dispensed with. While the breath still remains—why not recite?
Without knowing or realizing it, one suddenly utters the name of the Buddha from within the mouth. This is because one has a karmic affinity with the Buddha;
one only fears that the seven-foot body may suddenly fall across or that the three-inch tongue may easily break before this single phrase of "Buddha" can be fully recited.
Therefore, by means of ten recitations at the moment of death, one immediately attains rebirth in the Pure Land.
Regarding the Five Dhyānas (as explained by the Great Master Zhiyi): When the practitioner contemplates the Buddha, dwelling the mind upon a single object, it is called "dhyāna of concentrated mind.
This is because one clearly contemplates the Tathāgata’s jade-like brow-hair and golden marks, which are stilled and tranquil, for they are luminous and penetrate the subtle.

Furthermore, although the mind was previously concentrated, as the practice has not yet become habitual, one may unconsciously allow it to wander and scatter; now, one restrains it and causes it to return, clearly contemplating the gold.

This is called the dhyāna of restraining the mind. Furthermore, although restraining the mind achieves concentration, as it is not contemplation according to principle (*yoniśo-manasikāra*), it belongs entirely to the cultivation of phenomena (*dharma-prayoga*).
Now, realizing that the essence is fundamentally empty, who is there to concentrate and who is there to restrain? With neither Buddha nor thought, this is called the dhyāna of realizing the essence.
Furthermore, although the previous stage realized the essence, one still remained stuck in empty stillness; the infinite names and marks were obscurely unknown. Now, by means of non-...

Having attained this, one employs skillful means (*upāya*). Entering from emptiness into the provisional, one thoroughly illuminates the myriad dharmas and is no longer deluded or disturbed by the dust of emptiness;

this is called the dhyāna of skillful means. Furthermore, although previously one realized the reality (*tattva*) and employed skillful means, each remained based on either emptiness or existence, not departing from the two extremes.
Now, one observes that both stillness and agitation are fundamentally devoid of characteristics, such that the path of names and words is cut off.
When all conceptualizations are forgotten, it is called the "Dhyāna that Quells Discrimination Between the Two Extremes.

Fifth, [it is like] the morning bell of the Pure Land: now that a person inevitably faces evening after morning, cold after heat, youth inevitably leads to maturity, maturity to old age, and old age inevitably to death; from antiquity to the present it has been thus. If indeed...
If one makes plans for the morning but not for the evening, or for the summer heat but not for the winter cold, people will surely mock him as a fool.
Yet from childhood until middle age, and even into old age as one approaches death, one does not know to make such plans—is this not folly even more extreme?
When one suddenly comes into being, grows up in a state of dullness, and finally declines into old age and death—how deluded!
Vibrant and buoyant, yet one is boundlessly submerged in the river of affection and the sea of desire; endlessly dragged by the tether of fame and the shackles of profit.
In a single instant, all turns cold as ash; the fire is passed and the fuel changed—this is the final move at the end of one’s life.
Who can escape this? From now on, through death after death and birth after birth, one wanders through the six realms and the three miserable paths like a turning waterwheel.
Day by day, one pursues the karma of birth and death without seeking the means to liberation; it may be said that such a person pities others yet does not fear death themselves.
Those who truly fear death will surely seek the means to liberate themselves from birth and death. If...
If one seeks liberation, why abandon mindfulness of the Buddha? What other path could one follow? If one abandons the Pure Land, with whom can I return?
(From *The Morning Bell of the Pure Land*) Human life is like a bubble on water; birth and death are impermanent. Moreover, there is nothing in this world that is not suffering.
Should the great limit of one’s life suddenly arrive, how could the evils committed throughout one’s lifetime possibly be entirely absent? Furthermore, regarding the present moment...

To speak of it: to give rise to a single improper thought, to utter a single improper word, to look upon a single improper sight, to hear a single improper sound, or to perform a single improper deed—none of these fail to be faults and evils. How much more so for that which is eaten, which is the flesh of sentient beings;
and that which is worn, which is likewise obtained by killing sentient beings. Furthermore, how much more so regarding all the faults and evils that do not stop at this alone?

To eat meat and wear silk—when one reflects upon this, it is truly fearsome. After closing one's eyes [at death], one cannot avoid departing according to the conditions of one's karma, with no time of escape in sight.
Only the Western Pure Land is the most transcendent and direct path. A physical body is difficult to obtain;
while you are in good health, prepare for this great matter.
The Five Meanings (from the *Ratnarāja-śāstra*): Now, the essential point for dispersing [distractions] lies in the voice. If the voice is not stern, the mind will become trivial and flighty;

there is no fixed way for the voice to achieve such sternness. It is like pulling up the thatch by its roots—the one root being pulled out causes the others to follow in succession. Therefore, one must urge on the voice from behind.
To bring one’s life to its end in a single moment and forever bid farewell to a hundred anxieties—this is the first meaning. To look for it in what is near:
wherever its fame and radiance reach, ten thousand calamities melt away like ice, and the forest of merit flourishes as the pines grow lush across a thousand mountains—this is the second meaning.

To explain it from a distance: the golden countenance blazes forth, scattering the luster of precious flowers; they rain down with a glistening sound through the void, as if pointing directly at them.
All these sounds reach the palms. This is its third meaning. It is like pulling wood or stone that is heavy and will not move forward;

yet when a great sound issues forth as a proclamation, it is lifted up lightly and effortlessly. This is its fourth meaning. When waging war against the armies of Māra, the banners and drums face one another.
To employ the principles of prosody within the military chariot to ensure victory over powerful enemies—this is the fifth meaning. Possessing all these various meanings, what more could one desire?
Yet, this does not equal the perfection of both the bustling and the tranquil, the simultaneous application of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, which accords with the intent of the Buddha.
Is this not also appropriate?

In the *Lianzong baojian*, it is stated that by upholding the single phrase "Amitābha Buddha," within a single thought-moment, one accords with principle (*li*), all phenomena manifest before one, and the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) are fully realized. In giving, the mind is free from attachment; in maintaining the precepts...
One does not give rise to false conditions. Through patience, both subject and object are forgotten; through diligence, the mind is uninterrupted;
through meditative concentration, both movement and stillness are quiescent; and through wisdom, not even a hair’s breadth of conceptualization is established.
The Six Paramitas (as explained by Master Ouyi): To truly be able to practice nianfo (mindfulness of the Buddha) while letting go of body, mind, and the world is itself great generosity (*dāna*).

To truly be able to practice nianfo without again giving rise to greed, anger, or delusion is great observance of the precepts (*śīla*). To truly be able to practice nianfo without calculating right and wrong or self and others is great patience (*kṣānti*).

To truly be able to practice nianfo without even the slightest interruption or admixture [of other thoughts] is... [great vigor]. To truly be able to practice nianfo without being distracted by external objects is great meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). To truly be able to practice nianfo without harboring doubts or false views is great wisdom (*prajñā*).
This is great diligence: truly being able to practice mindfulness of the Buddha, no longer wandering in vain thoughts or pursuits. This is great meditative concentration (*samādhi*):
truly being able to practice mindfulness of the Buddha, not being deluded by other paths. This is great wisdom: try to examine yourself;

if body, mind, and the world have not yet been relinquished, and if thoughts of greed, anger, and ignorance still arise, or notions of right and wrong, and self and others persist—[then you have not yet attained these].

One still harbors lingering attachments; intermittent and mixed-up thoughts have not yet been entirely eliminated; discursive thoughts continue to pursue objects and have not yet been forever extinguished;
and various divergent paths can still delude the will. If this is the case, it does not constitute true mindfulness of the Buddha.
Six Kinds of Mindfulness (The Morning Bell of the Pure Land): To practice mindfulness of the Buddha with sincerity, one must possess six kinds of mindfulness.
First is courageous mindfulness. One must not be overly weak-willed; rather, one should be like a filial son seeking to avenge a deep grievance against his parents.
Even if it means traversing high cliffs, deep ravines, ghostly paths, or tiger dens, one must go forth without fear. Second is mindful compassion. One must not be overly detached... [text continues]

First, when he contemplates the Buddha, the hairs on his body all stand on end and his five internal organs feel as if they would tear apart, just like a young child remembering a compassionate mother who has turned her back on him, or an intelligent son mourning for his deceased father.

Thus, he feels a sense of poignant indignation; he thinks that the Great Peace has come, yet he cannot attain it, remaining like a failed candidate, solitary and impoverished, burdened by talent yet left in silence.
Every time he brings this to mind, he is nearly unable to go on living; thus, he feels a sense of longing and attachment.
It is because [the mind] is so utterly detached that it cannot regard even its most deeply cherished objects as its own;

though its soul and dreams are bound to them and it fears losing them, when a single object of pleasure appears before it, it leaps with joy and delight, like one who, cold, finds clothing, or one who, hungry, finds food.
Therefore, when a single adverse condition meets you, one should feel such intense regret and remorse as if having escaped from the jaws of death.
Thus, with mind and mouth as one, every word must flow forth from the very marrow of one's bones; only then is this the true state of mindfulness of the Buddha.

The six sense organs (*ṣaḍāyatana*)—adorned in a thousand ways—are for the sake of the eye, which is but half an inch; the hundred kinds of music are for the sake of the ear, which is but the size of a bean;
the sandalwood, aloeswood, and musk are for the sake of the two nostrils; the food spread over ten cubits are for the sake of the tongue, which is but three inches;
and the exquisite, beautiful, and charming forms are for the sake of this body, which is but foul and putrid. To follow after these...
To "meet and welcome" [the senses] is simply a state of wild dissipation. If one can discern this through and through, there will be no cause for affliction.
Because these six sense faculties exist, immeasurable matters arise and immeasurable karma is created. Therefore, it is like the kalpa-fire burning all worlds.
If one awakens to this principle, although one has not yet been born in the Pure Land, one is already as if born there.

The Sixfold Faith (as expounded by Master Ouyi): 1. **Faith in Oneself**: One believes that the single thought-moment of one's own present mind is fundamentally neither a physical lump of flesh nor a mere shadow of conditions.
Vertically, it has no beginning or end; horizontally, it is beyond all boundaries. Although it follows conditions throughout the day, it never changes.
The empty space of the ten directions and the lands as numerous as motes of dust have always been manifested within the single thought-moment of my own mind.

...of things. Although I am now confused, deluded, and inverted, if I can but turn my mind for a single thought, I will certainly attain birth within my own heart, where the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss is inherently present; of this there is no further doubt. This is called "faith in oneself.
Second, faith in others: one believes that Śākyamuni Tathāgata certainly has no deceptive speech, and that Amitābha Bhagavat certainly has no falsehoods.
Vow: The Buddhas of the six directions extend their broad and long tongues; their words are never double.
Following the true instructions of all Buddhas, I resolve to seek birth [in the Pure Land] without further doubt. This is called "faith through others. Third, faith in the cause:

I have deep faith that even calling the Name amidst distraction serves as the seed for attaining Buddhahood; how much more so when the mind is single-minded and undisturbed? How could one not attain it?

This is not a cause for the Pure Land; it is called the cause of faith. Regarding the four fruits of faith: one has deep faith that the gathering of supreme virtues in the Pure Land is entirely born from the samādhi of mindfulness of the Buddha.
It is, for example, like planting melon seeds and obtaining melons, or planting bean seeds and obtaining beans.
It is also like a shadow that must follow a form, or an echo that must respond to a sound; it can never be in vain. This is called the fruit of faith.
Regarding the five matters of faith: one has deep faith that the single thought-moment of the present is inexhaustible.
Therefore, all the worlds of the ten directions manifested by the mind are likewise inexhaustible. Truly, there exists the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Beyond hundreds of thousands of billions of lands lies a realm of supreme purity and adornment; this is not like the allegorical fictions of Zhuangzi.

This is called "faith in the facts. Sixth, regarding "faith in the principle": one has deep faith that although the Land of Ultimate Bliss is situated at a distance of hundreds of thousands of billions of lands, it does not, in reality, lie outside of this very present, infinitesimal thought-moment of my own mind.

The nature of my present single thought-moment has no reality outside of itself. Furthermore, I have deep faith that the Western Pure Land—whether its environment or its inhabitants, whether its Lord or his retinue—is entirely a reflection manifested within the wondrous, luminous, and true mind of my present single thought-moment.

The entirety of phenomena is identical to principle; the entirety of delusion is identical to truth; the entirety of cultivation is identical to nature; and the entirety of the other is identical to oneself. It is my own mind.
Because [the nature] is all-pervasive, the Buddha-mind is also all-pervasive. Because the Buddha-mind is all-pervasive, the mind-nature of all sentient beings is also all-pervasive.
It is like a thousand lamps in a single room: their lights mutually pervade one another, interpenetrating in successive layers without mutual obstruction. This is called "faith in the principle."

Sixth, one must not harbor the hope (as addressed in the *Wen Jingtu Ji*) that one may commit evil throughout a lifetime and yet attain rebirth in the Pure Land by reciting the Buddha’s name at the moment of death.

To be reborn while still carrying the burden of one's karmic offenses is possible only because one has possessed roots of goodness and the causes and conditions of merit from previous lives, thereby meeting a spiritual teacher (*kalyāṇamitra*) who can exhort one to practice mindfulness of the Buddha.

Such a stroke of fortune occurs but once in ten thousand cases. If one falls ill and approaches death, the "wind-blade" will dismember the body and the four elements will separate. At that time, the multitude...
Oppressed by suffering, one is frantic and terrified, unable to recite the Buddha’s name. Even if you were to die free from illness,
or if worldly affairs remain unfinished and worldly attachments have not ceased— such that the fear of life and death agitates the mind— if you are a layperson,
you will further be troubled by unsettled family matters and unattended funeral arrangements, with your wife weeping and children crying amidst a hundred kinds of anxieties.

When you are ill, you cannot recite the Buddha’s name. Even granting that before you die you have only slight ailments upon your body, you must endure the pain and suffering, crying out and groaning, seeking medicine and physicians, praying and repenting;
with such distracting thoughts flying about, you cannot recite the Buddha’s name. Furthermore, even granting that before you were ill you were merely advanced in years...
The signs of decay appear before you; you are exhausted and frail, filled with lamentation, sorrow, and affliction.

You can do nothing but arrange yourself on this aging body, unable to recite the Buddha’s name. Furthermore, even if it were before you grew old—when you were in the prime of youth—[you would still be unable to do so].
Precisely at the time one should be mindful of the Buddha, if the wild mind has not yet ceased, or if one is entangled in worldly affairs,
climbing here and clinging there, with distracted and chaotic thoughts, the karmic consciousness will be vast and murky, and one will be unable to practice mindfulness of the Buddha.
Furthermore, even if you are free and at ease, and possess the resolve to cultivate practice, if you cannot see through the appearances of the world, cannot let go of them, or cannot set them aside—
In meditative concentration, while sitting without interruption, suddenly a slight state of objective perception manifests before you.
The one master [of the mind] follows along with these delusions and cannot practice the Buddha-recitation. Try observing this during times of old age and illness;
even on days of youth and leisure, if there is even a single matter lingering in the mind, it is already impossible to practice Buddha-recitation—how much more so when waiting for the time of death?

Regarding the six purities (from the *Jingtu zhigui ji*): although the fundamental awakening (*benjue*) of sentient beings in the nine realms is inherently pure, as long as they have not heard the Great Dharma of the Perfect and Sudden, they remain defiled by the impurities of mind and land.

If sentient beings, with a pure faith, resolve to be reborn there, because their minds are focused, they shall see the Land of Bliss—its lotus ponds, jeweled trees, and pure environment—not departing from the present moment of thought. This...
For one at the stage of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*) who attends to names, the mind is pure and the land is pure. Thus the Sūtra says:

"Upon hearing me speak of the long duration of my lifespan, those who believe and understand with a profound mind shall see the Buddha constantly on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, surrounded by a great assembly of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas, preaching the Dharma.
This refers to the purity of the land through skillful means (*upāya*). If one destroys fundamental ignorance (*mūlāvidyā*), [the land is purified].

Ascending to the stage of the Ten Abidings, one realizes the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). This person belongs to the stage of partial truth; their mind is pure and their land is pure. As a sutra says:
"Furthermore, one sees this Sahā world, its ground made of lapis lazuli, level and even, with all the assemblies of bodhisattvas dwelling therein.
This is the purity of the Land of Real Retribution. If one ascends to the stage of Sublime Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), wisdom and severance are perfected.
These are the sages of the ultimate fruit; their minds are pure and their lands are pure. As the sutra says:
"Only Buddha and Buddha can fully exhaustively realize the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena. Śākyamuni is named Vairocana, pervading all places.

The dwelling place of that Buddha is called the Constant, Tranquil Light (*nitya-śānta-prabhā*), which is the nirvāṇa of the three virtues: permanence, bliss, self, and purity. This is the abode of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas.
Only when one dwells in such a place can it truly be called the ultimate purity of the mind and the purity of the Buddha-land.

Ignorant and worldly people, being deluded and lacking knowledge, claim that ordinary beings on the mundane ground can, without cultivation or realization, become identical to the Buddha’s purity. This is like commoners falsely styling themselves emperors;
they bring about their own destruction. What crime is greater than this slander of the Dharma?

The Sixfold Cultivation (Zheng Qingzhi’s *Exhortation to Practice the Pure Land*): When reciting the Buddha's name, if one chants with the mouth while contemplating with the mind, "Commit no evil"—is this not the Precepts?

If one fixes the mind on the pure realm until illusory objects are extinguished—this is not it the Concentration? If one contemplates that there is truly no contemplation and the lotus of the mind becomes serene—this is not it the Wisdom?
If a person can eliminate myriad anxieties and direct their single intent toward the Western Paradise, then they need not be struck with the staff.
"Ha!"—and thus one awakens to the capacity for the Perfect and Sudden [Teaching]. Without perusing the Great Canon, one attains the Eye of the True Dharma;
without maintaining the four modes of deportment, one attains great sovereignty. Neither defiled nor pure, neither bound nor liberated—at such a time, what are precepts, concentration, and wisdom?
What are meditation, doctrine, and discipline? My mind and the Buddha-mind are entirely without distinction.
This is the ultimate attainment of Pure Land cultivation.
Regarding the Six Medicines (*Fubao Zhinan*), the practice of *nianfo* consists solely in keeping the mind undistracted; there is no other method.
It is like using medicine to treat an illness: the patient merely looks at the medicine with their eyes and holds it in their hand, or perhaps brings it close to their nose.

Upon hearing of medicine, there are even more distant methods: storing the medicine in a vessel, soaking it in water, or boiling it with fire—all while saying, "I am using this medicine to treat the illness.
When the illness is not cured, they further claim, "This medicine is ineffective.
To repeatedly select such medical texts is truly pitiable; yet others cannot act on their behalf.

As for this drinking [of medicine], what can be done about it? Furthermore, if one merely seeks to complete the count of tens of thousands [of pills], this is simply a matter of buying medicine while refusing to take it at all.
Even if one were to accumulate such medicine until it resembles a hill or a mound, could the illness ever be cured?

Medicine is drunk with the mouth, whereas the Buddha is recited with the mind. Medicine must necessarily enter drop by drop through the mouth; the Buddha must necessarily enter sound by sound from the [lips].
It emerges from within the mind; this is the method for attaining true meditative concentration.

Regarding the seven kinds of excellence (from the *Amṛta-ṭīkā*): the merit of recollecting the Buddha possesses seven kinds of excellence. First, the excellence of having few words and being easy to practice.
First, by reciting even a single phrase of "Namo Amitābha Buddha," all people may practice mindfulness. Second, mindfulness through the object of the Buddha is superior;

with a single mind, one takes the Buddha’s physical marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) and the Pure Land as the object of contemplation. Third, it is superior for escaping calamities and attaining peace;
the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas protect those who practice mindfulness, so that they are free from all afflictions and hardships, remaining peaceful, joyful, and auspicious.
I. Excellence in the Extinction of Sin through Reciting the Name: A single recitation of the Buddha’s name extinguishes the heavy sins of birth and death accumulated over eighty billion kalpas.

II. Excellence in the Attainment of Merit through Sustained Recitation: A single invocation of the Buddha’s name surpasses the offering of the seven treasures of the four continents to the Buddhas and Arhats.
III. Excellence in the Realization of the Resulting Vision of the Buddha: Sentient beings who practice mindfulness of the Buddha will certainly behold the Buddha. Seven...
The merit of personally escorting [the deceased] to rebirth is superior. Transformation Buddhas and Bodhisattvas emit light to welcome the practitioner and lead them to rebirth in a Buddha-land.
(Master Lianchi on the Seven Right Mindfulnesses): One who truly leaves the home life for the sake of birth and death must desire to accomplish their goal in a single lifetime.
At all times, they should use these seven matters to admonish themselves and strive to maintain them. First, one must not accumulate wealth or build houses.

Do not harbor lingering attachment to the purchase of fields, nor to the acquisition of all manner of exquisite objects—such as scriptures and images—that have been handed down from antiquity or originate from renowned families.
With single-minded right mindfulness, you must not engage in various secondary meritorious activities that are not of primary importance.
Wait for the time when the great matter has been clarified; it will not be too late to perform them then. For now, simply set them aside.

Setting aside the gateway of the myriad practices, maintain single-minded right mindfulness. Third, do not give rise to a mind of greedy attachment toward beautiful forms, delicious flavors, and the like;

do not give rise to a mind of greedy attachment toward those who speak pleasant words and praise me. Do not give rise to a mind of anger and vexation toward ugly forms, unpalatable flavors, and the like;
do not [give rise to such a mind] toward those who speak ill of me, who revile me, or who insult me in various ways.
If anyone should offend or oppose me, I shall give rise to a mind of anger and vexation;

furthermore, regarding matters of the past or future, whether favorable or unfavorable, I shall completely set them aside and maintain a firm defense, keeping my mind focused on right mindfulness alone. Fourth, one must not compose poems or literary works.
1. Do not engage in calligraphy, whether in regular, cursive, or semi-cursive scripts; do not compose inscriptions or couplets; do not polish formal letters. 2. Do not peruse external secular texts;

do not discuss the gains and losses or the strengths and weaknesses of others. 3. Do not rely on mere personal opinions to teach or compose works with an arrogant mind; do not recklessly attempt to critique or evaluate [the teachings] when your own Zen realization is not yet thorough.
4. Seal your mouth and remain tongue-tied; maintain a single-minded focus on right mindfulness. 5. Do not associate with these five things.

When attending to invitations from relatives and friends, traveling to mountains to enjoy the scenery, engaging in miscellaneous talk and idle conversation, or dealing with various worldly matters—save for those tasks that must be resolved through principle and cannot be avoided—one should cease all other activities.

With single-minded right mindfulness, one must not indulge in greed, attachment, or negligence, nor yield to excessive sleep; for until the Great Matter is clarified, one must maintain steadfast resolve and endure.
Suffering. With single-minded right mindfulness: seventh, one must not compete with worldly people in talent or ability, nor strive for fame or power;

one must not claim what is not attained as attained, nor deceive by claiming what is not realized as realized; one must not falsely style oneself a "spiritual friend" (kalyāṇamitra) or arrogantly exalt oneself.

Rather, one should maintain humility and preserve simplicity, remaining in the stage of a student (*śaikṣa*) for the rest of one’s life, training oneself through constant refinement, ever diligent and ever progressing, with single-minded right mindfulness.
Contemplation:
The Seven Jewels (*Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*). First, gold; second, silver; third, lapis lazuli; fourth, crystal; fifth, musaragalva; sixth, ruby; seventh, emerald.
In the land of Ultimate Bliss there are ponds made of these seven jewels, and upon them are multi-storied pavilions, likewise composed of these.
These are adorned with the seven treasures; all are accomplished through the merits of Amitābha Buddha’s great vows and great practices that accord with his true nature.

Therefore, they are able to universally adorn the four kinds of pure lands and universally encompass all ordinary beings and sages of the ten directions and three periods of time, enabling them to attain rebirth there.
Seventh, it does not obstruct [one’s duties]: It is extremely easy to recite the name of Amitābha; it is extremely easy to be born in the Pure Land. This can be practiced by all people.
For those in office, it does not interfere with their official duties; for scholars, it does not hinder their studies; for merchants, it does not impede their trade;
for farmers, it does not prevent their cultivation; for women, it does not conflict with their domestic labors; and for those in public service...
It does not hinder one’s affairs; while among the monastic community, it does not hinder the practice of Zen meditation. Whatever one does, nothing stands in its way.
Whether performing prostrations and recitations at dawn or dusk, or finding leisure amidst busyness, one must simply dedicate the merit and make vows.
"I vow to be born in the Western Land; I shall certainly attain rebirth there.
(From the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra*) "A bodhisattva who accomplishes eight dharmas will move through this world without blemish and be born in a pure land.
They benefit sentient beings without expecting a reward, and they undergo all manner of sufferings on behalf of all sentient beings."
One should eliminate vexation. Dedicate all merits performed to them. Maintain an impartial mind toward sentient beings;
be humble and free from obstruction. Regard all bodhisattvas as Buddhas. When hearing sutras not previously heard, do not harbor doubt. Do not conflict with the śrāvakas.
Do not envy the offerings received by others, nor be arrogant regarding one's own gains; rather, within these circumstances, one should subdue the mind.
Constantly examine one’s own faults; do not speak of the shortcomings of others. Always with a single mind, seek all manner of merit. (From *The Morning Bell of the Pure Land*:

Regarding the Eight Recollections for Buddhanusmṛti) Whenever one wishes to practice buddhanusmṛti, one must first give rise to faith. One should believe that through buddhanusmṛti one will certainly be born in the Pure Land;

believe that through buddhanusmṛti all transgressions will certainly be extinguished; believe that through buddhanusmṛti one will certainly receive the protection of the Buddha; believe in buddhanusmṛti...
One attains the realization of Buddhahood with certainty. One believes that at the time of death, the Buddha will certainly come to welcome them.

One believes that those who share this faith in the Buddha will all attain rebirth in the Pure Land. One believes that those reborn through faith in the Buddha will certainly reach the stage of non-retrogression.
One believes that through faith in the Buddha, one is born in the Pure Land and will certainly not fall into the three evil realms.
The Water of Eight Qualities (*Amitābha Sūtra*): In the Land of Ultimate Bliss, there are ponds made of the seven treasures, filled with water possessing eight qualities.
What are these eight qualities? First is clarity and purity; that is, the water is limpid, still, and pure.
This is the quality of clarity and purity. Second is coolness; that is, the water is transparent and refreshing. This is the quality of coolness.
1. Merit (*guṇa*). 3. Sweetness: that is, its water is sweet, pleasant, and exquisite; this is the merit of sweetness. 4. Lightness and softness:
that is, its water is buoyant and gentle; this is the merit of lightness and softness. 5. Moisture:
that is, its water nourishes and moistens things; this is the merit of moisture. 6. Tranquility: that is, its water [is beneficial for] people...
If one drinks it, body and mind immediately attain peace, stability, and harmony; this is the merit of tranquility and harmony.
Seventh, the removal of afflictions: when people drink this water, they are able to eliminate afflictions such as hunger and thirst;
this is the merit of removing afflictions. Eighth, augmentation: when people drink this water, they are able to nurture their roots of goodness and increase them.
This further strengthens the four great elements; this is what is meant by increasing one's merit.
Regarding the eight applications (as explained by Chan Master Gu): first, take the Buddha as your vessel for crossing the sea of suffering, and I urge you to cross to the other shore early.

Second, take the observance of fasting and precepts as primary. Third, take the reforming of evil and the practicing of good. Fourth, take enlightened teachers and virtuous friends. Fifth, take [the study of] liberation...
Fifth, one employs the knowledge that cause leads to result. Sixth, one employs the presence of various skillful means. Seventh, one employs the accumulation of merit and virtue.
Eighth, one employs the mutual bestowing of blessings and conditions. Amidst walking, standing, sitting, and reclining, do not let the single name of Amitābha be interrupted.

You must believe that the cause is profound and the result is profound; you must ensure that even when not intentionally mindful, mindfulness arises spontaneously. If you can maintain this mindfulness in every thought-moment without it being empty, [you shall attain liberation].
Ensure that your recitation becomes a single, unified stream. While reciting, recognize the one who is reciting; Amitābha and you will appear together.
You will then enter the Samādhi of Buddha-Recitation and personally realize the Inner Court of Sukhāvatī. One of supreme attainment will see their own name inscribed upon the lotus seat.
Personally beholding Amitābha, they receive his prediction of enlightenment and become a companion to the Bodhisattvas, proceeding directly to the state of... [Nirvāṇa].
Ascending to Bodhi, though wandering at will through eternal kalpas, one returns by relying on this Way; it is certain that one shall attain Buddhahood without deficiency.
(The Family Treasure) The Eight Remembrances: Sincere mindfulness of the Buddha is the elixir; turning the hundred-and-eight beads in circulation is mindfulness.
Accomplishing the *śarīra*, one transcends birth and death; through mindfulness, one binds the seeds of Bodhi and realizes the identity of the holy and the ordinary.

If the mindful mind does not follow the flowing water, the mindful heart will always accompany the white clouds in leisure. Through mindfulness, the wondrous aperture opens to penetrate spiritual wisdom.

This verse is now left for you to contemplate. This verse was revealed by the Xuanzang (Lüzu) via spirit-writing; thus, between the two teachings of Buddhism and Daoism, how could there ever be a duality?
Generally speaking, the Samādhi of Buddha-remembrance does not involve the various stages of spiritual development nor does it fall within the ranks of the path;

it is a direct, transcendent entry into the Tathāgata’s Dharma-gate of the True Mark (dharmatā). As it is said: "To dissolve my inverted conceptions of billions of kalpas, and to attain the Dharmakāya without passing through the incalculable eons (asaṃkhyeya-kalpa)."
8. Ease of Rebirth (*Jingtu shiyi lun*): The radiance of Amitābha pervades the entire Dharma-realm; he embraces and never abandons those sentient beings who recite his name.
The holy and the ordinary are of one essence, as their spiritual capacity and the Buddha’s response correspond. Sentient beings are within the hearts of all Buddhas;
in every atom lies Sukhāvatī. Pure Land is within the minds of sentient beings; in every thought-moment is Amitābha. Viewed from this perspective, wisdom...
It is easy for those who can sever doubt to give rise [to this state]. It is easy for those in meditative concentration to give rise [to it], because they are not distracted.

It is easy for those who uphold the precepts to give rise [to it], because they are far removed from all defilements. It is easy for those who practice generosity to give rise [to it], because they have no sense of "mine. It is easy for those who practice patience to give rise [to it], because they are free from anger.
It is easy for those who practice diligence to give rise [to it], because they do not regress. It is not by creating merit or performing [meritorious acts] that one gives rise [to it].

Evil is easy to produce because the mind can be focused on a single [object]. Evil deeds already committed whose retribution has already manifested are easy to produce because one truly feels shame and fear.

Although there may be many good deeds, if one lacks sincere faith, lacks a profound resolve, and lacks a mind of dedication and aspiration, then one will not attain birth in the highest of the high grades. Alas! Amitābha is very easy to uphold; [Pure Land...]
The land is very easy to reach; yet sentient beings are unable to sustain themselves there or go thither. What can the Buddha do for them?
Regarding the nine grades (*navavidha-prakāra*) [in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra*], as for those of the highest grade of the highest birth:

if there are sentient beings who wish to be born in that land and give rise to three kinds of mind, they shall immediately attain rebirth. What are these three? First, the mind of utmost sincerity; second, the deep...
The mind. Third is the mind of dedication and aspiration. One who possesses these three minds will certainly be born in that land.
Furthermore, there are three kinds of sentient beings who shall attain rebirth there. What are the three? First, those with a compassionate heart who do not kill and who fulfill all the precepts.
Second, those who read and recite the Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtras. Third, those who practice the six remembrances and dedicate [their merit].
One should direct one's vows, aspiring to be born in that land. Possessing these merits, after one day up to seven days, one will immediately attain rebirth there.

At the time of being born in that land, because this person has been diligent and courageous, Amitābha Tathāgata, along with Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, countless transformation Buddhas, hundreds of thousands of bhikṣus, and the great assembly of śrāvakas, [will appear].

The various heavens and their palaces made of the seven treasures are measured out. Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, holding a vajra platform, together with Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva, arrives before the practitioner.
Amitābha Buddha emits a great radiance that illuminates the body of the practitioner.
The various bodhisattvas extend their hands to welcome him. Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta, together with countless bodhisattvas, praise the practitioner and encourage his mind.
Having seen this, the practitioner leaps for joy; he sees himself mounted upon a vajra platform, following behind the Buddha.
In the time it takes to snap one's fingers, he is reborn in that land. Once born there...
Having arrived at the land, he beheld the physical body of the Buddha, complete with all its marks; he beheld the various Bodhisattvas, complete with their physical forms and marks;

and he saw the jewel groves radiating light as they expounded the sublime Dharma. Upon hearing this, he immediately realized the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). In a mere moment, he attained this realization.
Having served various Buddhas throughout the worlds of the ten directions, they receive successive predictions of enlightenment in the presence of those Buddhas.
Upon returning to their own lands, they attain immeasurable hundreds of thousands of *dhāraṇī* gates; these are called those of the highest grade of the highest birth.

As for those of the highest grade of the middle birth: it is not necessary that they uphold, read, or recite the Vaipulya sutras, yet they skillfully understand their meaning and intent. Regarding the second...
First, one’s mind shall not be shaken; one shall have deep faith in cause and effect and refrain from slandering the Mahāyāna.

By dedicating these merits, one vows to seek rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. When the life of one who practices this comes to its end, Amitābha Buddha, surrounded by a vast assembly of followers including Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta, will hold a purple-golden platform.
They arrive before the practitioner and praise him, saying: "O Son of the Dharma, you practice the Mahāyāna and understand the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
For this reason, we have now come to welcome you. Together with a thousand transformation Buddhas, they simultaneously extend their hands.

The practitioner sees himself seated upon a purple-gold pedestal; with palms joined and hands crossed, he praises the Buddhas. In the space of a single thought-moment, he is immediately reborn in that land. (7)
Within the jeweled pond, this purple-gold terrace is like a great precious flower that blooms after one night has passed.

The practitioner’s body becomes the color of purple-polished gold, and beneath their feet there are also lotus flowers made of the seven treasures. The Buddha and the bodhisattvas simultaneously emit light that illuminates the practitioner’s body;
their eyes immediately open and become clear. Due to their prior habitual practice, they universally hear various sounds, all of which exclusively preach [the Dharma].
Regarding the profound ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), he descended from the golden platform, prostrated before the Buddha with palms joined, and praised the World-Honored One.
After seven days had passed, he immediately attained non-retrogression (*avaivartika*) regarding *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that very moment, he was able to fly through the air, traveling everywhere throughout the ten directions to serve various Buddhas at their respective abodes.
They cultivate various samādhis for the duration of one small kalpa, attain the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharmakṣānti), and receive a prediction of enlightenment in their presence.
These are called those of the highest grade who are born by the middle way. Those of the highest grade who are born by the lower way also believe in cause and effect and do not slander the Mahāyāna;
they merely give rise to the mind set on the unsurpassed path and dedicate these merits, vowing to seek rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. When the practitioner’s life...

At the time of death, Amitābha Buddha, along with Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta, together with all the bodhisattvas, will hold golden lotus flowers and manifest as five hundred transformed Buddhas to welcome this person. These five hundred transformed Buddhas will simultaneously extend their hands and praise them, saying:
"O son of the Dharma, you are now pure; you have given rise to the mind of unsurpassed enlightenment. We have come to welcome you. Thus they shall see [the Buddhas].
At that moment, one sees oneself sitting upon a golden lotus flower; once seated, the flower closes.

Following behind the World-Honored One, one immediately attains rebirth within a pond of the seven treasures. After one day and one night, the lotus flower opens; within seven days, one is able to see the Buddha.
Although one sees the Buddha’s body, the mind is not yet clear regarding his various marks and signs of excellence (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*). Regarding the three...
After seven days, one sees clearly and hears various sounds, all of which expound the sublime Dharma.

One travels through the ten directions, making offerings to the Buddhas, and before those Buddhas, hears the most profound Dharma. After three minor kalpas, one attains the "Gate of Illumination of the Hundred Dharmas" and dwells on the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).
This is called the "Lower Birth of the Superior Grade. As for the "Upper Birth of the Middle Grade": if...
There are sentient beings who uphold the five precepts, observe the eightfold fast, and practice all the various moralities;
they do not commit the five heinous crimes and are free from all faults and afflictions. By dedicating these roots of goodness, they vow to be reborn in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss.
At the time of their death, Amitābha Buddha, surrounded by a retinue of bhikṣus, emits golden...
A colored light reaches that person and expounds upon suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self, praising the renunciation of the household life as the means to escape all sufferings.
Upon seeing this, the practitioner’s heart is filled with great joy, and they perceive themselves sitting upon a lotus pedestal.
Kneeling with palms joined, they pay homage to the Buddha. Before their heads have even been raised, they attain rebirth in the World of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*).
As soon as the lotus flower opens, they hear various sounds praising the Four Noble Truths;

at that very moment, they immediately attain the path of an Arhat, endowed with the three knowledges (*trividyā*), the six supernatural powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), and the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*). This is called the "Superior Grade of the Middle Class."

Regarding those born [in the intermediate state]: as for those born in the middle grade, if there are sentient beings who observe the eightfold precepts for one day and one night, or observe the śrāmaṇera precepts for one day and one night, or observe the full set of precepts for one day and one night.
Their deportment is flawless. By dedicating these merits, they vow to seek rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

Perfumed by the fragrance of the precepts, when such a practitioner is about to pass away, they will see Amitābha Buddha together with his retinue, emitting golden light and holding a lotus flower made of the seven treasures, appearing before the practitioner. The practitioner will personally hear from the sky:
A voice praised him, saying: "O son of good family, because you, a virtuous person, have followed the teachings of all Buddhas of the three periods of time, I have come to welcome you.
The practitioner sees himself sitting upon a lotus flower, which then closes;
he is born in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss within a jeweled pond. After seven days have passed, the lotus flower opens. Once the flower has opened—
Having done so, they open their eyes and join their palms in reverence, praising the World-Honored One. Hearing the Dharma, they rejoice and attain the stage of Srotāpanna.

After half a kalpa has passed, they become Arhats. These are called those who are reborn in the middle grade within the middle level. As for those who are reborn in the lower grade within the middle level:
if there are good men or good women who filially support their parents and practice worldly benevolence and kindness, when the life of such a person is about to end—

At the time of death, he encountered a spiritual friend who extensively expounded for him the blissful matters of Amitābha Buddha’s land and also taught the forty-eight vows of the Bhikṣu Dharmākara. Having heard these things, he immediately passed away;
in the time it takes a strong man to bend and extend his arm, he was reborn in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss. After seven days had passed, he encountered...
Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta, hearing the Dharma, rejoiced and attained the stage of Srotāpanna; after the passing of one small kalpa, they became Arhats.
These are called those of the lower grade of middle birth. As for those of the upper grade of lower birth:
there may be sentient beings who have committed various evil deeds, yet do not slander the Vaipulya sūtras; such deluded people commit many [sins].

Regarding those who commit evil deeds and lack a sense of shame or remorse, when their lives are about to end, they may encounter a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) who recites for them the titles of the twelve divisions of the Mahāyāna sūtras.
By hearing the names of these various sūtras, they eliminate the most grievous karmic obstacles accumulated over a thousand kalpas.
Furthermore, the wise one instructs them to join their palms and, with hands clasped, to recite "Namo Amitābha Buddha."
"By virtue of reciting the Buddha's name, one shall eliminate the sins of birth and death accumulated over fifty billion kalpas.

At that time, that Buddha will immediately dispatch emanated Buddhas, an emanated Avalokiteśvara, and an emanated Mahāsthāmaprāpta to the practitioner’s presence and praise them, saying: 'O son of good family!'"
"Because you have invoked the name of the Buddha, all your sins are extinguished; I have come to welcome you.
Having spoken these words, the practitioner immediately sees the light of the manifested Buddha filling his room. Upon seeing this, he rejoices and then passes away.
Riding upon a precious lotus flower, they follow behind the manifested Buddhas and are born within a pool of jewels. After seven times seven days have passed, the lotus flowers finally bloom.

At the moment the flowers bloom, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara of Great Compassion and the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta emit great radiance and stand before those individuals, preaching the profound twelvefold scriptures for them; having heard this, they believe and understand.

They resolve their minds upon the unsurpassed path to enlightenment. After ten minor kalpas, they become fully endowed with the gate of illumination of the hundred dharmas and attain entry into the first stage (*bhūmi*).

This is called "inferior-grade superior rebirth. As for those of "inferior-grade middle rebirth," there may be sentient beings who violate the five precepts, the eight precepts, or the full set of monastic precepts.
Such foolish people steal the property of the Sangha as a whole or misappropriate the property belonging to the present assembly of monks.
They preach the Dharma impurely and lack shame or remorse. Adorned with various evil karmas, such sinners ought to fall into hell because of their evil deeds.
When their lives are about to end, the manifold fires of hell arrive all at once;
yet, meeting a virtuous friend who, out of great compassion, immediately praises and explains for them the ten [names] of Amitābha Buddha...

[The Buddha] extolled the power and majesty [of that Buddha], widely praising his light and spiritual powers, as well as his precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.
Upon hearing this, the person shall have the offenses of birth and death accumulated over eighty billion kalpas eliminated.
The fierce fires of hell will transform into a cool breeze, blowing celestial flowers; upon each flower, there are transformed Buddhas and Bodhisattvas who come to welcome [the practitioner].
Upon meeting this person, in the space of a single thought-moment, they immediately attain rebirth within a lotus flower inside a pond of the seven treasures.
After six kalpas have passed, the lotus flower finally opens. Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta, with their Brahma-voices, comfort that person and preach for them the profound Mahāyāna sūtras.
Having heard this Dharma, they immediately give rise to [the aspiration for enlightenment] at that very moment.
The mind of unsurpassed enlightenment. This is called the middle birth of the lower grade. As for those of the lower birth of the lower grade:
there may be sentient beings who have committed unwholesome deeds, the five heinous crimes, and the ten evil acts, possessing all manner of unwholesomeness.
Such foolish people, because of their evil karma, ought to fall into the evil realms and undergo suffering without end for many kalpas. Such foolish people, when facing [death]...
At the time of death, one encounters a spiritual friend who provides various forms of consolation and expounds the sublime Dharma, instructing one to practice mindfulness of the Buddha.
That person, being oppressed by suffering, has no leisure to practice mindfulness of the Buddha. The virtuous friend tells them:

"If you are unable to practice mindfulness of that Buddha, you should instead invoke the name of Amitāyus Buddha. Thus, with a sincere heart, they cause the sound of the invocation to be uninterrupted for ten full recitations.
By reciting "Namo Amitābha Buddha," through the power of invoking the Buddha’s name, one eliminates the sins of birth and death accumulated over eighty billion kalpas in every moment of thought.
At the time of death, one sees a golden lotus flower, like a sun-disk, appearing before that person.
In the space of a single thought-moment, one attains rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Within the lotus flower, [one is fully...]

After twelve great kalpas, the lotus flower finally opens. Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta, with voices of great compassion, extensively expound for them the true reality of all dharmas and the methods for eliminating and extinguishing transgressions. Having heard this, they rejoice and immediately give rise to the bodhicitta at that very moment.
These are called those born in the lowest grade of the lower level.

The Ninth Grade (*Xīfāng gōngjù*): When the three minds are fully developed and the profound principle of the Truth is clearly understood, one follows to the Golden Terrace and immediately realizes non-arising;

this is the "Highest Birth of the Highest Grade. Having realized the emptiness of all phenomena, one is free from any agitation; by merely making a vow, one is born there, without the necessity of recitation. The "Middle Birth of the Highest Grade":
One simply arouses the aspiration for the Way but has not yet exhausted the subtle principles; upon reaching that realm, they attain enlightenment. One obtains...

The Prediction of Enlightenment. Regarding those of the superior grade who are born in the lower level: having long maintained the various precepts, they are reborn according to their wishes; upon hearing the teachings on suffering and emptiness, they attain arhatship.
Regarding those of the middle grade who are born in the upper level: for one day and one night, they uphold the precepts and make vows;

when the lotus flower opens, they behold the Buddha and immediately enter the stream of the sages. Regarding those of the middle grade who are born in the middle level: being filial, fraternal, benevolent, and compassionate, they are enlightened by a spiritual friend and encounter the two...

The Bodhisattva, having heard the Dharma and attained deliverance, is reborn in the middle grade, lower birth. One who has accumulated evil throughout their life and has not encountered a virtuous teacher, yet utters the Buddha’s name even once, is reborn in a lotus pond in the lower grade, upper birth.
One whose violation of the precepts is grave and whose karmic retribution is deep, with the fires of hell already approaching, [is reborn in the lower grade, middle birth].

Hearing the Dharma, they turn their minds [toward enlightenment] and are welcomed by the assembly of sages; this is birth in the Middle Grade of the Lower Tier. Those who have committed the ten evil deeds or the five heinous crimes, though oppressed by suffering at the moment of death, are taught to recite the Name ten times;
the lotus flower opens to a golden hue, and this is birth in the Lower Grade of the Lower Tier. Throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time, there is only this One Vehicle.
Once one has entered through its gate, nothing is lacking and nothing is superfluous; all nine grades return to the same destination.

The Ninth Patriarch (as recounted by Dharma Master Shizhi Xiao): Since the establishment of the Lotus Society was initiated by Master Huiyuan of Mount Lu as its founding patriarch, there have been no generations among those who have succeeded to this Way over the past several centuries that have lacked worthy individuals.
All of them have looked up to embody the Buddha’s compassion and grandly opened the gates of salvation;
though separated by different eras, they shared the same spirit and were all excellent guides for the multitude. What is recorded in the biographies is indeed impossible to conceal. Therefore:
The chroniclers of successive dynasties have recorded these matters to form a lineage of patriarchs. Subsequently, some have designated Cijue as the eighth patriarch and Lianchi as the ninth.
The First Patriarch was the Great Master Bianjue of Mount Lu, whose name was Huiyuan.
The Second Patriarch was the Dharma Master Guangming of Chang’an, whose name was Shandao. The Third Patriarch was the Banzhou [Samantabhadra] Master of Mount Nanyue...
Shang, whose taboo name was Chengyuan; the Fourth Patriarch Yunfeng Wuhui Guoshi, whose taboo name was Fazhao;
the Fifth Patriarch Xinding Taiyan Fashi, whose taboo name was Shaokang; the Sixth Patriarch Yongming Yijue Chanshi, whose taboo name was Yanshou;
the Seventh Patriarch Zhaqing Yuanjing Fashi, whose taboo name was Shengchang; the Eighth Patriarch Changlu Cijue Chanshi, whose taboo name was...
Zongze. The Ninth Patriarch, the Great Master Yunqi Lianchi, whose name was Zhuhong. (As recounted by Layman Baoguang:

At the assembly at Donglin, he manifested in the body of a layman; having received his prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*) within meditative concentration, he immediately attained the highest grade.
With Liu Yimin as the leader, Lianchi said: "The *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra* sets forth the primary cause for pure practice."

Filial piety toward one’s parents is the foremost virtue. Now, while you, Yimin, have fulfilled your filial duties to the utmost, you have further entered deeply into the *nien-fo san-mei* (Buddha-recollection samādhi).
Having repeatedly experienced auspicious responses, it is fitting that you shall attain rebirth in the highest grade.

This serves as a model for all ages for lay practitioners cultivating the Pure Land path; following the intent of establishing patriarchs for the Lotus Society, we take Yimin as the First Patriarch. Furthermore...
Based on those whose deeds and conduct were most prominent, nine patriarchs were subsequently established. The First Patriarch was Liu Chengzhi, courtesy name Zhongsī, styled Yimin.
The Second Patriarch was Bai Juyi, courtesy name Lètiān, styled Xiāngshān Jūshì.
The Third Patriarch was Wáng Rìxiū, courtesy name Xūzhōng, styled Lóngshū Jūshì. The Fourth Patriarch was Gě Fán, courtesy name [blank]. The Fifth Patriarch was Wáng...
The Sixth Ancestor was Gu, courtesy name Minzhong; the Seventh Ancestor was Yang Jie, courtesy name Cigong, styled Wuzi;
the Eighth Ancestor was Feng Ji, styled Budong Jushi; the Ninth Ancestor was Qian Xiangzu, styled Zhian Jushi;
and the Tenth Ancestor was Ding Mingdeng, styled Lianlü.

The Ten Minds (*Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra*): If there are sentient beings who give rise to ten kinds of mind and single-mindedly contemplate that Buddha, such persons shall, at the end of their lives, attain rebirth there.
First is the mind free from harm. Those who contemplate the Buddha always give rise to a mind of great compassion toward all sentient beings;
they do not inflict injury or harm, but cause them to obtain happiness. This is called the mind free from harm.
Second is the mind free from affliction. One who recollects the Buddha maintains tranquility of body and mind;
toward all sentient beings, they constantly give rise to great compassion, feeling deep pity and sorrow so as to enable them to escape suffering—this is called the mind free from affliction.
Third is the mind that delights in protection. One who recollects the Buddha must, regarding the True Dharma taught by the Buddha, never begrudge their own body.
To protect and cherish one's life is called the mind that delights in protection. Fourth is the mind free from attachment.
One who recollects the Buddha constantly uses wisdom to observe all phenomena and does not give rise to attachment; this is called the mind free from attachment.
Fifth is the mind that gives rise to pure intention. One who recollects the Buddha is able to remain detached from the defiled phenomena of the world.

Furthermore, regarding matters such as gain and offerings, one should always give rise to a mind of contentment; this is called "arousing a pure mental state. Sixth is the "mind free from forgetfulness":

a person who practices mindfulness of the Buddha seeks rebirth in the Pure Land and the attainment of the Buddha’s omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*), never abandoning these thoughts for even a single moment at any time;
this is called the "mind free from forgetfulness. Seventh is the "mind free from inferiority": [the practitioner of] mindfulness of the Buddha...
A person who constantly practices a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings, honoring and respecting them without giving rise to contempt or arrogance—this is called having no inferior mind.
Eighth is the mind of certainty in birth. A person who recollects the Buddha does not cling to worldly discourse;
they develop deep, correct faith in the path of unsurpassed *bodhi* and ultimately remain free from confusion. This is called...
1. The mind of certainty. 2. The mind free from affliction. One who recollects the Buddha cultivates meritorious practices and plants various roots of goodness;
their mind is always far removed from all afflictions and defilements—this is called the mind free from affliction. 3. The mind of mindfulness.
One who recollects the Buddha, though contemplating the Tathāgata’s marks and signs of excellence, does not give rise to attachment.
With a mind of such intent, one constantly recollects that Buddha within a state of non-thought; this is called "arousing the mind of recollection.

(From the *Jingtu zhigui ji*, "The Ten Minds of Faith": Those who wish to understand birth and death and practice pure karma should give rise to ten kinds of faith, maintaining them without forgetting, and will certainly be born in the Pure Land.
First, faith: that the Dharma taught by the Buddha is the sincere word from his golden mouth.)

1. Faith that it is true and not false. 2. Faith that ordinary beings remain in delusion; their consciousness-spirits do not perish, and they circulate through the six realms of existence without ceasing. 3.
Faith that practicing in this world, one does not escape saṃsāra unless the fruits of the Path have been attained. 4.
Faith that as long as one has not emerged from saṃsāra, even if born in the heavens, one cannot avoid falling back down. 5. Faith that the sentient beings of the Land of Ultimate Bliss are born...
6. Faith: Sentient beings who make a vow to be born in the Pure Land will certainly attain rebirth there, never again falling back.
7. Faith: Reciting the Buddha’s name even once can extinguish the heavy sins of birth and death accumulated over eighty billion kalpas. 8. Faith:
For those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha, Amitābha Buddha’s supernatural powers and radiant light embrace them and never abandon them. 9. Faith: Mindfulness of the Buddha...
Such a person shall be constantly protected and mindful of by the Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the worlds of the ten directions, through their shared supernatural powers.
Once the ten stages of faith have been realized and they are born in the Pure Land, their lifespan shall be immeasurable; in a single lifetime, they shall attain unsurpassed Bodhi.
The Ten Unimpedednesses (*Daśāsaṅga*) (from the *Jingtu zhigui ji*): Contemplating the Buddha within the mind, relying on objects to manifest the nature.
Mind after mind is free from dependence; phenomenon after phenomenon is entirely true. There are those who do not understand this and thus recklessly give rise to doubt and slander.

Therefore, I shall now use ten kinds of unimpededness to reveal the perfect fusion of the Pure Land, to wash away clinging attachments, and to clarify right faith. When the single mind and its object are identical to the One Dharma, practice...
A single thought-moment of a person is the mind that contemplates; Amitābha’s Pure Land is the object contemplated.

Since there is no phenomenon outside of mind, the pure lands of all Buddhas are entirely one's own mind. Since there is no mind outside of phenomena, this mind is entirely the Dharma-body of all Buddhas.
Mind and object are ungraspable, yet mind and object are vividly present; they mutually dissolve and mutually exist.
It is beyond thought and beyond discourse. Thus, the Sūtra says: "When you all bring the Buddha to mind, this very mind is the thirty-two marks and eighty secondary characteristics.
Here, the two—the cultivated and the innate—are non-dual. The Pure Land of Mind is the principle inherently possessed;
it is the entirety of cultivation existing within the nature. To make the vow for rebirth is the matter of following conditions; it is the entirety of the nature manifesting as cultivation.

It is cultivation (*bhāvanā*). Because cultivation and nature are non-dual, although the pure lands of all Buddhas are primordially manifest, one must necessarily achieve rebirth therein through the fulfillment of pure karma. Thus, the Sūtra says: "This mind creates the Buddha; this mind is the Buddha."

The ocean of the Buddhas, the Truly and Fully Enlightened Ones, arises from the mind and thoughts. The principle of the three causes and effects is identical because sentient beings and Buddhas share the same essence.
While the Buddhas have already attained awakening and sentient beings remain in delusion, though their states of delusion and awakening differ, their nature is eternally equal.
Therefore, one who recollects the Buddha is recollecting the fundamental nature of all sentient beings. Thus, the Sūtra says:

It is said: "As it is with the mind, so it is with the Buddha; as it is with the Buddha, so it is with sentient beings. Thus, the mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are without distinction.

Herein, both the ultimate and the conventional are simultaneously extinguished. All phenomena are fundamentally empty; not even a speck of dust can be found. Yet, they are established according to conditions.
Phenomena and phenomena are distinct, because all phenomena are empty. Mind and Buddha cannot be apprehended, because all phenomena are provisional.
Mind and Buddha are distinct, because they exist within all phenomena. They are neither existent nor empty; they are non-dual.
It transcends thought and transcends discourse. Thus, a sutra says: "The physical dimensions of Amitāyus Buddha are boundless;
they are not within the reach of the mental power of ordinary beings. Nevertheless, by virtue of that Tathāgata’s power of past vows, those who bring him to mind will surely achieve accomplishment.
Furthermore, a sutra says: "The form-body is not the Buddha, and the voice is likewise so; yet it is also not apart from form and sound."
Beholding the Buddha’s supernormal powers: the fivefold interpenetration of the environment and its inhabitants. The adornment of the land is the *niśraya-vipāka* (the retributive environment);
the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are the *samyak-pariṇāma* (the primary retribution). A single mind encompasses all lands; within every single atom, all Buddhas appear.

Furthermore, because the fundamental nature of the sentient beings of the nine realms is inherently identical, the setting sun and the adornments of the land of ice are all manifested solely by the mind.
The water-birds and the forest trees all proclaim the wondrous Dharma; thus, the six classes of beings—superior and inferior alike—are of one and the same essence.
The Dharma-body of all Buddhas arises from the Truth as a response, like a mirror manifesting images; beauty or ugliness depends on the capacity of the observer.
It is like water giving rise to waves, which vary in size according to the wind. Because capacities possess sharpness or dullness, the responses appear superior or inferior;
yet the essence of the Dharma-body is fundamentally unmoving. Thus, a sutra says: "The supernatural powers of Amitābha Buddha are as he wishes, throughout the ten directions."
In the realm of sovereign transformation, one may manifest a vast body that fills the void of space, or manifest a small body of one *zhang* and six *chi*, or eight *chi*.
Because the many are identical to the one, a single mind and a single mote of dust pervade all Buddha-fields;
because the one is identical to the many, all Buddha-fields are entirely contained within a single mind and a single mote of dust. This is for the purpose of making the mind single-minded.
Because it is one, and because it is easily accomplished, one is led to focus one’s mindfulness on a single Buddha;
yet that one Buddha is all Buddhas. Thus a sutra says: "He who sees the Buddha of Immeasurable Life sees all the Buddhas of the ten directions.
8. Mastery over breadth and narrowness: because the Dharma-realm of the ten directions is not separate from a single mote of dust. A single mote of dust is extremely minute, yet its measure...

They share the same dharma-realm. Although a Buddha-land is vast, it does not depart from a single speck of dust; though the distance be a hundred thousand leagues, it does not exceed the space of a square inch.
Thus a sutra says: "Amitābha Buddha is not far from here; it is like seeing the reflection of one's own face within a mirror."

The nine [realms] have been without interval from antiquity, because the three time periods are not separate from a single thought-moment. Since the prior limit (*pūrvānta*) cannot be apprehended, there is no past;
since the subsequent limit (*aparānta*) cannot be apprehended, there is no future; and since the intermediate limit (*madhyānta*) cannot be apprehended, there is no present.
Because the shifting flow of temporal phenomena is fundamentally eternally abiding, a sutra says: "To contemplate that which is far distant is as if..."
Today, in a mere moment, one traverses the service of all Buddhas throughout the worlds of the ten directions. The ten modes of quiescence and function are unimpeded;

that is to say, while blazingly active in manifestation, one does not stir from the fundamental limit (*dharmadhātu*). It is like water giving rise to waves: the waves are entirely the water. As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says:

"Without arising from the meditative concentration of cessation, one manifests all dignified postures. And as the *I Ching* says: "Quiescent and unmoving, yet upon being stimulated, it immediately penetrates all things."
It is quiescent yet functional; thus, it abandons defilement until it is exhausted and takes up purity until its source is reached. It is functional yet eternally quiescent;

therefore, although there is taking and abandoning, in reality there is no taking and abandoning. For this reason, fervent mindfulness of the Buddha is equal to non-mindfulness, and fervent rebirth in the Pure Land is equal to non-arising.
Within the state of non-seeing, there is no obstruction to seeing the Buddha; within the state of non-arising...

One is spontaneously reborn [in the Pure Land]. Because for the practitioner of the Perfect and Sudden Teaching, speech, silence, movement, and stillness at all times are identical to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the Sūtra says: "That which adorns the Buddha-lands is not adorning;
that which is the parinirvāṇa of immeasurable sentient beings is in truth no sentient being who attains parinirvāṇa. This is precisely what is meant.

The Ten Superiorities (of the Amitābha Repentance Method): Amitābha Buddha possesses ten superiorities. First, the superiority of being able to fulfill all requests; second, the superiority of personally welcoming one to rebirth;
third, the superiority of receiving his light and transcending the world; fourth, the superiority of attaining the Dharma upon hearing his name;

fifth, the superiority of transforming one's substance upon hearing his name; sixth, the superiority of cultivating reverence upon hearing his name; seventh, the superiority of realizing the fruits of the path upon hearing his name; eighth, the superiority of receiving [the teachings] upon hearing his name... [and so forth].

1. Superiority of birth; 2. Superiority of the land; 3. Superiority of the assembly; 4. Superiority of the lifespan; 5. Superiority of the absence of suffering; 6. Superiority of the absence of fear; 7.

Superiority of the absence of evil destinies; 8. Superiority of the absence of women; 9. Superiority of possessing merit upon hearing the name; 10. Superiority of non-retrogression upon hearing the name. (From Ci'en’s *General Praise*: Comparing An-yang (Sukhāvatī) with the celestial palaces, there are ten points of superiority: first, the superiority of the abode of the Lord of Transformation.
1. The superiority of the long life of those to be converted; 2. The superiority of not being bound by the realms (*dhātu*); 3. The superiority of purity and freedom from desire;

4. The superiority of women not dwelling [there]; 5. The superiority of non-retrogression in practice; 6. The superiority of purity and freedom from defilement; 7. The superiority of the adornment of the land; 8.
The superiority of mindfulness of the Buddha gathering the emotions; 9. The superiority of rebirth through ten recitations.

The Ten Superiorities of the Pure Land (The Amitābha Repentance Method): There are ten superiorities of the Pure Land. First, the superiority of encountering the Triple Gem in this very life. Second, the superiority of swiftly attaining the supreme Dharma. Third, the superiority of obtaining a sublime physical form at birth.

Fourth, the superiority of being free from evil and possessing only goodness. Fifth, the superiority of being free from suffering and experiencing pure bliss. Sixth, the superiority of having all necessities provided according to one's thoughts.

Seventh, the superiority of a long and far-reaching lifespan. Eighth, the superiority of non-retrogression in spiritual practice. Ninth, [the superiority of] being born in the presence of the Buddha. Tenth, the superiority of attaining Buddhahood without delay.
