1. Superiority in being non-bound by realms; 2. Superiority in the adornment of the land; 3.

Superiority in the ease of rebirth as taught in the sutras; 4. Superiority in achieving rebirth through brief cultivation; 5. Superiority in the protection and mindfulness of the holy assembly; 6. Superiority in being gathered by the light [of Amitābha]; 7. Superiority in riding upon the Buddha... [The Ten Superiorities for Rebirth in the Western Land]. (Amitābha Repentance Method) There are ten superiorities regarding rebirth in the West.

First, the superiority of the ease of rebirth as stated in the sutra. Second, the superiority of achieving it with only a small amount of cultivation. Third, the superiority of being protected and mindful of by the holy assembly. Fourth, the superiority of being gathered by the light. Fifth, riding upon the Buddha... [End of fragment]
1. Superiority of the power of the vow; 2. Superiority of the transformation-master personally welcoming [the practitioner]; 3. Superiority of being witnessed and certified by all Buddhas;
4. Superiority of being able to extinguish all transgressions; 5. Superiority of being praised together by all sutras; 6. Superiority of being practiced alone when the Dharma has perished.
Ten Benefits (from the *Sūtra on the Dharma Gate of Praising the Pure Land*): Those who uphold the names of the Buddhas shall obtain ten kinds of benefits in this present life.
First, they will always receive the protection of all the great powerful devas and spirits who remain invisible.
Second, they will always receive the constant protection that follows them from all Bodhisattvas. Third, they will always receive the protective mindfulness of all Buddhas day and night. A...
First, Amitābha Buddha constantly emits light to gather and protect this person.
Second, no evil spirits whatsoever can cause them harm; all snakes, dragons, poisons, and drugs shall be unable to affect them.

Third, they shall not suffer from water or fire, enemies or bandits, swords, arrows, imprisonment, untimely death, or unjust rebirths. Fourth, all previously committed transgressions shall be entirely...
The karmic debts of those whose lives were taken will be extinguished; they shall receive liberation and no longer face retribution.
Seventh, one’s dreams at night will be upright, or one may dream of the sublime and wondrous physical marks of Amitābha Buddha. Eighth, the mind will be constantly joyful.
First, their complexion will be radiant and their physical vigor will be full and flourishing; second, all their undertakings will be auspicious and successful.
Third, they will always be honored, supported, and joyfully prostrated to by all the people of the world, just as if they were venerating a Buddha.
Fourth, at the time of death, their minds will be free from fear, right mindfulness will manifest before them, and they will behold Amitābha Buddha and the various sages.
The assembly shall be guided to rebirth in the Pure Land, where they will enjoy supreme and wondrous bliss throughout the bounds of the future.
Regarding the Ten Eases for Rebirth in the Pure Land (*Mida Chánfǎ*): First, because Amitābha’s vows are profound, rebirth is easy.

(As in various sutras: 1. It is easy to attain birth in the two Pure Lands without obstruction (*Amitāyurdhyāna-sūtra*); 2. It is easy to be sustained by the Buddhas of the ten directions (*Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra*); 3.
It is easy to be assisted and perfected by a Buddha of the eastern quarter (*Sukhāvatī-vyūha-sūtra*); 4. It is easy to be welcomed by the two Great Sages (*Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha-sūtra*);
5. It is easy to be led away by the eight great Bodhisattvas (*Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra*); 6. It is easy to practice the ten [virtuous actions] (*Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha-sūtra*).
1. Wishing to attain birth [in the Pure Land] with ease (*Avataṃsaka Sūtra*). 2. Transcribing a single sūtra to attain birth with ease (*Niyatāloka Sūtra*). 3.

Dedication of scattered merits to attain birth with ease (*Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra*). 4. Recollecting the Buddha for a short time to attain birth with ease (*Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*, the Sixteen Contemplations).

The Ten Ease-factors for Rebirth in Sukhāvatī (The Amitābha Repentance Method): There are ten ease-factors for rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. First, it is easy to attain rebirth through faith, understanding, and the arousal of the bodhicitta.

Second, it is easy to attain rebirth by practicing even a small amount of merit. Third, it is easy to attain rebirth by practicing any single visualization. Fourth, it is easy to attain rebirth through the compassionate light and vows of [Amitābha] that encompass all beings.
Fifth, it is easy to attain rebirth through the praise and exhortation found in various teachings. Sixth, it is easy to attain rebirth through the praise and exhortation of all Buddhas.

1. Birth is easy: it is easy to attain birth through the protective empowerment of the seven classes of noble ones. 2. Birth is easy: it is easy to attain birth through the transformative guidance and gathering of the two sages.

3. Birth is easy: it is easy to attain birth by recollecting the eradication of all transgressions. 4. Birth is easy: it is easy to attain birth through the welcoming reception of the sages at the moment of death.
The Ten Eases (Expounded by the Repentance Master Ciyun). Regarding the ten ease of the Pure Land: First, one constantly beholds the Buddha.
Since Amitāyus Buddha attained Buddhahood, ten great kalpas have passed; He dwells eternally and does not perish. Second, one constantly hears the sound of the Dharma.
The Buddha, the bodhisattvas, the forest trees, and the waterfowl constantly proclaim the wondrous Dharma. Third, holy sages assemble. Avalokiteśvara, [Mahāsthāmaprāpta], and... [text continues]
First, one becomes their supreme companion, for all the most virtuous people assemble in one place. Second, one distances oneself from demonic obstacles;
even though there may be celestial Māras, they all protect the Buddha-dharma so that practitioners may swiftly achieve accomplishment. Third, one does not undergo saṃsāra;
through lotus-birth transformation, one no longer revolves within the painful realms of birth and death. Fourth, one is forever free from evil...
First, as for the Path: in that Buddha-land, the three evil realms do not exist, for even their names are never heard. Seventh, as for the seven superior conditions that assist the Path:
jade towers, precious palaces, exquisite garments, and fine delicacies all serve as requisites to aid the Path.

Eighth, as for immeasurable lifespan: the life span of sentient beings is equal to that of the Buddha; even if ordinary humans and devas were to exhaust the full extent of their intellectual power [to calculate it], [it would remain beyond measure].
Because their number cannot be known, nine enter the stage of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*). Those beings born there are all *avaivartika* (non-retrogressive), because they do not regress.
Eleven have fulfilled their practice; they constantly follow and learn from the Buddha, for in one more birth they shall attain unsurpassed *bodhi*.
The Ten Kinds of Merit (*Karmavibhaṅga-sūtra*): There are ten kinds of merit in chanting the Buddha’s name with a loud voice.

First, it can dispel sleep. Second, the celestial Māras are struck with terror. Third, the sound pervades the ten directions. Fourth, suffering ceases in the three evil realms. Fifth, external sounds do not enter.
Sixth, it prevents the mind from becoming distracted. Seventh, it inspires courageous diligence. Eighth, all Buddhas rejoice. Ninth...
Samādhi manifests before one. Ten times one will be reborn in the Pure Land. (Master Cizhao said: With single-minded focus on this one thought, hold the name of Amitābha Buddha.
This one thought alone is my Original Teacher; this one thought alone is the Transformation Buddha; this one thought alone is...
This single thought is the fierce general who shatters hell; this single thought is the precious sword that slays the multitudes of evil;
this single thought is the bright lamp that illuminates the darkness; this single thought is the great ship that crosses the sea of suffering;
this single thought is the excellent remedy for escaping birth and death; this single thought is the exit from the three...
The path through the realms is simply this single thought-moment, which is the Original Nature Amitābha; it is simply this single thought-moment that reaches the Pure Land of Mind-Only.
(From the *Miaoying Lu*): In the practice of reciting the Buddha’s name ten times, there is the inconceivable principle of the blooming of lotus flowers.

In a single thought-moment, one contemplates the Buddha’s merit-water as pure and clear, with golden sand shimmering in its void brilliance. In a single thought-moment, one contemplates the Buddha’s wisdom-seed as wondrous and perfect, within a jewel pond of profound stillness.
In a single thought-moment, one contemplates the Buddha’s roots of goodness as firm and solid, the wondrous treasury of the ocean-seal.

In a single thought-moment, one contemplates the sprouts of the Buddha-dharma as first emerging, sharing the same essence as empty space. In a single thought-moment, one contemplates the lotus of the Buddha’s faith as gradually growing, established in a stage from which there is no regression. In a single thought-moment...
The Buddha’s vows have reached full maturity; his conditioned activities are unimpeded. First, the Buddha’s cultivation of form varies according to each being, manifesting in four ways.
Second, the fragrance of the Buddha’s precepts is truly pure, pervasively heard throughout the ten directions. Third, the flowers of the Buddha’s awakening are in full bloom.
Adorned with merit and virtue, one recollects that the Buddha-fruit is perfectly accomplished; the power of wisdom is vast and great.

Regarding the ten doubts (from the Treatise of Master Zhiyi): first, there is the doubt that [the Buddhas] lack great compassion. [This is because] all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas take great compassion as their primary activity.
If they wish to rescue and deliver sentient beings, they ought only to vow to be born within the triple world, amidst the five turbidities and the three miserable realms.
To save suffering sentient beings, for what reason would one seek birth in a Pure Land for one’s own peace, abandoning sentient beings?
This would constitute a lack of great compassion, being solely for one's own benefit and obstructing the path to Bodhi. Second, the doubt that all phenomena are unborn.
The essence of all phenomena is empty; they are originally unarisen and quiescently extinguished in equality.

To now abandon this and seek that—to seek birth in the Western Pure Land of Amitābha—is it not to act contrary to principle? Furthermore, a sutra says: "If you seek a pure land, first purify your mind;
because the mind is pure, the Buddha-land is pure. How can this be reconciled? For the three Buddha-lands are equal.
Doubt: The pure lands of all Buddhas throughout the ten directions are equal in their dharmatā, and their merits are likewise equal.
A practitioner should universally recollect all such merits in order to be born in all pure lands; yet now, one seeks only the pure land of a single Buddha.
This contradicts the principle of equality. How, then, can one be born in a pure land? Fourth is the doubt regarding the exclusive mindfulness of the West:
if one is equally mindful of seeking birth in the pure land of a single Buddha, why not instead follow one's mindfulness toward the pure land of any Buddha among those of the ten directions?
One will attain rebirth accordingly; why then must one single-mindedly contemplate Amitābha Buddha alone? Fifth, the doubt regarding the heavy fetters of the ordinary person:
Ordinary beings who are bound by all fetters possess thick and heavy evil karma. Not even a hair’s breadth of any affliction has been severed, yet the Western Pure Land transcends the triple world.
How can such an ordinary being bound by all fetters attain rebirth there? Sixth, the doubt regarding the attainment of non-retrogression: Suppose...
How can ordinary beings bound by all fetters, who constantly give rise to wrong views, the three poisons, and so forth,

be born in that land and immediately attain non-retrogression, transcending the triple world? How can those of the highest grade who practice the ten wholesome deeds, free from the seven doubts regarding Tuṣita and Maitreya Bodhisattva—
who is in his final birth before becoming a Buddha— be born there and see him attain Buddhahood?
Maitreya Bodhisattva will descend to be born [in this world] in accordance with the times; within his three assemblies, one will spontaneously attain the fruits of sainthood.

Why, then, must one seek rebirth in the Pure Land of the West? Regarding the doubt concerning rebirth through eighty recitations: since beginningless time, sentient beings have created immeasurable karma.
In this present life, though possessing a single physical form, they do not encounter a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), and furthermore, they continue to commit all manner of [unwholesome deeds].

Regarding those who have committed sinful karma and have done no evil that they did not perform, how can it be that at the moment of death, through the accomplishment of ten recitations, they immediately attain rebirth and transcend the affairs of karmic bondage within the three realms? How can this be reconciled? Inferior and weak persons harbor doubts, thinking:

"The Western Land is ten thousand billion Buddha-fields away from here; being ordinary beings of inferior strength, how can we possibly arrive there? Furthermore, regarding the *Wangsheng lun* (Treatise on Rebirth)...
It is said: "Women and those with impaired faculties, as well as those of the two vehicles' lineage, will not be born [there].
Since this teaching exists, one should know that women and those with impaired faculties certainly cannot attain rebirth there. Tenth:

Regarding the doubt concerning what karmic actions to perform—now, desiring to seek birth in the Western Land with certainty, I do not yet know what karmic actions to perform, nor what to take as the seed for attaining birth there.
"In that land, moreover, ordinary laypeople all have wives and children; it is not yet known whether those who have not severed lustful desire can be born there.
Thus he raised ten such doubts as questions. Furthermore, each was answered with clarity and precision; as the text is voluminous, it is not recorded here. Yang Cigong said:
"The Great Master cited the words of the Sage to resolve the doubts of the multitude; this is no mere work of Fazang."
In future lives, one will be unable to reach this state.

Regarding the "Ten Kinds of People Who Do Not Mindfully Recite [the Buddha's Name] at the End of Life" (from the *Wen Jingtu Ji*), there are ten types of individuals who fail to achieve mindfulness of the Buddha when their lives come to an end:

First, they may not necessarily encounter virtuous friends, and thus lack the opportunity for someone to exhort them to recite the Buddha’s name. Second, they may be entangled by the suffering of illness, such that their spirits become clouded and their faculties impaired.
1. Distraction; 2. Illness; 3. Impaired speech due to wind-disorders, such that one cannot utter names; 4. Madness and mental derangement, such that focused contemplation is difficult to achieve;
5. Encountering fire or water, leaving no leisure for sincere resolve; 6. Suddenly meeting tigers or wolves, causing panic and haste; 7.
Having wicked companions at the critical moment, who destroy the aspiration for the Way; 8. Eating to excess until satiated.
Fainting leads to death. Ninth, one may suddenly perish in the midst of military arrays and battle. Tenth, one may fall from a high cliff and sustain injuries that end one’s life.

These are the ten difficulties (as explained by the Venerable Master Ciyun in his *Cānzhǔ*). It is difficult to attain the Way in the five turbidities, whereas practicing in the Pure Land is easy. Now, by means of...
The ten difficulties of the Sahā world are shown as follows: First, one does not constantly encounter a Buddha. Within the perilous paths of the three realms, the Buddha serves as the guide;
yet because the karma of sentient beings is heavy, they are born when no Buddha is present. Śākyamuni has already entered parinirvāṇa, and Maitreya has not yet appeared.

The worthy sages remain hidden, while false teachings blaze ever more fiercely. Second, one does not hear the preaching of the Dharma. In this degenerate age of the Semblance Dharma, all spoken words are diluted and corrupt.

First, they discourse only on the heterodox and evil doctrines of non-Buddhists; because they do not hear the True Dharma, they are ensnared by the three types of evil friends and associate with wicked companions.
Seeking gain and offerings, they mislead and delude practitioners, causing them to fall into the evil realms.

Fourth, they are troubled and disturbed by the various māras and the ninety-six kinds of heterodox and evil persons, who corrupt and disrupt the True Dharma, preventing practitioners from achieving success.
First, because the five wheels of rebirth revolve without ceasing in a continuous cycle; like drawing water from a well, the wheel has no rest.

Second, because it is difficult to escape the six realms of existence; wandering through the three worlds, one receives retribution according to karma, and even if born in the heavens, one cannot avoid eventual downfall.
Third, because worldly conditions obstruct the Path; submerged in the toil of mundane defilements, they become hindrances to the supramundane Dharma.

Therefore: (8) life is short; although humans live for a hundred years, those who meet with untimely death are many, and time passes so swiftly that it is difficult for a Bodhisattva to accomplish the Great Way.

(9) there is regression in practice; in this land, one must sever the delusions of views and thought before one can attain non-retrogression, for practitioners at the initial stage cannot yet avoid falling back. (10) it is difficult to achieve in even dust-like kalpas.
For example, during the era of the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, there were followers who heard the Dharma but regressed from the Great Vehicle and clung to the Lesser Vehicle.

Although they remained on the stage of the śrāvaka for kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, because they had not yet accomplished the Great Way despite this vast duration of time, [they were not yet liberated].

Ten Difficulties in Believing (as taught by Master Lianchi): Pure Land is a teaching that is difficult to believe. There are ten reasons why it is called "difficult to believe. First, we currently dwell in this defiled land;

having been accustomed to it for a long time, our minds are at ease. When we suddenly hear of the pure and magnificent adornments of that land, we doubt that such a thing exists—this is the first difficulty in believing.
Second, even if one believes in that land, one may further doubt whether rebirth can be attained in all the Buddha-fields of the ten directions.
First, there is the difficulty of believing that one will certainly be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

Second, even if one believes in being born there, one further doubts how it is possible to travel to the Land of Ultimate Bliss from this Sahā world across ten trillion *krośas*—how can one reach such a vast distance? This is the third difficulty of belief.
Even if one believes it is not far off, one further doubts that ordinary beings on this broad earth, burdened by deep karmic obstacles, could so suddenly attain rebirth in that land;

this is the fourth difficulty in believing. Even if one believes they can be reborn there, one further doubts that to be born in this Pure Land, there must necessarily be wondrous Dharma-gates and manifold meritorious practices;
how is it that merely by holding the Name, one can thus attain rebirth? This is the [fifth] difficulty.
Fifth is the difficulty of faith: even if one believes in and holds to the Name, one may still doubt that by reciting this title one can achieve success only after passing through many kalpas;
how then could one attain birth in that land in a single day or seven days? This is the sixth difficulty of faith.

Even if one believes that birth is attained within seven days, one may further doubt that taking birth in the seven realms of existence does not escape the modes of birth from a womb, an egg, moisture, or transformation; how then [could it be otherwise]?

That land is entirely born through transformation from lotus flowers—this is the seventh difficulty to believe. Even if one believes in birth from lotuses, one further doubts that those who have newly begun their path to enlightenment would encounter many conditions for regression;
how could they attain the stage of non-regression upon being born in that land in a single lifetime? This is the eighth difficulty to believe.

Even if one believes in non-regression, one further doubts that this [teaching] is merely a provisional means to guide sentient beings of dull faculties, while those of superior wisdom and sharp faculties [would require something more].
It is not necessary that those with dull faculties will be born there; this is the ninth difficulty in producing faith.
Even if they possess faith and have sharp faculties, they may still doubt whether other sutras state that a Buddha exists or does not exist, or that a Pure Land exists or does not exist;
thus they remain undecided in their hesitation. This is the tenth difficulty in producing faith. To now expound this Dharma in this world is like entering into a state of nakedness.
In the kingdom, he displayed his majestic demeanor and pointed out black and white to those born blind. This is called a "difficult task.
This is called the inconceivable merit of benefiting others.
The Ten Losses (from the *Jingtu zhigui ji*): There are ten kinds of losses for those with heavy karmic obstructions who are unwilling to advance in their practice.

He personally beheld Amitābha and received his prediction of enlightenment face-to-face. He practiced all the six perfections and four immeasurables without exception;

Sighing that the paths of human life are many, one must quickly and earnestly recite the name of Amitābha Buddha. Do not let your time be wasted in the river of溺愛 (溺愛, *ni-ài*, drowning love/attachment).
With this single phrase of "Amitābha," take charge yourself; there is no other dharma to be contemplated.

This is the clear, direct pointing to the path home, so that the fourfold assembly may together ascend to the field of Great Enlightenment. Take this single phrase of "Amitābha" as the *huatou* (critical phrase) and hold it up alone.
There is no need for further seeking; when the work is thoroughly penetrated, the lump of clay is shattered. Even the iron Buddha perspires all over his body.
One phrase of Amitābha is superior to sitting meditation. One sound is not finished, and another follows.
When the work reaches its peak in every thought and every moment, everywhere is the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. Amitābha Buddha is the King of the Dharma. The waves of the river of craving...
Within, they construct a vessel; with a single-minded vow, they wish to deliver those submerged in the cycle of existence, so that all may reach the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.

It is produced by the four conditions, accomplished by the six causes, and subsumed within the five fruits. If, in a single thought-moment, one harbors anger or engages in sexual misconduct, this is the karma for the hells.

Obstruction. If there are sentient beings who encounter this light, their three impurities are extinguished;

their bodies and minds become supple, and they leap for joy as wholesome thoughts arise. If those in the three miserable realms or places of diligent suffering behold this radiance, they all obtain rest.
After their lives end, they all receive liberation. There was once a person condemned to hell who, while still in the world...
On this day, having previously read the sutras and teachings on Amitābha’s Pure Land rebirth, I gained some understanding of the causes, conditions, and karmic retributions of past lives.

With a sincere mind and right mindfulness, I take refuge in Namu Amitābha Buddha, ensuring my voice does not cease for ten full recitations. [The shackles and locks...]
Liberated, one is received by Amitābha and departs through the air, immediately attaining rebirth in the Western Pure Land.

(The Ritual for Mindful Recollection, Twelve Vows) Those who wish to be born in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*An-yang*) must rely upon making vows. If one does not make vows, by what means can one attain rebirth?
Therefore, one makes a vow with a sincere heart, saying: "May my illusory body be free from illness and suffering; may I be liberated from the three miserable realms."
The Gate of the Eight Difficulties: May all karmic obstructions from past lives be extinguished; may the afflictions and the six sense faculties be eliminated;

may my body remain untainted by contact with the perverse and the non-righteous; may I emerge from the dust of the five turbidities of this Sahā world; and may I diligently cultivate the path without ever regressing.
May I enter the gate of liberation of the Tathāgata. May my consciousness remain undisturbed at the time of death. May transformation Buddhas come in their entirety to welcome me.
May I serve Amitābha and encounter the assembly of sages. May I realize the indestructible Vajra-body.
The Twelve Inconceivables (*Guiyuan Zhizhi*): That land of Amitābha Buddha is inconceivable in its radiance,
inconceivable in its lifespan, inconceivable in its compassion, inconceivable in its power of vows, inconceivable in its supernormal powers,
inconceivable in its wisdom, inconceivable in its samādhis, inconceivable in its eloquence, and inconceivable...

The emanated bodies preach the Dharma in an inconceivable manner, deliver sentient beings in an inconceivable manner, and possess the two kinds of adornments—the primary and the secondary—in an inconceivable manner, fully complete in all their various aspects. Do you now possess these fully, or not?

If you do not, you must with utmost sincerity pay homage to the Buddha, recite his name, and seek birth in the Pure Land. Why is this? Because those who practice while clinging to partiality and remaining deluded...
It is like a lame person traveling by land; in a single day, they cover no more than a few li.
In contrast, practicing the rites and recitations for rebirth is like boarding a boat to enter a waterway; with a favorable wind, one arrives at a thousand li in a mere instant.

It is also like a weak man who, following a Universal Monarch (cakravartin), travels around the four continents in a single day and night; this is not through his own strength, but through the power of the Universal Monarch.
It is also like people in this world who, when caught in the perils of official service, must rely on those with power to rescue them if they lack the strength to escape themselves;
or like a person pulling a heavy object who, unable to manage it by their own power, must rely on the strength of many others before it can be moved.
Reciting the liturgy and seeking rebirth in the Pure Land is likewise so.

Regarding the twelve powers (*dvādaśabala*) [from the *Lianzong baojian*]: those who cultivate the practice of Pure Land rely on the power of the Buddha’s vows and take the Buddha’s precious physical marks as their object of contemplation.
Thus, it is like a person who stays close to a sovereign; who would dare to offend them?
Moreover, Amitābha Buddha possesses the power of great compassion, the power of great vow, the power of great wisdom, the power of great samādhi, and the power of... [great majesty].

He possesses the power of majestic spiritual authority; he possesses the power to utterly crush all that is heterodox; he possesses the power to subdue Māra; he possesses the power of the divine eye for seeing afar;

he possesses the power of the divine ear for hearing from a distance; he possesses the power of penetrating insight into the minds of others; he possesses the power of radiant light that universally illumines and gathers in sentient beings;
and he possesses the power of unspeakable, inconceivable, immeasurable, and most supreme merit. How could it be...?

When rising, one must examine oneself: whether there is a mind of stinginess and greed, a mind of anger and resentment, a mind of deluded attachment, a mind of jealousy, a mind of deceit and madness, a mind of self-centeredness, a mind of arrogance, a mind of flattery and crookedness, a mind of false views, or a mind of contempt.
Regarding the mind of subject and object, as well as all adverse and favorable conditions, and all unwholesome states of mind produced by defilement:

for one who practices the mindfulness of the Buddha according to the "Fourteen Methods for Guarding the Mind" (The Ten Gate Teachings on the Pure Land), when evil thoughts arise, one must urgently practice mindfulness of the Buddha.
One should constantly guard all deep faith, sincere resolve, the mind of aspiration and dedication, and compassion.
The mind of compassion; the mind of humility; the mind of equanimity; the mind of skillful means; the mind of patience; the mind of ethical discipline; the mind of joy and relinquishment;
the mind of meditative concentration; the mind of diligence; the mind of bodhicitta; and all virtuous minds.

Regarding the fourteen characteristics (from the *Ratnarāja-śāstra*): the Tathāgata, the Hero of the World, examined all various concentrations and determined that the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi* is the king among meditations.
All other samādhis that possess dependence or opposition are merely the concentrations of commoners.

However, the *ratnarāja-samādhi* does not abide in noble characteristics, nor does it abide in base characteristics, false characteristics, correct characteristics, or the characteristics of birth and death.

The mark of nirvāṇa, the mark of afflictions, the mark of bodhi, the mark of stillness, the mark of distraction, the mark of attaining perfect enlightenment, the mark of delivering sentient beings, the mark of sitting at the site of enlightenment, and the mark of non-abiding—all such marks are entirely non-abiding.
They are like awakening from a dream; they are vast and devoid of coming or going. Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "Neither going nor coming—this is the Buddha."

Fifteen Reflections on Nianfo (Spoken by Master Lianchi): Now, those who study the Buddha-dharma should not seek outward adornment; mere external appearances are of secondary value, for true practice is what matters.
Lay practitioners need not necessarily don black robes and clerical caps; those with their hair unshorn may simply wear their ordinary clothes.
Likewise, when practicing nianfo, it is not strictly necessary to strike the fish-shaped gong or beat the drum; those who prefer stillness may do so.

One may naturally remain in silent stillness; reciting the Buddha’s name does not necessarily require forming groups or holding assemblies. Those who fear worldly affairs may simply close their doors;
reciting the Buddha’s name does not necessarily require entering a temple to listen to sutras. Those who can read may follow the teachings themselves;
offering incense for hundreds of miles is not as good as sitting peacefully in one's own home hall. Reciting the Buddha’s name is better than making offerings to heterodox deities.

Master, reciting the Buddha’s name while being unfilial toward one’s parents is not as good as practicing filial piety; reciting the Buddha’s name while extensively associating with demonic friends is not as good as remaining solitary and pure;
reciting the Buddha’s name while making offerings for the sake of future lives is not as good as performing meritorious deeds in the present;

reciting the Buddha’s name while making vows for protection and averting calamities is not as good as repenting and reforming oneself; and reciting the Buddha’s name while studying the texts of non-Buddhist paths is not as good as being illiterate.
To recite the Buddha's name while engaging in ignorant and deluded talk of Chan principles is not as good as being sincere in upholding the precepts.

To recite the Buddha's name while seeking supernatural powers from malevolent spirits is not as good as maintaining correct faith in cause and effect. To speak of the essentials of reciting the Buddha's name: it is simply to rectify the mind and extinguish evil.
To thus recollect the Buddha is called being a "good person" (satpuruṣa), for one gathers the mind and eliminates distraction.
To thus recollect the Buddha is called being a "worthy person" (ārya), for one awakens the mind and severs delusions. To thus recollect the Buddha is called being a "sage" (muni).
Sixteenth, regarding "this and that" (*Nien-fo Chih-chih*): The sentient beings of that land have no manifold sufferings, but experience only various joys;
therefore, it is named "Ultimate Bliss" (*Sukhāvatī*). Now, let us contrast this with the *Sahā* world: here, one possesses a physical body of flesh and blood, and all who are born undergo suffering;
there, one is born through transformation from a lotus flower, and thus lacks the suffering of birth. Here, the seasons shift and change, leading to senescence and decay.

The sun encroaches upon them; thus, they are not shifted by cold or heat and suffer no pain of aging. Here, however, the four elements are difficult to harmonize, and many illnesses and afflictions arise.
There, their transformed bodies are fragrant and pure, and they suffer no pain of disease. Here, those who reach seventy are rare.
This world is impermanent and fleeting; there, lifespans are immeasurable and there is no suffering of death.

This world is characterized by attachment to kin; where there is love, there must be separation. There, there are no parents, wives, or children, and thus no suffering of being separated from those one loves.
This world is filled with enemies and adversaries; where there is enmity, there must be encounter. There, there are assemblies of the most virtuous, and no encounter with those one hates.
This [state] is one of suffering from hunger and cold, with insatiable greed for acquisition; that [state] is one where clothing, food, and precious jewels are spontaneously provided for enjoyment.
This [state] is one where the physical form is haggard and the six sense faculties are often impaired; that [state] is one where the appearance is dignified and the body possesses radiance.
This [state] is one of wandering through birth and death; that [state] is one where non-arising is eternally realized. This [state] consists of the four realms of existence.
...of suffering. There, even the names of the three evil realms do not exist. Here, there are thorns, pits, and ravines;

the ground is uneven, high and low, and filled with filth such as earth, stones, sand, and mud. There, the ground is made of gold, jewel-trees reach toward the heavens, towers soar with the seven treasures, and flowers of four colors bloom.
Here, the twin śāla trees have already perished and the Dragon Flower tree has yet to appear. There, there is no...
In this world, the Honored One of Immeasurable Life currently preaches the Dharma; yet here, Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta can only look up to their illustrious names from afar.
There, however, he is personally the supreme friend to those two sublime beings. Here, various māras and heterodox teachers disturb and confuse one’s correct cultivation;

there, the Buddha’s transformation unifies all under his rule, leaving no trace of māras or heterodoxy. Here, seductive forms and licentious charms delude the practitioner; there, such things do not exist.
There, the retribution is pure and there are truly no women; here, malevolent beasts and demons clamor with perverse sounds, while there, waterfowl and forest trees all proclaim the wondrous Dharma.
When these two lands are compared, the conditions of their environments are utterly distinct.
Exhorting the people of this world, they take great delight; how could they fail to leap for joy toward the Land of Bliss?
The Sixteen Contemplations (Verses on the Sūtra of Immeasurable Life):
Part One, The Contemplation of the Setting Sun.
The ocean of mind is vast and boundless, its waters meeting the sky; A hundred thousand samādhis are spontaneously accomplished.
Behold the setting sun like a suspended drum; In a single thought-moment, one ascends the City of Peace and Bliss.
2. The Contemplation on the Two Waters.
The waters of meditative concentration are vast and expansive like the great ocean; when not a single ripple stirs, the water becomes even clearer.
In an instant, it transforms into a ground of lapis lazuli, where palaces stand in错落 (chaotic yet harmonious) array, reflecting a brilliant clarity.
This is the visualization of the third stage.
The earth is as level as the palm of a hand, with hills and mounds submerged;

there are great golden banners rising from below to support boundless towers and terraces made entirely of the seven treasures. One knows not who shall ascend them on another day—this is the Contemplation of the Four Trees.
The trees of the seven treasures rustle in the gentle breeze, Proclaiming exhaustively impermanence, suffering, and emptiness.
If one hears this but once and attains the stage of non-retrogression, There is no need for further cultivation over many kalpas.
The Contemplation of the Five Pools.
Water flows from fourteen branches of mani-jewels, divided by golden channels into flower ponds;
amidst the flowers, the sound of the Dharma is played, mournful and elegant. Born of the radiance of pearls, its plumage is marvelous;
contemplate it as the six-storied pavilion.
A hundred billion tiers of towers made of the seven treasures, With the celestial music of the devas filling the halls, playing spontaneously;
Furthermore, there is suspended music in the air, All proclaiming the merit of the three refuges and every thought-moment.
Contemplating the seven-flower seat.
The great precious lotus has suddenly blossomed; A hundred thousand necklaces hang upon the golden terrace.
Everyone possesses their own share to ascend it; To never turn back would be a pitiable state of mind.
*Eightfold Contemplation of the Buddha’s Image*.
Lotus flowers bloom in succession upon the pond; A mass of purple-gold light stands towering and majestic.
One must constantly observe this in every thought-moment; Go and listen as the Tathāgata praises it as "Excellent!"—this is the visualization of the nine dharma-bodies.
Images of purple-golden hue fill the void; Their deep blue eyes are as clear and serene as the ocean.
Do not marvel that the clouds of their bodies are limitless; From the beginning, they have never departed from the single mind.
The Contemplation of the Ten Avalokiteśvaras.
From the beginning, his compassionate vows have remained ever-fresh; manifesting forms throughout the ten realms, he delivers suffering beings.
Whether encountering the adverse or the favorable, his mind remains composed; how could it hinder him from continuing to cultivate causes while already possessing the fruit?
(11) Contemplation on the Visualization of Śrī-Ābhāsvara.
Wearing a jeweled vase as a crown upon his head, with eyes like blue lotuses and a complexion of purple-gold,
he walks with such power that the three thousandfold world-system trembles; he is able to awaken those intoxicated by ignorance through the twelvefold Dharma-methods of wisdom-contemplation.
Constantly cultivating the conditions for the Pure Land day and night, suddenly the Three Sages stood before one's door;
they praised him with earnestness and stroked his head, enabling him in an instant to sit upon a precious lotus.
(The Thirteenth Contemplation on Miscellaneous Thoughts)
Myriad thousands of emanated Buddhas, Their large and small golden bodies seated with solemn dignity;
Jade trees, crystal groves, and precious palaces— At last, celestial music surpasses that of all other heavens.
The Fourteenth: Contemplation of the Superior Birth in the Highest Grade.
Years of diligent practice have expanded your wisdom; how joyful your journey today!
The Buddha comes in person to welcome you as heavenly music resounds, and Guanyin personally holds a purple-gold platform for you.
(Fifteenth: Birth in the Middle Grade of the Middle Division.)
Observing the precepts and maintaining the fast are great causes; suddenly one hears the earnest words of the Transformation Buddha upon a blue lotus by the sands of the Golden River.
Therein, one briefly forms bonds of friendship with the various worthies.
(16th: Lower Grade, Lower Birth Contemplation)
How enviable is the profound wisdom of the commoner, Who can turn their mind away from hell even now;
Though they may remain within the palace for many kalpas, They personally hear the sound of Avalokiteśvara preaching the Dharma.
*Sixteen Contemplations (Direct Pointing to the Recitation of the Buddha)* If one can, within this gate of the Pure Land, Diligently practice day and night without ceasing...
Cease! Accord with the Buddha’s teaching. Regard the various sensory objects of sound and form in this land as a hell, as a sea of suffering, and as a burning house.
Regard all precious things as instruments of torment. Regard food, drink, and clothing as pus, blood, and iron skin.
Regard your kinsmen as yakṣas, rākṣasas, and man-eating ghosts; how much more so those who have been born [into such states]?
Death does not wait; one wanders through long kalpas in a constant state of flux. One should truly cultivate weary detachment toward worldly acquaintances.

If, within the scriptures, one hears of that Buddha’s power of vows and the adornments of his land, then in every thought-moment, one should contemplate that principle, giving rise to the perception of peace and security, the perception of it as a precious treasure, the perception of it as a family inheritance, and the perception of it as the place of liberation. [One should do this] regarding Amitābha Tathāgata and the Bodhisattvas.
One should regard the Sangha as one’s compassionate father, as one’s compassionate mother, as those who provide guidance, and as a bridge to the shore of liberation.
Amidst fear and urgent distress, if one calls their name, they will respond; the merit shall not be in vain, for they will arrive in an instant.

One should conceive the thought that they come swiftly to provide protection and rescue, and the thought that through mindfulness one attains deliverance. To practice in this manner brings immeasurable merit.

Benefit for the Body:
Thirty Verses on Self-Rejoicing (*Mida Chanfa*). If the assembly knows how to rejoice in themselves, they must further cultivate the supramundane mind.
The Buddha said: "Hell is difficult to escape from; we have all together already attained liberation from this suffering. This is...

First, we rejoice in ourselves: it is difficult for hungry ghosts to escape their state, yet we have all together already attained freedom from their agonizing suffering. Second, we rejoice in ourselves:
it is difficult for animals to abandon their condition, yet we have all together already attained freedom from receiving such retribution. Third, we rejoice in ourselves:
having been born in a remote land where benevolence and righteousness were unknown, we have all together already attained residence in the Central Kingdom where the Way and its teachings prevail.

To have personally received these sublime instructions—this is my first self-congratulation. To have been born in the Heaven of Longevity, yet not knowing how to plant roots of merit, and now having mutually attained this state, we are able to further establish causes for the future—this is my fifth self-congratulation. A human body is difficult to obtain; once lost, it cannot be recovered.
That we have mutually obtained a human body—this is my sixth self-congratulation. Those with impaired faculties do not participate in the roots of goodness. [We who are complete in our senses...]
To be endowed with purity and to attain the profound Dharma-gate—this is the seventh self-congratulation. Worldly wisdom and eloquence, conversely, become obstacles;
to unite our minds and take refuge in the True Dharma—this is the eighth self-congratulation. The Buddha said: "To see the Buddha is difficult.
We have already attained the opportunity to behold his sacred image—this is the ninth self-congratulation. The Buddha said: "Furthermore, to hear the Dharma is difficult. We, together...
Having already obtained the consumption of ambrosia (*amṛta*), this is the tenth self-congratulation. The Buddha said: "To leave the household life is difficult.

You have all already been able to bid farewell to kin and sever your attachments to return toward and enter the Way; this is the eleventh self-congratulation. The Buddha said: "Benefiting oneself is easy; benefiting others is difficult.
Today you have all performed one prostration and one salutation for the sake of the ten directions; this is the [twelfth]..."
Second is rejoicing in oneself. The Buddha said: "To endure toil and suffer hardship is difficult. Today, you have all exerted yourselves with diligence;
whatever you have done was not for your own sake. This is the thirteenth form of rejoicing in oneself. The Buddha said: "To recite and chant the scriptures is difficult."
That we, this great assembly, have together attained the opportunity to read and recite [this teaching] is our fourteenth self-congratulation.
That seated meditation is difficult, yet now we see those whose minds are stilled and whose intentions are fixed in concentration is our fifteenth self-congratulation. The Buddha said:

"This teaching is difficult to encounter, difficult to believe, and difficult to know; now that we have encountered this teaching, it is easy to believe and easy to know"—this is our sixteenth self-congratulation. The Buddha said: Previously...
In former lives, I did not encounter this teaching; therefore, I did not escape the cycle of birth and death within the three realms and six paths.
Now that I have encountered this teaching, it is certain that in this very life I shall directly emerge from the cycle of birth and death within the three realms and six paths.

This is my seventeenth self-congratulation. The Buddha said: "Sentient beings are turbid and evil; their obstructions are heavy and their merit is meager. Although this teaching exists, they are deluded by it."

"First, self-congratulation: I have known [the truth]. Having known it, I previously failed to practice; now, encountering this teaching, I am able both to know and to practice—this is my eighteenth self-congratulation.
The Buddha said: 'Those who do not know this teaching cultivate various miscellaneous virtues, lacking a resolute mind, and thus do not escape saṃsāra.
Now, encountering this teaching, I shall cultivate one practice exclusively and will certainly escape saṃsāra—this is my nineteenth self-congratulation. The Buddha said: 'I lacked virtue...'"
Ordinary people, at the time of their death, mostly perceive evil visions or encounter adverse conditions;

they do not hear the Dharma of the sutras, and being entangled by their sinful karma, they wail in terror as they enter hell, seeking salvation but finding no way. Now, they have received this teaching.
At the time of death, encountering favorable conditions and meeting virtuous friends who instruct one to practice this method and explain it in detail—

one may hear a virtuous friend teach the recitation of the ten recitations, or one may oneself recite "Namo Amitābha" ten times.
Recite the name of Amitābha Buddha continuously until the ten invocations are complete; then, evil conditions will immediately vanish and wholesome conditions will manifest before you.
That person will personally see Amitābha Buddha, Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, and the assembly of the Pure Land, coming together to welcome them.

may those who hear my name likewise be able to repay their filial debt to their fathers. My second vow is this:

when I first resolved to attain enlightenment, it was out of a desire to repay the profound kindness of my compassionate mother, Great Lotus of Gold, who nurtured me; I pray that through the compassionate power of the Triple Gem, may I...
May all my mothers, who have given birth to me throughout beginningless lifetimes, be reborn in the Pure Land and swiftly realize Bodhi.
May those who hear my name also be able to repay their debt of gratitude to their mothers. My third vow is:
I vow to deliver all sentient beings within the Dharma-realm and the realm of empty space until they have all attained Buddhahood; only then shall I myself enter Nirvana. My fourth vow—
First, I vow that my lustful impulses shall be severed from both body and mind, and even the nature of such severance shall be non-existent;
may those who hear my name likewise attain the permanent eradication of the root of lust.

Second, I vow that my karmic habituations of killing shall be extinguished without remainder, and may those who hear my name universally give rise to the power of compassion. Third, I vow that my ignorance and darkness...
May the karma of slandering the Triple Gem be extinguished without remainder. May those who hear my name be able to develop right faith in the Triple Gem.
My seventh vow is: may all my unwholesome karmas be completely purified, and may those who hear my name [attain this].
I shall abide securely in the holy life. My eighth vow is: May I be reborn with certainty in the World of Ultimate Bliss;
may I swiftly realize unsurpassed bodhi and manifest emanations throughout lands as numerous as atoms to deliver sentient beings, without weariness or fatigue until the end of the future.
The ninth vow: May I, in birth after birth throughout all ages, never forget my original vow, and skillfully transform sentient beings within the world of the five turbidities.
The tenth vow: May I, wherever I may be, propagate and spread the True Dharma without any demonic obstacles.
The eleventh vow: May I attain immeasurable wisdom and be able to thoroughly penetrate and understand all Buddhas.

The Dharma. As for the twelfth vow: may I attain immeasurable eloquence to guide the deluded masses, subdue those of external paths, and be entirely fearless, like the roar of a lion. As for the thirteenth vow:
may I attain immeasurable supernormal powers to travel everywhere to the lands of the ten directions, to serve all Tathāgatas and spiritual friends within all ocean-like assemblies.

There is nothing that cannot be granted. The fourteenth vow is: May I be able to produce various subtle and wondrous sounds to praise the Three Jewels throughout the bounds of the future, causing all sentient beings to know where they may take refuge. The fifteenth vow is:
May I be able to produce all manner of subtle and exquisite offerings at will to worship the Triple Gem, acting as a great field of merit for all sentient beings.
As for the sixteenth vow: may I [dedicate] all the merits possessed by all sentient beings throughout the ten directions.
I rejoice in all of them, so that they may achieve unsurpassed bodhi. As for the seventeenth vow:
when the Tathāgatas of the ten directions attain perfect enlightenment, I shall first entreat them to turn the great wheel of Dharma and reveal the unsurpassed path of awakening to sentient beings.
As for the eighteenth vow: when the Tathāgatas of the ten directions enter parinirvāṇa, I shall entreat them all, saying: "Do not..."
Entering nirvana yet abiding eternally in the world to benefit all sentient beings. As for the nineteenth vow:
among the assemblies of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, they shall recognize me as the Great Dharma Prince;
and within all the ocean-like assemblies, the Buddhas shall praise my merit, wisdom, compassion, and power of vows as being no different from those of Avalokiteśvara or Kṣitigarbha. (2)
The tenth vow is: May the light of great compassion illuminate all the hells;
may those who are touched by my light have their various sufferings transformed into supreme and wondrous bliss at that very moment. The twenty-first vow is: May the light of great compassion...
May it illuminate all hungry ghosts. Those who touch my light shall, at that very moment, cast off their hungry ghost bodies and attain birth in the Pure Land.
The twenty-second vow is: May I, through the light of great compassion, illuminate all animals.
Those who receive my light shall be freed from all fears, and after casting off their bodies, attain birth in the Pure Land. The twenty-third vow is: May I, through great [compassion]...
The light of compassion illuminates all spirits and deities. Those who encounter my light shall all abandon their hearts of anger and awaken to the Buddha-way;
they shall cast off all ugliness and obtain pure bodies. As for the twenty-fourth vow: I vow that by means of the light of great compassion...

I illuminate all sentient beings afflicted by suffering. Those who receive my light shall have their illnesses eliminated, their six sense faculties made complete, and be liberated from all calamities and hardships.
All immeasurable terrors shall be cast away; they shall live long in health and give rise to the aspiration for Bodhi.
Should they approach the end of their lives, they shall be reborn immediately in the Pure Land. As for the twenty-five vows, I vow that through great compassion—

Radiant light shines upon and touches all that has form or is formless, all that possesses thought or is thoughtless, as well as all Māras and non-Buddhists, causing their bodies and minds to abandon all false views and attain penetration into the Buddha Vehicle. The twenty-sixth vow is:

may the light of great compassion shine upon and touch humans and devas, causing them not to become deluded by sensual pleasures or by the attachment to and aversion toward meditative concentrations, so that each may diligently seek [the Way].

Unsurpassed Bodhi. Regarding the twenty-seventh vow: I vow that with the light of great compassion, I shall illumine all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, causing them to relinquish the unconditioned and swiftly realize the Buddha Vehicle. Regarding the twenty-eighth vow:
I vow that with the voice of great compassion, I shall reveal and instruct all sentient beings, causing all sentient beings to attain definitive and clear awakening. Not...
They cherish the three realms and take no pleasure in other vehicles, seeking only unsurpassed bodhi. The twenty-ninth vow is:

by means of the power of great compassion, may I accord with the various requests of sentient beings and always cause them to have their wishes fulfilled, so that they may develop deep faith in my Dharma.
The thirtieth vow is: for the sake of saving and delivering sentient beings, I vow that—

Throughout the ten directions, he manifests in the form of a Buddha or appears in pure lands to gather in sentient beings; these lands are so magnificently adorned that they surpass even the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Alternatively, he appears in defiled lands to transform and guide sentient beings, employing immeasurable skillful means to subdue evil associates.
Regarding the thirty-first vow: For the sake of delivering sentient beings, I vow to manifest my body in accordance with their various types.
Within each type, I shall be of noble lineage, preeminent, and possess sovereign majesty and virtue, so that all of their kind may respect and cherish me.
In accordance with these instructions, until the attainment of Bodhi, regarding the thirty-two vows:

wherever there is no Buddha-dharma, wherever all dharmas have ceased, and wherever the Buddha-dharma cannot be practiced, I vow to manifest my body therein through the skillful means of great compassion.
Concealing and revealing myself for the sake of great transformation, I shall serve as a lamp in the long night to rescue and deliver those submerged in darkness, leading them forth.
The Ocean of Suffering. Regarding the thirty-three vows: I vow that whenever sentient beings are hungry or thirsty, I shall manifest as food and drink;
in times of pestilence, I shall manifest as medicinal herbs; in times of cold and frost, I shall manifest as clothing;
in times of heat and affliction, I shall manifest as a cooling breeze; in places of peril and obstruction, I shall manifest as a ferry or a bridge—and so on for all sentient beings.

All that is required shall be manifested and produced, so that all sentient beings—whether they wear it, eat it, lean upon it, or tread upon it—shall all attain peace and happiness and resolve their minds toward Bodhicitta. As for the thirty-four vows:

if there are sentient beings who joyfully seek the Buddha Vehicle, once they have heard my name, they shall not cast off their physical bodies but shall attain the Bodhi of a Buddha and realize ultimate perfection.
The thirty-fifth vow: If there are bodhisattvas who adorn Buddha-lands, upon hearing my name, their lands shall be superior and more wondrous than even Sukhāvatī.
Yet, if they wish to manifest in defiled lands, they shall obtain immeasurable skillful means to skillfully transform those beings who are stubborn and difficult to convert.
The thirty-sixth vow: If there are sentient beings who wish to see the pure [lands] of the various Buddhas...
Earth. Hearing the sound of the Dharma being preached, I vow that they shall all be able to see and hear it. As for the thirty-seventh vow:
if there are sentient beings who wish to go to countless worlds to make offerings to the Triple Gem, I vow that in a single moment of thought, [they may do so].

It is universally and pervasively attained. Regarding the thirty-eighth vow: if any sentient beings desire to be born in the pure lands of the Buddhas and hear my name, they shall immediately attain rebirth there in accordance with their vows. Regarding the thirty-ninth vow:
if any sentient beings share my vow, they shall swiftly attain immeasurable wisdom, skillful means, and sovereign majestic power. Regarding the fortieth vow:

As for this: if there are sentient beings who delight in seeking the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*), I vow to cause them to swiftly ascend to the fruits of sainthood (*āryaphala*), whereupon they immediately turn their minds toward the Bodhisattva Vehicle (*bodhisattvayāna*).
Regarding the forty-first vow: I vow that all Bodhisattvas practicing throughout the ten directions...
Upon hearing my name, they shall proceed directly to Bodhi, forever free from the works of Māra. The forty-second vow is:

I vow that throughout the ten directions, may all malevolent spirits, heterodox teachers, and followers of external paths, upon hearing my name, immediately abandon their false views and together return to Right Enlightenment.

The forty-third vow is: If there are sentient beings whose bodies are burdened with the five heinous crimes and the ten evil deeds, or who have committed the four pārājika offenses or the eight pārājika offenses, when...
Falling into the great hells, I vow that by the power of my mind of great compassion, I shall cause them to know how to seek pity and repent;
I will manifest a supreme and wondrous form-body before those individuals, stroke their heads to comfort them, and ensure that the roots of their offenses are forever uprooted.

Regarding the forty-four vows for the arousal of the bodhicitta: if there are sentient beings who either slander my Dharma or revile my name, although their karmic obstructions are heavy, I vow that through the power of impartial great compassion, I shall cause them to extinguish their evil.
May I swiftly attain Bodhi. Regarding the forty-fifth vow: May my compassionate eye be most utterly pure, universally beholding the entirety of the realm of empty space;
may all those in places of extreme suffering be brought to peace and happiness, and may all extremely wicked sentient beings be made virtuous and good.
Regarding the forty-sixth vow: May my hand of seals be most utterly adorned, in every thought-moment...
From within, there emerge clouds of all manner of offerings, clouds of various precious jewels,
clouds of garments, clouds of all necessary utensils, clouds of food and drink, clouds of medicines, clouds of samādhis, clouds of dhāraṇīs,
clouds of eloquence, and clouds of radiant light, pervading the entire realm of empty space to benefit sentient beings throughout the bounds of the future.
There shall be no interruption. Regarding the forty-seventh vow: I vow that my name shall be most supreme and far-reaching, pervading the entirety of the ten directions without exception;
even to the places where the Dharma has perished, my name shall not cease to exist.
May I constantly cause all sentient beings, whether they hear it or recite it, to attain complete liberation. Regarding the forty-eighth vow: I vow that my form-body shall be most...
Extremely subtle, he was adorned by the marks of a great man (*mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa*) as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields.
Each mark possessed secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*) as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields;
each secondary characteristic possessed [attributes] as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields.
There were light rays as numerous as the atoms of a world-system of dust.
Each and every light ray manifested colors as numerous as the atoms of unspeakably unspeakable Buddha-fields, adorning and embellishing the realms.

Each emitted sounds as numerous as the atoms of unspeakably unspeakable Buddha-fields, proclaiming the sublime Dharma. Each produced [fragrances] as numerous as the atoms of unspeakably unspeakable Buddha-fields...

Fragrances as numerous as atoms fill all things everywhere, from which emerge unspeakably unspeakable numbers of most sublime foods and drinks, as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable Buddha-fields, to provide offerings for all.
There falls a rain of garments and various requisites, as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable Buddha-fields, universally bestowed upon all. All these appear unspeakably...
There were transformation Buddhas as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably many Buddha-fields, teaching and transforming all beings.
Each of these transformation Buddhas had as their retinue transformation Bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields.
Each of these Bodhisattvas [had as their retinue... as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields.

There were as many sublime adornments as there are atoms in a world-system, and each individual adornment performed as many vast Buddha-activities as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields.
Each of these Buddha-activities benefited sentient beings in as many worlds as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields. Any sentient beings who saw them...
Through this first Buddha-activity, one shall behold my subtle and wondrous form-body.
Those who behold my body shall be able to attain equality with me and swiftly achieve Buddhahood.
*Jingtu Ganzhu* (The Blue Bead of the Pure Land), Part Two: Postscript.
In the summer of the Jisi year, while seeking respite from the heat in the meditation hall of Dao’an Temple, I paid my respects to the Elder Xuzhou and respectfully inquired of him.
Regarding the general purport of the Buddha-dharma, the Elder illustrated that the Three Teachings originally possess no difference, for they reside solely in the single character "mind.
Indeed, "refining it to the utmost and making it one, truly holding fast to the Mean" is the mind-transmission of the sages handed down from generation to generation.

"Pure wisdom is wondrously perfect, utterly transcending the sense organs and their objects" is the heart-seal of the Buddhas realized through mutual verification. "Seven returns and nine cycles" refers to the practice of cultivation.
This is the Great Jewel, the heart-essence transmitted from sage to sage. It is like the brilliant light of the sun in the sky obscured by drifting clouds;

so too, people are clouded by delusive thoughts and discrimination, unable to perceive their own nature. Thus they rise and fall, circling and descending through the various realms of existence with no end in sight.
Is this not truly a matter of great sorrow and pity? If one can turn the light back to reflect within and investigate the source, [one shall realize it].
"Thoroughly. Thus, it is said that all phenomena in the myriad of existences do not lie outside this single mind. Upon hearing this, it was like a needle piercing the crown of my head;

although I could not achieve sudden enlightenment through words alone, whenever a circumstance or object arose to touch my senses, a single thought of vigorous introspection would cause both self and objects to become empty, leaving my breast clear and expansive. Is this not indeed the result of the Elder’s cultivation?
How powerful! The lay practitioner Bao Guang of the Zongren lineage showed me a volume titled *The Dark Pearl of the Pure Land*, compiled by the Elder himself.
This work gathers those elements pertaining to numerical categories from the sutras and treatises on the Pure Land;
it serves as a guide for returning to the source of the mind and a compassionate vessel for crossing the ocean of vows. Thus, one can especially perceive therein his vow to deliver all beings.

The master craftsman has exerted great effort. I can do no more than look up to him with profound admiration. I have respectfully selected one point from the Dharma instructions I received on the previous day to append to the end of this scroll. Thus it is said.
Respectfully inscribed at the end of the late spring of the Gengchen year by the Layman Baohua, Liu Xue of Daebang.
